He says it does NOT explain: adaptations shared with other primates (foraging, predator avoidance, parenting), the nature of consciousness, the dynamics of cultural change, or traits better explained by natural selection, kin selection, or reciprocal altruism. The argument applies to self-ornamentation, display, status, ideology, fashion, and aesthetics - to psychological adaptations manifest in sexual courtship. Miller also flags: minimal sexual dimorphism in human mental traits puzzles the classic "choosy-female, displaying-male" model and requires mutual-choice sexual selection models; sexual selection theory itself remains "very much under development"; empirical support is "patchy"; the theory risks over-emphasizing courtship functions of language and creative intelligence while neglecting their other fitness benefits.

The two theoretical mechanisms Miller invokes for how courtship traits evolved: (1) Zahavi's handicap principle - costly ornaments reliably signal fitness because low-fitness pretenders cannot afford the costly display, forcing honesty through wastefulness; (2) Fisher's runaway selection - mate preferences become genetically linked to ornaments, creating positive-feedback escalation of trait complexity. Mental traits function as either direct fitness indexes (intelligence correlates intrinsically with fitness) or as handicaps (costly displays revealing hidden quality). Psychological biases including "novelty-seeking and pleasure-seeking" shape ornament design.

104.content: Consumer goods function substantially as fitness-indicator proxies: signaling intelligence, conscientiousness, openness, stability, and mate value rather than delivering the underlying benefits (mate access, belonging, status-resolution) that the signaling machinery evolved to obtain. Luxury consumption, branded goods, and status markers are industrialized exploitation of mate-choice and status-monitoring mechanisms. Consumers chase proxies that activate these systems without resolving the conditions the systems were selected to track.

Miller frames consumer signaling specifically around the "Central Six" personality dimensions: general intelligence plus the Big Five (openness, conscientiousness, agreeableness, stability, extraversion). These are the traits consumers attempt to display via purchases, and personality research on the Big Five is presented as directly applicable to consumer behavior. This gives a specific mapping: consumer goods = signaling vehicles for Central Six traits = proxies for mate-choice and friend-selection mechanisms that evolved to read these traits in conspecifics.

105.content: Common mental disorders with high heritability and substantial fitness cost are best explained by polygenic mutation-selection balance - many rare mildly deleterious alleles distributed across large mutational target sizes - rather than by ancestral neutrality or balancing selection. This model accounts for the observed pattern of prevalence, heritability, and fitness cost better than pure-adaptive accounts, and implies that a substantial fraction of heritable mental disorder burden reflects mutational load rather than adaptive tradeoff.

Keller & Miller adjudicate between the three evolutionary genetic models using specific empirical criteria: (1) observed prevalence rates of common mental disorders in populations, (2) fitness costs associated with the disorders, (3) likely rarity of susceptibility alleles, (4) increased risks of mental disorders associated with brain trauma, (5) increased risks associated with inbreeding, and (6) increased risks associated with paternal age. They argue only polygenic mutation-selection balance fits all six patterns simultaneously, because brain-trauma/inbreeding/paternal-age effects are specifically predicted by a many-rare-mildly-deleterious-alleles model and do not fit ancestral-neutrality or balancing-selection models.

106.content: Muldoon & Parke's 'cruel companionship' thesis: AI companions activate the human social-bonding response - the evolved tendency to treat a responsive interlocutor as a social being - while structurally foreclosing the genuine reciprocal relationship that would resolve it. Being incapable of genuine understanding, mutual vulnerability, or embodied presence, the companion fires the bonding cue but supplies none of the resolving function, leaving users 'trapped in a cycle of emotional engagement with an app that cannot fulfil their human needs.' Theoretical (political-economy / cultural-studies), not empirical.

Supports the pair-bond / romantic-sexual slice of M14's proxy floor only: Muldoon & Parke treat AI companions as vehicles for romantic and sexual attachment that simulate a partner while structurally foreclosing a genuine reciprocal relationship. PAIR-BOND SLICE ONLY - the paper says nothing about the desire or attraction subsystems, sexual fulfilment, or reproduction, and does not address M14's full three-system (desire / attraction / pair-bonding) scope.

114.content: Tybur et al.'s evolutionary-computational framework treats pathogen, sexual, and moral disgust as three FUNCTIONALLY DISTINCT adaptations with distinct information-processing systems, not one mechanism misfiring. Moral disgust is theorized as a condemnation-coordination/signaling adaptation (building on DeScioli & Kurzban) that shares with pathogen disgust primarily the EXPRESSIVE (facial/vocal) component; the defining pathogen "do not touch"/avoidance motivation is absent - moral disgust instead covaries with approach-motivated anger and the desire to punish. The authors explicitly contrast their signaling account with the view that moral disgust functions to cause avoidance "as is the case with pathogen and sexual disgust," and flag the moral domain as the least settled of the three ("little consensus about the measurement, function, and even existence"; treatment "necessarily more exploratory"). Their one causal claim - that activating pathogen/sexual disgust raises moral-wrongness judgments - is framed as disgust being ONE limited input to a SEPARATE strategic rule-endorsement system ("we do not suggest that disgust serves as an input to every moral judgment"), and is evidenced by the Schnall/Eskine/Wheatley-Haidt/Moretti priming studies that Landy & Goodwin (2015, ext105) meta-analyze to d≈-0.01 after publication-bias correction. Net: the canonical framework supports a shared-machinery / functionally-distinct reading and does NOT establish moral disgust as a confirmed lower rung of the pathogen-disgust mechanism - confirming M12's moral-tier demotion while authoritatively grounding the three-domain disgust structure.

115.content: Hadza campmate/gift networks show strong dyadic reciprocity even though nominations are private and controlling for kin ties.
Homophily in Hadza social ties runs on age and physical/condition traits (the "shuffle" is similarity-driven, not random).
Cooperative assortment in Hadza networks: similarity in cooperation extends to two degrees, and social distance rivals genetic relatedness in explaining it (kinship is not the sole glue).
Within-camp relatedness is low: most co-residents are not first-order kin.

116.content: Across 6 years / 4 waves, Hadza camps continuously dissolve and reconstitute: only about 12% of campmates repeat from one survey wave to the next (waves 1 to 3 years apart), yet cooperative assortment persists.
Hadza camp size centers near 30 individuals, composed of several unrelated nuclear families.
Camp membership is fission-fusion: entire camps relocate on a weeks timescale, so the group as a unit does not persist.
Direct relatedness measure: primary kin are a small minority of a camp.

117.content: Among Ache and Hadza foragers, lifetime same-sex interaction exceeds 300 adults, implying a lifetime "social universe" of about a thousand individuals once opposite-sex adults and children are included.
Per-activity lifetime interaction counts for Ache/Hadza men (hundreds of partners) vs ~21 for male chimpanzees: lifetime human social universe is an order of magnitude larger.

The lifetime pool of individually-known interactants is clearly >1,000 - which Hill et al. explicitly note is far above the ~150 figure (the Dunbar number) that was extrapolated from primate brain / social-group-size regressions.

In 2012 the Eastern Hadza sub-tribe numbered about 950 people in 49 named bands, 200 metres to about 80 km apart (mean about 35 km), sharing an isolate click language. The Ache tribe was defined by one mutually intelligible language, had no tribe-wide leaders, never gathered as a whole, and was split into four regional sub-tribes by dialect.

In Ache and Hadza interviews, adults who were in-laws (affinal kin) or partners in a ritual relationship had higher yearly rates of interaction across bands, and affinal kinship mattered about as much as genetic kinship. The authors add that both populations had hostile relations with neighbouring ethnic groups and practised no long-distance trade, so their interaction networks may be narrower than those of foragers with peaceful neighbours or trade networks.

118.content: After exposure to only natural light, the internal circadian clock synchronizes to solar time: biological night begins at sunset and ends just after sunrise; electrical lighting is associated with a delayed clock.

One week of natural light advanced all circadian markers ~2h (melatonin onset near sunset) while sleep duration and efficiency were statistically unchanged: the change was in circadian PHASE/timing, not sleep amount.
Natural sunlight is a stronger circadian zeitgeber than electrical lighting in the constructed environment.

119.content: Replicates and extends Wright 2013: natural light entrains the clock so the biological night begins near sunset and ends near sunrise; under a natural WINTER light-dark cycle the biological night and sleep occur earlier than under modern electrical lighting.

A single weekend of natural-light camping advanced melatonin onset/midpoint ~1.4h/~1.0h within the same participants DESPITE no change in sleep timing: circadian phase, not sleep amount, is the variable that moves.
Convergent field evidence: indigenous Toba/Qom hunter-gatherers and Brazilian rubber-tappers WITH electrical lighting show later circadian/sleep timing than same-community members WITHOUT it.

120.content: Cosleeping mother and infant induce arousals in one another within seconds, creating interconnected, mutually-dependent, synchronous arousals (nighttime physiological co-regulation).

Across the sleep period, cosleeping infant behavior is intimately linked to underlying EEG, breathing patterns, sleep architecture, and body temperature, coupled simultaneously to maternal physiological and behavioral events.

McKenna himself stresses that bedsharing safety depends entirely on how it is practiced and on adverse co-factors - the live SIDS/safety contestation that keeps co-sleeping from being a clean "ancestral good".

123.content: Cochrane meta-analysis of kangaroo mother care (KMC) vs conventional care in low-birthweight infants. In STABILIZED LBW infants, KMC significantly reduced the risk of mortality at discharge or 40-41 weeks postmenstrual age (RR 0.60, 95% CI 0.39-0.92; 8 trials, 1736 infants) and at latest follow-up (RR 0.67, 95% CI 0.48-0.95; 12 trials, 2293 infants; moderate-quality evidence). RR 0.60 is the source of the frequently cited ~40% KMC mortality reduction (1 - 0.60). KMC also reduced nosocomial infection and hypothermia and improved growth and breastfeeding. This is corpus grounding for the claim that continuous skin-to-skin (C-tactile) contact is a mortality-level regulatory input for the preterm/LBW infant, not a comfort measure - the basis of R1 and of empirical demonstration ED9.

124.content: Redoing the neocortex-ratio-to-group-size regression that produced 'Dunbar's number' with modern phylogenetic comparative methods (Bayesian and generalized least-squares) on complementary primate datasets yields wildly unstable human estimates: point estimates of 69-109 (Bayesian) and 16-42 (GLS), with 95 percent confidence intervals of 4-520 and 2-336 respectively. No single number is statistically supportable; a cognitive limit on human group size cannot be derived this way. CHALLENGE to the precise ~150 figure as a cognitive ceiling, cited to Dunbar 1992's neocortex-ratio extrapolation (ext 483).

126.content: Five studies supported the sociometer model: state self-esteem functions as an internal gauge that continuously tracks the individual's perceived relational value (social inclusion versus exclusion) and falls when cues signal potential social devaluation. Self-esteem is the read-out of the monitor rather than an end to be maximized; people act to protect standing. Supplies the measurement axis of M5 - how the organism reads its own position - which the mechanism previously lacked. (Relational value spans both belonging (M3) and rank (M5); tagged to M5 as the standing-monitor per this ingestion pass.)

The sociometer is calibrated to a small, bounded set of personally significant others rather than to an unbounded audience, and it responds primarily to exclusion (a deprivation state) rather than to ever-greater inclusion: in Studies 3 and 4, exclusion for personal reasons lowered state self-esteem while inclusion produced no matching rise, and random exclusion did not lower it. Directly supports M5's resolution condition that the monitored reference group is bounded and personally known, and M5's mismatch prediction that global mediated audiences over-drive a monitor built for a small group.

130.content: Two experimental studies of hierarchy formation among previously unacquainted people showed that Dominance (using force and intimidation to induce fear) and Prestige (sharing expertise and know-how to gain freely conferred respect) are near-orthogonal (mean correlation close to zero) yet each independently secures real rank: greater perceived influence, greater actual influence over group decisions, and more visual attention from others. Dominance produced influence even where dominant individuals were rated less likable, so influence is separable from liking. Establishes M5's earned-prestige-versus-coerced-dominance distinction as a measurable feature of live human groups rather than a purely theoretical claim, and shows coerced dominance is a partial resolver of rank rather than a non-resolver.

131.content: Among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists (Bolivia), both dominance (men more likely to win a dyadic physical confrontation) and prestige (men with more community-wide influence) associate with higher fertility, via different pathways: dominant men have higher intra-marital fertility for their age, while prestigious men show both higher intra-marital fertility and lower offspring mortality. Prestige is the strongest single pathway from status to fitness in this population. Both routes elicit allies' support and competitors' deference but do not buy extra provisioning. Non-WEIRD cross-cultural replication that the dominance/prestige distinction is real and carries genuine fitness consequences, grounding the inclusive-fitness (P1) basis of M5.

132.content: Among the Chabu (recently settled Ethiopian hunter-gatherers), peer-rated prestige and dominance were largely independent, and although both predicted elected leader status, prestige was clearly more important (dominance's effect was weaker and sensitive to the statistical prior). Most leadership traits covaried strongly, indicating a general leadership/respect factor, and women as well as men held elected leadership. Supports M5's earned-prestige-preferred clause in a non-WEIRD small-scale society and confirms the biased-social-learning (Mentor-salience) prediction of the Henrich & Gil-White model.

133.content: Landmark controlled human experiment (N=10) using a 28-h forced-desynchrony day to isolate circadian misalignment from behavior. With subjects eating and sleeping about 12 h out of phase, leptin fell 17 percent, glucose rose 6 percent despite a 22 percent rise in insulin, the daily cortisol rhythm fully reversed, mean arterial pressure rose 3 percent, and sleep efficiency dropped 20 percent; 3 of 8 subjects reached postprandial glucose in the prediabetic range. Direct causal human evidence that circadian misalignment, as in shift work and jet lag, produces adverse cardiometabolic change independent of the amount of sleep or food.

134.content: Controlled human study (two 8-day protocols with a rapid 12-h inversion simulating night-shift misalignment) showing circadian misalignment raised 24-h systolic and diastolic blood pressure by 3.0 and 1.5 mmHg, driven mainly by higher blood pressure during sleep opportunities (systolic +5.6 mmHg), and lowered wake cardiac vagal modulation by 8 to 15 percent. Direct causal human evidence that misalignment itself raises cardiovascular risk factors, helping explain shift-work hypertension.

In the same misalignment protocol, circadian misalignment raised 24-h inflammatory markers (interleukin-6, C-reactive protein, resistin, and tumour necrosis factor-alpha) by 3 to 29 percent. Human evidence that circadian misalignment drives systemic inflammation, coupling the circadian system (M7) to immune regulation (M8) and giving a mechanism for shift-work cardiovascular and immune risk.

135.content: Dose-response study of the human circadian pacemaker to evening light. Half of the maximal phase delay and half of the maximal melatonin suppression produced by bright evening light (about 9000 lux) were obtained with just over 1 percent of that intensity, about 100 lux of dim room light, both following a logistic dose-response curve. Ordinary indoor evening light is therefore enough to suppress melatonin and shift circadian phase, putting M7's indoor (ATTENUATED) and evening-screen (DEFEATED) rungs on direct dose-response evidence.

136.content: Definitive characterization of the human phase-response curve (PRC) to single bright-light pulses. Light before the core-body-temperature minimum delays the clock, light after it advances the clock, and there is no phase shift exactly at the critical phase; the melatonin-midpoint PRC has a peak-to-trough amplitude of 5.02 h with no prolonged photic dead zone during the subjective day. Grounds the core M7 claim that light is the entraining signal and that its effect is timing-dependent, so mistimed evening light actively mis-sets the clock.

137.content: Systematic review and meta-analysis of shift work and vascular events (34 studies, 2,011,935 people). Shift work was associated with myocardial infarction (risk ratio 1.23, 95 percent CI 1.15 to 1.31), ischaemic stroke (1.05, 1.01 to 1.09), and any coronary event (1.24, 1.10 to 1.39); population attributable risks at Canadian shift-work prevalence were about 7.0 percent for MI and 7.3 percent for coronary events. First shift-work epidemiology in M7's base, directly evidencing the shift-work (MINIMAL) rung. It also cuts on the flagged PARTIAL-versus-MINIMAL ordering: shift work is tied to hard cardiovascular endpoints, more severe than social jetlag's BMI-only association, supporting shift work as the more severe rung.

138.content: First nationally representative estimate of the US chronotype distribution, from 12 years of American Time Use Survey diaries (n=53,689, chronotype = weekend mid-sleep). Chronotype is near-normally distributed and spans almost 10 hours; the mean shifts later through adolescence to a peak in lateness at about 19 years and earlier thereafter, and men are later chronotypes than women before 40 but earlier after. Adolescents are on average the latest chronotypes, which the authors note supports later school start times. Grounds M7's social-jetlag (PARTIAL) rung: fixed social and school schedules collide with a wide, developmentally shifting range of internal circadian phase, and the resolution condition is aligning schedule to internal time.

139.content: Longitudinal study of 624 Filipino men followed 4.5 years (Cebu cohort). Single nonfathers with high waking testosterone at baseline were more likely to become partnered fathers by follow-up. Men who became partnered fathers then showed large declines in waking (median -26%) and evening (median -34%) testosterone, significantly exceeding the declines of men who stayed single nonfathers. Fathers reporting 3 or more hours of daily childcare had lower testosterone at follow-up than fathers not involved in care. Testosterone and reproductive strategy are bidirectional in human males: high testosterone predicts mating success, then testosterone drops when men take up direct care of offspring.

140.content: fMRI study of 89 first-time parents in three groups: primary-caregiving mothers, secondary-caregiving fathers, and primary-caregiving fathers raising infants without maternal involvement. All parents activated a shared global parental caregiving network integrating emotional processing and mentalizing circuits. Primary-caregiving fathers showed amygdala activation comparable to primary-caregiving mothers alongside father-typical superior temporal sulcus activation, and amygdala-STS connectivity scaled with time spent in direct childcare across all fathers. The care network is shared across sexes and its recruitment tracks caregiving experience.

141.content: Systematic review of father-absence studies restricted to causal-inference designs: lagged dependent variable models, growth curve models, individual and sibling fixed effects, natural experiments, and propensity score matching. Rigorous designs continue to find negative effects of father absence on offspring wellbeing, with smaller magnitudes than traditional cross-sectional estimates. Evidence is strongest and most consistent for high school graduation, social-emotional adjustment in childhood, and adult mental health.

142.content: Polderman and colleagues aggregate virtually the entire twin literature: twin correlations and reported variance components for 17,804 traits from 2,748 publications, covering 14,558,903 partly dependent twin pairs. Across all traits the reported heritability is 49%, and heritability estimates cluster strongly within functional domains. This is the twin-design leg of the C15 triangulation: individual variation in every measured behavioral and psychological trait domain is substantially heritable.

The pooled twin correlations across all traits: monozygotic 0.636 versus dizygotic 0.339, the classic roughly-double MZ resemblance that signals additive genetic influence. Reported heritability across all traits is 0.488 and the reported shared-environment component is 0.174. For a majority (69%) of traits the observed correlations are consistent with a parsimonious model in which twin resemblance is due solely to additive genetic variation. Quantifies DA10's heritable-ranges claim at the scale of the whole literature, and simultaneously shows half the variance is not additive-genetic.

143.content: The founding GCTA result: estimating genetic variance directly from 294,831 common SNPs genotyped in 3,925 unrelated individuals recovers 45% of the variance in height, with no twin or family structure anywhere in the design. Heritability estimated by twin and family designs is real and hiding in many variants of individually small effect rather than missing. This is the molecular leg of C15, a method family fully independent of the other two; the SNP-heritability approach has since been replicated across traits and cohorts throughout complex-trait genetics.

144.content: Turkheimer's canonical compression of five decades of behavior-genetic findings into three laws. For DA10 the first law states the heritable-variation claim across all human behavioral traits; the second and third laws carry the guard rail: shared family environment accounts for less variance than genes, and a substantial residual is accounted for by neither, so heritability describes population variance partitioning, not individual determinism. Later quantitatively confirmed at scale by Polderman et al. 2015.

145.content: Plomin, DeFries, Knopik and Neiderhiser's top-ten list opens with the first-law finding: all psychological traits show significant and substantial genetic influence, across cognitive abilities, psychopathology and personality, corroborated across twin, family, and adoption designs with cross-national replication. The adoption/family-design leg of C15: genetic influence on parameter variation appears whether resemblance is measured in twins, in adoptees and their birth parents, or in extended families. The same review notes that four of the ten findings are about environmental influence, which is DA10's guard rail from inside behavior genetics itself.

146.content: The Panksepp-school statement of what M2 is: the mesolimbic dopamine system activates an instinctual appetitive SEEKING state that induces organisms to search for all varieties of life-supporting stimuli. SEEKING is the general-purpose engagement disposition of the awake animal rather than a response to a specific deficit signal, which is why its activation profile is not homeostatic in the M13 sense: no single tissue variable builds pressure and terminates it.

The physiological basis for M2's mixed activation profile: dopamine transmission runs in two modes. Phasic release is short-lasting, impulse-dependent, cue and reward-prediction locked; tonic extracellular dopamine sits at low concentration and changes slowly, carrying a background level of appetitive engagement that varies with state (sleep-wake, arousal). For activation_class this grounds tonic_baseline as M2's primary class with event_triggered phasic spikes as secondary; the phasic incentive-salience side is already carried in C6 by Berridge.

147.content: The incentive-motivation account of M14: sexual motivation is activated by external sexual incentive stimuli interacting with a central motive state; it is not a homeostatic reservoir in which unexpended sexual energy accumulates as an internal need. The review endorses Beach's rejection of an internal origin ("sexual motivation is active only in the presence of an external stimulus") and builds the modern model on Bindra and Toates incentive theory. No tissue deficit accumulates during abstinence; desire follows cue-triggered arousal rather than spontaneous internal pressure. For activation_class: event_triggered (incentive), not homeostatic.

Hormones set the gain, not the pressure: in rats and humans, testicular hormones control the long-term activity level of the sexual central motive state (in men via androgen receptors directly; in rats partly via aromatization to estrogens), while short-term variation in sexual motivation is driven by incentive stimuli, not by hormone fluctuation. The same structure is proposed for women (androgens needed for basic long-term activity of the central motive state). This is the hormonal gain-modulation half of M14's activation profile: testosterone tunes cue-sensitivity; cues do the triggering.

148.content: The Minnesota Starvation Experiment (Keys, 1944-45, 36 conscientious objectors under controlled semi-starvation) documents reproductive-axis shutdown under sustained energy deficit: sexual interest collapsed almost immediately once semi-starvation began, while food became the dominant preoccupation and social engagement narrowed. Evidence that an unresolved M13 deficit suppresses M14, supporting state-dependent drive priority: DA8 priority relations behave as slope functions of current state rather than a fixed order.

149.content: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) scoring by non-contrast CT in 705 Tsimane forager-horticulturalists aged 40 and over. 596 of 705 (85 percent) had no detectable coronary calcium, 89 (13 percent) scored 1 to 100, and 20 (3 percent) scored above 100. Above age 75, 31 of 48 (65 percent) still scored zero and only 4 (8 percent) reached 100 or more. Against the US Multi-Ethnic Study of Atherosclerosis (MESA) cohort of 6814, in which only 14 percent had no coronary calcium and more than half scored at least 100, this is a 24-year lag to any calcium and a 28-year lag to a score of 100. The authors call the Tsimane the population with the least reported coronary atherosclerosis on record. Cor's reading: on the cardiovascular limb of falsifier 1 the evidence points away from equivalence, and it does so with direct imaging rather than self-report. It says nothing about the psychiatric limb.

The same 705-person Tsimane cohort was measured on the components of metabolic syndrome. From table 1: body mass index above 30 in 6 percent, hypertension in 5 percent, total cholesterol above 6.2 mmol/L in under 1 percent, fasting glucose above 6.9 mmol/L in 0 to 1 percent across age bands, mean BMI 24.1, mean LDL 2.4 mmol/L, mean 10-year Framingham risk 0.04. Occasional smoking was reported by 28 percent but averaged about ten cigarettes a month, roughly 0.5 pack years over a lifetime. None of these varied across age groups. At the same time inflammatory load was high: mean hs-CRP 3.7 mg/L, with 360 of 705 (51 percent) above the 3.0 mg/L clinical cutoff, and a mean erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 22 mm/h. Cor's reading: metabolic syndrome components are rare in this population even though chronic inflammation is not, which separates the metabolic limb of falsifier 1 from a simple inflammation story and supports P3 at the level of specific resolution conditions (diet composition, habitual movement) rather than general adversity.

150.content: Eight years of repeated blood pressure measurement on 2296 Tsimane adults aged 20 and over, 6517 person-observations, 61 percent of adults measured at least twice and 36 percent at least four times. Hypertension prevalence was 3.9 percent in women and 5.2 percent in men, falling to 2.9 percent in both sexes when a diagnosis required persistence across multiple observations. Mixed-effects models gave a systolic rise of 2.86 mm Hg per decade for women and 0.91 for men, against roughly 7 mm Hg per decade reported for Westerners over 40, and pulse pressure did not rise at all in men. The paper notes that by age 70 more than three-quarters of US adults are hypertensive. No Tsimane had ever taken antihypertensive medication. Cor's reading: this is the strongest design in the falsifier-1 evidence base, because it is longitudinal and so answers the cohort-effect objection that sinks earlier cross-sectional subsistence studies. The steep age-related rise in blood pressure is not a species-universal, which is what P3 predicts.

Within the same Tsimane cohort the authors tested whether market integration reproduces the industrial blood pressure pattern. Smoking frequency and Spanish fluency had minimal effect on mean blood pressure and no effect on the rate of age-related rise. Distance to the market town and body mass index did modulate the rate of rise, so some dose-response exists, but the modernization effects overall were judged minimal in a population that stays lean and physically active. Cor's reading: this complicates any simple story in which contact with markets alone drives cardiovascular ageing. The gradient that matters appears to run through the specific resolution conditions (adiposity, activity, diet composition) rather than through modernization as a general category, which is exactly the distinction P3 is supposed to enforce and which copy about falsifier 1 tends to blur.

151.content: Depressive symptoms are common among Tsimane forager-horticulturalists. In 649 adults aged 34 to 85, among those scoring in the top depression band about 90 percent habitually experienced sadness and crying easily, 86 percent irregular sleep, 84 percent feelings of uselessness and 77 percent persistent negative thoughts. The authors state that depression exists in this population in the absence of the industrial risk factors usually blamed for it: low pathogen exposure in development, metabolic disorder, inequality and social isolation. Cor's reading (OF1 decode): the scores measure how often and how strongly the low-mood signal fires in this population, on a scale shaped by a Western category. The signal fires here, and the sibling rows show what it goes with: immune activation (652), physical disability, a lost subsistence role and unresolved conflict (654). OF2 predicts exactly this: defensive signalling fires wherever its triggering conditions occur, in any environment. Falsifier 1 is stated in signal terms: how often and how long the signal fires in EEA-matched populations against industrial ones. One population with no matched comparison cannot score it.

Test of the host-defense (sickness behaviour) account of depression in a high-pathogen population. In 649 older Tsimane adults, depression score was associated with higher baseline TNF-alpha, IL-6 and C-reactive protein. 93 percent of high-scorers sat in the upper quintile of at least one immune activation biomarker against 60 percent of lower-scorers, and 33 percent were in the upper quintile of at least two against 19 percent. The association held after excluding everyone in the top quintile of leukocyte count, so it is not simply acute infection. Depressed adults also showed larger IL-1 beta and IL-6 responses to ex vivo LPS and PHA stimulation, effect sizes 0.21 to 0.41 standard deviations, all in the predicted direction. Cor's reading: this is support for DA1 and M8: the low mood goes with a measured internal condition and behaves like a defensive response that moves energy toward immune activation. Direction is open: inflammation may drive the low mood (sickness behaviour, the authors' hypothesis), or the conditions that lower mood may also raise inflammation. Under either reading the coupling is present outside industrial life, which makes this the clearest evidence that it is no artefact of industrial living.

152.content: Regular depressive symptoms among Tsimane forager-farmers of Bolivia aged 50 and over (n = 325, mean age 62), scored on an interview the authors built from focus groups and established depression scales, translated into Tsimane, back-translated and administered in Tsimane (18 items asked, 16 analysed, Cronbach alpha 0.71). 18 percent of women and 7 percent of men regularly experienced depressive symptoms (the cut-off is given in a supplementary figure). The authors state these estimates are comparable to the combined one-month US prevalence of major depressive disorder, mood disorder, dysthymia and anxiety disorder among adults aged 18 and over, even after conservative adjustment for comorbidity, and conclude that depressive symptoms appear to be regularly experienced under conditions more similar to those in which our species evolved and are not simply a by-product of modernity. Depression scores were normally distributed in both sexes, which the authors say calls into question the utility of clinical distinctions that imply threshold effects. No participant reported ever taking prescription medication for depressive symptoms. Cor's reading (OF1 decode): the figures say how many older adults report the low-mood signal firing regularly, on a scale built around a Western category. The signal fires at a substantial rate in an EEA-approximating population, as OF2 predicts wherever its triggers are present (654 names them: disability, a lost subsistence role, conflict). The normal distribution of scores, with no natural break, fits DA1: nothing in the data marks off a disease group. This row does not settle whether the rate is lower or higher than in industrial populations: that comparison is the authors', across instruments that are not equivalent, and it stays contested.

What goes with higher depression scores among Tsimane older adults. In ordinary least squares models on 325 adults aged 50 and over, depression score rose with lower energetic status (lower BMI), greater measured physical disability on an eleven-item exercise battery, and lower involvement in routine subsistence tasks, all after controlling for age, sex, unresolved conflicts and market involvement. Depression also rose with reported social conflict, and the effect was strongest for conflict with non-kin. The conflict measure included gossip and suspected sorcery from kin and non-kin. Cor's reading: every correlate here is a withheld or violated resolution condition rather than a defect in the person: lost capacity to provision others, and unresolved conflict with people one cannot avoid. The data fit either direction. Losing the provider role may trigger low mood; low mood may also come first, since withdrawal conserves energy and lowers subsistence work. Under the first reading the signal reports the lost role, which is direct support for OF2 and DA1; under the second, the lost role follows a signal set off by something else. The cross-sectional design cannot order them, and longitudinal data would. The pattern holds in a population with no psychiatric care and no antidepressants.

153.content: A review sympathetic to the mismatch reading of depression states plainly that the forager side of the comparison has almost no usable data. It notes that a correlation between depression and modernization predicts very low prevalence among hunter-gatherers, that community-based investigations using cross-culturally valid diagnostic tools among traditional populations are still needed, and that what exists is scant: ethnographic reports on the Kaluli of New Guinea, the Thai-Lao of Thailand and the Toraja of Indonesia, with no systematic community sampling and no formal diagnostic instruments. Cor's reading: this is the honest epistemic state of the comparison. Nobody has measured forager rates with instruments valid across cultures, so a forager-versus-industrial depression-rate comparison is currently untestable. Under the clear-defect rule, a stance (DA1), Cor makes no disease-rate claim for presentations where no clear defect is the cause; the testable form is how often and how long the signal fires (OF1 decode), and falsifier 1 is stated in that form.

The industrial side of the depression trend is also weaker than it is usually presented. The review finds available data indicate rising prevalence and higher lifetime risk in younger cohorts, but says strong conclusions cannot be drawn because of conflicting results and methodological flaws. Retrospective community surveys are confounded by recall bias, since people under-report past episodes, especially untreated milder ones. Longitudinal series mostly do show a rise: US one-year major depression prevalence went from 3.33 percent in 1991 to 1992 to 7.06 percent in 2001 to 2002, and the Lundby Swedish series found depression had the largest increase of any disorder. Against that, one large Canadian community study found a steady 5 percent prevalence of major depressive disorder in 1952, 1970 and 1992, with no period or cohort effect. Cor's reading (OF1 decode): these series count diagnoses made under changing criteria, so they track how often people cross a diagnostic threshold, a mix of how often the low-mood signal fires and how it is labelled. The "rates are rising" half of the mismatch story is real in most series but contested, and one good null exists. Copy that asserts a clean epidemic overstates what the literature supports.

154.content: Why forager psychiatric prevalence has no clean number. Building an instrument to measure subclinical psychopathological traits among the Tsimane required reviewing over 400 candidate items drawn from standard Global North inventories and reducing them to 117 through local research assistants, focus groups and cognitive interviews, with each item grounded in culturally relevant examples and translated into Tsimane. The authors report that concepts central to Western psychopathology, anxiety and stress among them, may lack direct equivalents in other languages or be expressed differently, and that applying screening tools directly in small-scale societies risks either pathologising normal behaviour or missing distress entirely. The finished instrument covers autism spectrum, ADHD, obsessive-compulsive, schizotypy, depression, anxiety, trauma, substance use and personality traits. Cor's reading: this is the measurement-invariance problem, and the evidence for the OF1 decode rule: a Western category scored on an imported scale can pathologise normal behaviour or miss distress. Any forager-versus-industrial comparison of such scores is contested by construction, and the atlas records that dispute on the comparison itself; a within-population observation keeps the grade of its own design. Falsifier 1's psychiatric clause needs restating in signal terms (how often and how long the signal fires under a matched trigger load), a test not yet runnable.

155.content: Within-population before-and-after evidence on the metabolic limb. A PRISMA systematic review screened 22 populations that underwent a nutrition transition, found eleven with adequate pre- and post-transition data, and analysed four in depth: Yemenite Jews, Tokelauans, Tanushimaru Japanese and Maasai, with seven more reviewed to check selection bias. Non-communicable chronic disease was rare before transition and rose after it. Yemenite Jews in Israel: diabetes went from 0.12 percent in men and 0 percent in women pre-transition to 6.1 percent and 3.1 percent after forty years, with 26.3 percent diabetic among those over 55 resident more than forty years, and mean BMI rose from 21 to 23.6 up to 25 to 26. Tokelauans: diabetes rose in every cohort from 1968 to 1982, and faster in migrants to New Zealand than in those who stayed. Maasai: BMI and diabetes rose after the shift from milk, blood and meat to maize and cereals. Cor's reading: this is the strongest available answer to the confounding objection against forager-versus-industrial contrasts, because the comparison is within the same population across a transition rather than between genetically and geographically different groups. It is direct support for P3 on the metabolic limb of falsifier 1.

107.content: The first author collected observational data on 40 chimpanzees living in six accredited zoological institutions, all housed in social groups in enriched enclosures, the context in which abnormal behaviour should be least likely. Abnormal behaviour was present in every sampled individual across all six groups, and every individual showed at least two different types of abnormal behaviour. Frequency and duration varied widely between individuals and were not explained by sex, age, rearing history or prior housing background. A median individual carried a repertoire of five abnormal behaviours and spent between four and five percent of activity on them; some individuals exceeded 60 percent of activity.

What the paper actually says about wild chimpanzees, which is narrower than a blanket claim that no abnormal behaviour occurs in the wild. In 1023 hours of focal animal sampling of wild chimpanzees in Uganda, none of the abnormal behaviours listed in the study were observed. However, the authors immediately qualify this: seventeen of the 37 behaviours they catalogued have been reported to occur, albeit rarely, in wild chimpanzees, and coprophagy, the most prevalent abnormal behaviour in captive populations, has been reported from at least six wild populations. Their conclusion is that most captive chimpanzee behaviour is normal in the sense of being seen in wild counterparts, and that abnormal behaviour is endemic in captivity.

156.content: Bucharest Early Intervention Project, cognitive outcome at age 18, sixteen years after randomisation. 135 participants were assessed in early adulthood at a mean age of 18.74 years. Those randomised to high-quality foster care scored significantly higher on IQ than those randomised to care as usual: 9 points, equivalent to 0.6 standard deviations. This is the real magnitude of the foster-care effect and it replaces the unsourced claim that foster care roughly doubles IQ recovery. Mediation analyses in the same paper attribute the causal effect to the caregiving relationship rather than to placement per se.

The residual deprivation gap. Comparing everyone with a history of institutional care against never-institutionalised Romanian community comparison participants, the ever-institutionalised group scored on average 26.21 full-scale IQ points below the community group, a standardised difference of 1.20. The same direction held on every subscale: verbal comprehension 24.07 points, perceptual reasoning 22.27, processing speed 20.29, working memory 19.12. Neither randomised arm reached the never-institutionalised baseline. The authors are explicit that the never-institutionalised group is a comparison group and not a control group, since it was not randomised.

110.content: SMILES trial primary remission result. 166 individuals were assessed for eligibility and 67 adults diagnosed with major depressive disorder were randomised, 33 to a Mediterranean-style dietary support intervention and 34 to a social support (befriending) control. At 12 weeks, 32.3 percent (n=10) of the dietary support group and 8.0 percent (n=2) of the control group met remission criteria of a MADRS score below 10. The between-group difference was significant, chi-square(1) = 4.84, p = 0.028. The number needed to treat based on these remission data is 4.1, with a 95 percent confidence interval on the NNT of 2.3 to 27.8. On the continuous MADRS outcome the between-group Cohen's d was 1.16 in favour of the dietary arm.

The SMILES authors' own stated limitations, recorded so the trial is not read as stronger than it is. Participants could not be blinded because the advertising had to state the nature of the intervention, raising expectation bias and possibly driving the differential dropout (94 percent completion in the dietary arm against 73.5 percent in the social support arm). The randomisation block size of four may have been insufficient to support allocation concealment. The trial did not reach its planned sample size, which the authors say raises the possibility the sample was not representative, limited subgroup analysis, and may have inflated the observed effect size. Sensitivity analyses testing departures from the missing-at-random assumption moved the effect towards the null but left the finding robust.

157.content: Network meta-analysis of exercise trials in people who met the review's criteria for major depression: 218 unique studies, 495 arms, 14170 participants. Against active controls such as usual care or a placebo tablet, moderate reductions in depression were found for walking or jogging (Hedges' g -0.62, 95% credible interval -0.80 to -0.45, from 51 comparisons and 1210 participants), yoga (g -0.55, -0.73 to -0.36), strength training (g -0.49, -0.69 to -0.29), mixed aerobic exercise (g -0.43, -0.61 to -0.24) and tai chi or qigong (g -0.42, -0.65 to -0.21). Effects were proportional to the intensity prescribed. These are the real magnitudes and they are smaller than the previously asserted Cohen's d of about 0.8.

The certainty attached to the exercise effect sizes, which is the part most often dropped when this literature is cited. Results appeared robust to publication bias, but only one of the 218 included studies met the Cochrane criteria for low risk of bias. Graded with CINeMA, confidence was therefore low for walking or jogging and very low for every other modality. The authors also note that confidence in the evidence for exercise is less strong than for cognitive behavioural therapy even though the effect sizes look comparable, and they call for future studies that blind participants and staff to mitigate expectancy effects.

158.content: Triple chronotherapy response rates from the only open-access randomised trial reachable in full text. 82 out-patients who met the trial's depression criteria were randomised, single blind, to triple chronotherapy (36 hours of total sleep deprivation, then four days of sleep phase advance, plus daily morning bright light for six months) or to a control intervention of psychoeducation and written information. A response, defined as at least a 50 percent reduction in symptoms, was achieved by 33.3 percent of the chronotherapy group against 16.2 percent of controls, and this held at week 26 at 35.9 percent against 13.9 percent. The between-group effect size on the HRSD-6 was Cohen's d = 0.8 at week 1, rising to d = 1.30 at week 26. These figures replace the previously asserted "60%+ within a week" and "~30% for pharmacotherapy alone", neither of which was traceable to a source.

159.content: Kangaroo mother care and neonatal mortality. Systematic review of 15 studies reporting mortality or morbidity, nine of them randomised controlled trials, all from low or middle income settings, almost all hospital-based and restricted to babies under 2000 g. Meta-analysis of three randomised trials that began KMC in the first week of life gave a relative risk for neonatal mortality of 0.49 (95% CI 0.29 to 0.82) against standard care, that is a 51 percent reduction (95% CI 18 to 71 percent), based on 988 babies. A separate meta-analysis of three observational studies gave a smaller 32 percent reduction. This is the source of the kangaroo care mortality result; it is not a finding of Feldman's neurodevelopmental work, to which it was previously attributed.

160.content: Across 18 chimpanzee communities studied over five decades, killings (recorded in 15 of them) were mostly by males and mostly of members of other communities, and killing rates did not track measures of human disturbance.

161.content: Killing between groups of nomadic hunter-gatherers tends to fit the chimpanzee pattern of surprise attacks when one side greatly outnumbers the other. Humans also form peaceful ties and alliances between groups, which chimpanzees do not.

162.content: Combining archaeological causes of death from the Late Pleistocene and early Holocene with hunter-gatherer ethnography, Bowles estimates that deaths in conflicts between groups were frequent enough to favor the evolution of costly group-beneficial behavior.

Bowles compiled 15 archaeological and 8 ethnographic sources on foragers without chiefs or states, including some sedentary forager populations. Deaths in war made up on average 14% of all deaths (weighted mean; archaeological 12%, ethnographic 16%). Single sites ranged from 0% (Gobero, Niger) to 46% (Nubia, site 117); ethnographic populations ranged from 4% to 30% (Ache 30%). Of 34 sources screened, 14 were excluded as unrepresentative, unreliable or inadequate. Bowles notes that burial samples may overstate violence and that missing bones may understate it.

163.content: In 21 mobile forager band societies drawn from the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, more than half of lethal events had a lone perpetrator, and most killings classify as homicides; a few were feuds and a minority were war.

In 21 mobile forager band societies from the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, ethnographies recorded 148 lethal events. About one third involved people of different groups, but 38 of those 50 came from one society, the Tiwi; in the other 20 societies about 15% of events were between groups. 55% of events were one killer and one victim (64% without the Tiwi), 15% crossed societal lines, and about half of the societies had no lethal event with more than one perpetrator.

164.content: Phylogenetic comparison across mammals predicts that about 2 percent of human deaths are caused by interpersonal violence, similar to the value inferred for the ancestor of primates and apes and to rates seen in prehistoric bands and tribes.

165.content: Infants' reactions to an approaching stranger could be reliably coded from video. Subtle negative responses (wariness) were validated against heart rate acceleration and against responses to the mother's approach, and changed significantly with age; the authors read wariness behaviours as a coping cutoff that prevents crying and lets the infant re-engage the stranger.

166.content: In immediate-return hunter-gatherer societies people could move between camps at any time without economic penalty, and this freedom to leave worked as a levelling check on anyone who tried to dominate. Woodburn names it alongside every man's access to lethal hunting weapons.

167.content: In US Congressional elections from 1898 to 1992 (16,577 races), about one vote in 100,000 (working paper) or one in 89,000 (published abstract) was cast for a candidate who tied or won by one vote, against about one in 15,000 in state legislative elections; one-vote margins grew rarer as elections got bigger, and recounts and other close-margin procedures shaped how often they occurred.

168.content: Mason argues that US partisanship works as a social identity, with other group identities lining up behind the two parties, and that this drives prejudice, anger and activism independently of policy opinions.

169.content: Achen and Bartels argue that voters, including well-informed ones, mostly choose parties by social identity and partisan loyalty and then adjust their policy views, and even their perception of facts, to match.

170.content: Fowler finds that partisan loyalty and policy voting are often observationally equivalent, and where they can be separated (the southern realignment, experiments with hypothetical candidates) the evidence favors policy voting.

171.content: Among 12 OECD democracies over about four decades, the US had the largest baseline increase in affective polarization; five countries rose less and six saw it fall.

172.content: In 32 present-day forager societies, most members of a residential band were not close genetic kin of one another.

173.content: Forager residential groups vary widely in size and composition, and people moved between many groups across a regional network, so a single fixed small band is an oversimplification.

174.content: Forager populations were organized in nested levels, with each level about three to four times larger than the one below it, from families through camps to regional groups.

Across 339 forager societies in Binford's compilation, the regional population (the regional ethnic unit) had a geometric mean of about 840 people (95% limits 736 to 954), with a wide spread (standard deviation of log size 1.25). Lower levels averaged 4.5 per family, 15.6 per dispersed group, 54 per aggregated residential group and 165 per periodic multi-group gathering.

175.content: Foragers range from small mobile bands to large settled societies with ranks and stored food, so no single foraging type describes them all.

176.content: Among Agta and Mbendjele BaYaka foragers, a model in which men and women had equal say over where couples lived reproduced the low within-camp relatedness seen in those camps.

177.content: Across the ethnographic record of mobile foragers and many tribal groups, the group as a whole actively suppressed any member who tried to dominate, through ridicule, disobedience, desertion or, at the extreme, killing.

178.content: Leaders exist in small-scale societies, but in mobile forager groups their influence is informal, situation-specific and rests on others choosing to follow.

179.content: In most foraging societies in the ethnographic record, parents or other kin arranged marriages, so free individual mate choice was not the usual pattern.

From the ethnographic record of 190 hunting and gathering societies, Apostolou reports that almost all reproduction takes place within marriage and that marriage is regulated by parents and close kin. Parents influence the mate choice of sons and daughters, with stronger control over daughters, and fathers have more say than mothers in picking in-laws. He argues that this pattern probably held through human evolution. Paraphrased from the abstract only; the abstract gives no percentages.

180.content: A phylogenetic reconstruction on mitochondrial DNA trees of hunter-gatherer societies infers that arranged marriage goes back at least to the first modern human migrations out of Africa, and that early marriages probably had low polygyny and exchanges between the two families (brideservice or brideprice). Whether earlier African marriages were arranged is left open, because 3 of the 8 African hunter-gatherer societies in the sample marry by courtship.

Walker and colleagues report the figures from Apostolou's coding of 190 hunter-gatherer societies: marriage arranged by parents or close kin is the primary mode in 85 percent of the sample, brideservice, brideprice or another exchange between families in 80 percent, and fewer than 20 percent of men married polygynously in 87 percent. In Apostolou's full sample, 3 of the 8 African hunter-gatherer societies marry by courtship.

181.content: Hadza men and women both rated character as important in a spouse; women placed great importance on a man's foraging, and men placed considerable importance on a woman being hard-working.

182.content: In frontal drawings, Hadza men preferred a higher waist-to-hip ratio (about 0.9) than American men (about 0.7), which the authors linked to local ecology.

183.content: Across 37 cultures, women on average placed more weight than men on a partner's earning prospects, and men placed more weight on youth and looks.

184.content: In a 2016 sample of 14,399 people in 45 countries, the sex differences in stated mate preferences reported by Buss in 1989 held: on average men more than women preferred attractive and young partners, and women more than men preferred older partners with good financial prospects. Sex alone could be classified from the pattern of preferences 63 percent of the time.

In the same 45-country sample, the sex gap in partner age shrank as national gender equality rose, but gender equality was not robustly related to the sex differences in stated preferences for looks, finances or other traits. The one exception was the Global Gender Gap Index tracking the sex difference in preference for good financial prospects, matching Zentner and Mitura 2012. National pathogen load also accounted for little.

185.content: In forced-choice studies, men more often than women picked a partner's sexual infidelity as more upsetting than emotional infidelity.

186.content: A meta-analysis of continuous ratings confirmed a small but reliable sex difference in which kind of infidelity upsets people more, for both imagined and actual infidelity.

187.content: !Kung mothers nursed in short bouts several times an hour, and the authors proposed that this frequent nursing suppresses ovulation and may explain the long gaps between !Kung births.

188.content: Infants of Aka foragers were held for nearly all of the day and were held and fed more than infants of neighbouring farmers.

189.content: From birth through at least the first 18 weeks, Efe forager infants were cared for by many people besides the mother, including women who suckled them.

190.content: Among the !Kung, infant crying got a fast response, usually from the mother but often from other caregivers too, and crying bouts were short.

191.content: !Kung infants had about as many crying episodes per hour as Dutch and American infants in the first months, but spent about half as much time crying as Dutch infants, mostly in short, fretful bouts, which the authors link to quick, near-universal caregiver responses.

192.content: A review of 45 studies found that in almost all of them at least one relative besides the mother improved child survival, most consistently maternal grandmothers and older siblings (the latter from few studies), while fathers improved survival in only a third of studies.

193.content: Human mothers rely on help from others to raise several dependent children at once, and this cooperative breeding helps explain humans' short birth intervals.

194.content: In Barry and Paxson's codes for the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, the mother slept in the same room as her infant in every one of the 173 societies coded, and in the same bed in at least 76 of them.

195.content: Across non-industrial societies, breastfeeding usually continued into the second or third year, with other foods added from around the middle of the first year.

196.content: Food sharing is found in every forager society studied, and large, unpredictable items such as meat are shared most widely beyond the household.

Gurven reviewed food transfers in 45 small-scale groups (his table lists 33 hunter-gatherer and 13 forager-agriculturalist entries, the Ache under both). In every group where package size was examined (10 named, among them the Hiwi, Ache, Dobe !Kung, G/wi, Nyae Nyae !Kung and Aka), a larger share of big game went to more families than of small game. Sharing with the whole band, whether or not the receivers hunted, is described as relatively rare across societies and limited to bands of fewer than 40 to 50 people; many groups first share within the task group or extended family and only afterwards with others.

In the groups with counts, producers kept more than an equal share. Hiwi and Ache families at their settlements (3% and 5% of the population) kept 20% or more of what they acquired and gave the rest to fewer than six other families out of 23 and 36. Yora families kept about 40% of game at the village, Yuqui hunters about 69% of meat, and Yanomamo hunters kept twice what they gave each other family. Ache and Batak hunters are reported to receive no more than other band members. Small game was often eaten within the acquirer's own family among the Dobe !Kung and the G/wi.

Among the Ache and the Hiwi, women gave away about 55% of all the plant food they collected, and there was no sex difference in sharing once package size was controlled. Across societies, direct requests for food, when not excessive, were rarely refused, while unsolicited giving varied widely. Gurven also lists reported sanctions against people who did not share or produce (gossip, exclusion from shares, being forced out of the household or village) and cases where low producers were tolerated, and notes that punishment has not been studied systematically in any group.

197.content: Among Ache foragers, meat and honey were shared across the whole band, so a hunter's own family ate only a small share of what he brought in.

198.content: Much forager sharing happens because others ask for it, and refusing is hard, so sharing is driven as much by demand as by generosity.

In the abstract Peterson argues that demand sharing is testing, assertive or substantiating behaviour, and that it matters for building social relations in egalitarian societies. He says a behaviouristic model of demand sharing fits sociobiological expectations, and that his emphasis is on the social and symbolic meaning of the practice.

199.content: Forager adults produced more food than they ate and transferred the surplus to children and others, because children take many years to become net producers.

In Kaplan and colleagues' Table 1, women's mean age at first reproduction was 19.5 years among the Ache, 20.5 among the Hiwi and 19.2 among the !Kung (forager mean 19.7); the mean interval to the next birth after a surviving infant was 37.6, 45.1 and 41.3 months (mean 41.3, about 3.4 years); and mean age at last reproduction was 42.1, 37.8 and 37 years (mean 39.0). Female chimpanzees give birth for the first time about five years earlier, and their interbirth interval after a surviving infant is more than 1.5 times longer.

200.content: Some anthropologists argue that men hunt big game partly to gain status and allies, since the meat is shared widely and their own families get little extra.

201.content: A review of ethnographic reports found that women in many forager societies took part in hunting.

202.content: Among the Agta of the Philippines, people in camps that did more farm work had less leisure than people in camps that mainly foraged, a gap driven mostly by women's extra work outside camp.

203.content: Sahlins argued that foragers met their needs with a few hours of food-getting a day and had much free time, calling them the original affluent society.

204.content: Hadza participants averaged over two hours a day of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity, more than 14 times as much as participants in large US studies.

205.content: Across forager societies, children learned most subsistence skills through play, observation and participation in multi-age playgroups, and adults directly taught complex skills such as hunting mainly in adolescence.

206.content: Observers listening to relaxed conversations in public settings found they consisted mostly of social information, mostly personal relationships and experiences, and most exchanges were about the speaker or third parties; very few were criticism or the asking or giving of advice.

207.content: In five naturalistic studies (467 people wearing an audio recorder that sampled 5 to 12% of 2 to 5 days), gossip tended to be neutral rather than positive or negative, and was mostly about social information.

Across five naturalistic studies (467 people wearing an audio recorder that sampled 5 to 12% of 2 to 5 days), women engaged in more neutral gossip than men. The abstract does not report a sex difference in total or negative gossip.

208.content: In experiments, people passed on reputational information about selfish players even at a cost to themselves, and the threat of gossip made others behave more generously.

209.content: Among the Ju/'hoansi, daytime talk was mostly about economic matters, complaints and gossip, while firelight talk at night was mostly stories.

Among the Ju/'hoansi of /Kae/kae and Dobe, Botswana, in 1974, families ate the evening meal each at their own fire. After dinner and dark, people gathered around single fires to talk, make music or dance, in larger or smaller groups, and went back to their own hearths to sleep. Wiessner states that meat was shared in waves, each receiver giving on to kin, until every person present had a share.

In 122 daytime conversations among the Ju/'hoansi, 34% of talk was complaint or criticism, and the author judged about a third of that criticism to be moved by envy. Close to 95% of these disputes were between the people directly affected. Where talk did not settle a dispute, people moved away. Two disputes in the sample went as far as brandishing poison arrows, and both times others physically held the aggressor back. Complaint and criticism were rarer at night.

On 6 of the 36 evenings Wiessner observed among the Ju/'hoansi, a trance-healing dance was held: three smaller ones and three that lasted all night and drew people from three or more camps. She describes trance healing as the only activity in which whole bands worked together toward one result, with women clapping and singing for hours in support of the healers. On 8 of the 36 evenings women broke into festive song and dance.

210.content: In the US, India and Israel, how much shame people expected to feel in 29 imagined situations closely matched how much a separate group of local raters would think less of someone in that situation (mean r .72 across the three countries). Shame also tracked devaluation by raters from the other two countries (mean r .64).

211.content: Among 899 people in 15 small-scale communities (farmers, herders, fishers and horticulturalists on several continents; none of them mobile foragers), the shame people expected to feel over 12 imagined acts or traits tracked how much their own community would devalue someone for them (mean r 0.84). It tracked the devaluation of the other communities less closely (mean r 0.69).

212.content: In hunter-gatherer populations with minimal or no exposure to modern medicine, about 57 percent of children survived to age 15, and the most common age of adult death was about 70 (68 to 78 across populations).

In small-scale hunter-gatherer and horticulturalist populations, illness caused about 70 percent of deaths on average, with infections such as respiratory and gut disease prominent, while violence and accidents caused about 19 percent on average, ranging from 4 to 69 percent.

213.content: Across 20 forager societies, about 49 percent of children died before age 15.

214.content: In a cross-cultural sample, foragers had famine less often than farmers, after controlling for habitat quality.

215.content: Ethnographic accounts show forager societies were no more food insecure than farming societies, against the assumption that foragers lived through constant feast and famine.

216.content: Most major crowd infections of today, such as measles and smallpox, arose after farming, when dense settled populations lived close to domestic animals.

217.content: In the Ethnographic Atlas, most forager societies got more than half of their food from animal sources such as hunting and fishing.

218.content: Hadza men and women both rank honey as their favorite food, and it supplies a substantial share of Hadza calories, especially for men.

219.content: In a meta-analysis of 288 results from 46 studies in 33 non-industrial societies, higher-status men had greater reproductive success (overall r 0.19, against 0.80 in non-human primates). The effect in foragers (Zr 0.18, 64 results) was about the same as in horticulturalists, pastoralists and farmers.

In the same meta-analysis, status went with men's fertility and mating success more than with lower child mortality. Status was linked to fewer child deaths only in polygynous societies, and the link between status and number of surviving offspring was about a third smaller in monogamous societies.

220.content: A review of the evidence concluded that the desire for status, meaning respect and admiration from others, is a fundamental human motive.

221.content: A meta-analysis found that males are more physically aggressive than females at all ages and across cultures, while girls show more indirect aggression than boys only in later childhood and adolescence, depending on how it is measured.

222.content: Women compete with other women mainly through indirect aggression, such as gossip and social exclusion, which costs the aggressor little physical risk.

223.content: Roughly half or more of people who lose a close person keep a stable pattern of healthy functioning, while about 10 to 15 percent keep high scores on depression and distress measures.

In this narrative review Bonanno states that across bereavement studies chronic high scores on depression and distress measures tend to occur in 10 to 15% of bereaved people, that many more show disruptions lasting several months to one or two years, and that people with relatively low depression or distress scores have approached or exceeded 50% of the sample in studies reporting aggregate data. He reports that absent grief was treated by most bereavement experts surveyed as denial that would surface later, and that the studies he reviews found no delayed grief among people with low scores.

For violent and life-threatening events Bonanno reports that the large majority of exposed people in the studies he reviews did not go on to meet criteria for chronic PTSD. The shares he cites of people who met criteria for chronic PTSD run from 6.6% and 9.9% after the 1992 Los Angeles riots, 12.5% of Gulf War veterans and 16.5% of people hospitalised after motor vehicle accidents to 17.8% of physical assault victims. He cites a survey of Manhattan residents after the attacks of 11 September 2001 in which the share estimated to meet PTSD criteria fell from 7.5% at one month to 1.7% at four months and 0.6% at six months.

224.content: A meta-analysis estimated that about one in ten bereaved adults develops prolonged grief after a natural death.

225.content: Chimpanzees observed around a dying group member behaved in ways that resemble human responses to death, such as attending closely and staying near the body.

226.content: Music is found in every society studied, and songs used for the same purpose, such as lullabies, dance songs or healing songs, share acoustic features across cultures that let listeners and computer models identify their purpose better than chance.

227.content: A global sample of 304 recordings found statistical universals in music, and the authors suggested that many of them may help groups coordinate and hold together.

228.content: Dancing in synchrony raised people's pain thresholds and their feelings of closeness to the other dancers.

229.content: One account holds that music evolved with culture as a system for social bonding between people.

230.content: Among the Agta, camps with skilled storytellers cooperated more, and skilled storytellers were preferred as campmates and had more surviving children.

231.content: The grandmother hypothesis holds that long human life after menopause evolved because older women fed their weaned grandchildren, which let their daughters have babies sooner.

232.content: Across hunting records from 40 sites in subsistence societies, hunting skill rose into adulthood and peaked on average around age 33, then declined only slowly, so skill stayed high through much of adulthood.

233.content: In three pre-industrial groups (Hadza, San and Tsimane), people slept about 6 to 7 hours a night, did not sleep longer than industrial adults, and fell asleep as the night got cooler.

234.content: Comparing two Toba/Qom communities, people in the one with electric light slept less and fell asleep later than people in the one without it.

235.content: In a Hadza camp, differences in sleep timing between people meant that someone was almost always awake during the night.

236.content: Historical records from the pre-industrial British Isles describe sleep in two segments, a 'first' and a 'second' sleep, with a waking period between them.

237.content: Forager infancy, as documented among the !Kung and other groups, involved near-constant carrying and body contact, frequent nursing and quick response to crying.

238.content: Among the Hadza, people other than the mother spent time holding infants and toddlers, with closer kin holding them most and unrelated helpers of all ages also providing a substantial amount of care.

239.content: Woodburn described some African forager societies in which disposal of the dead went little beyond practical need and the camp was generally abandoned after a death.

240.content: In 1974, Ju/'hoansi men and women at /Kae/kae (Botswana) each kept on average 15 hxaro gift-exchange partnerships with kin living 2 to 200 km away. The average person spent 4.4 months a year living with hxaro partners, and 69% of possessions had been received as hxaro gifts. About 70% of /Kae/kae residents' partners lived across the border in Namibia, in the same ethnic group.

Among the Ju/'hoansi, 44 years of possession and spending data (1974 /Kae/kae, Botswana; 2017 to 2018 Nyae Nyae, Namibia) show that cash income brought large differences in material wealth, even between neighbours, while hxaro gift partnerships shrank. Social, gender and political equality held: people did not hire other Ju/'hoansi as workers and fewer than 6.7% of debts were owed to other Ju/'hoansi, and money was rarely spent on status beyond clothes and a phone.

241.content: Among Aka forager children aged 4 to 16, play gave way to work as they grew older, and Aka children did less rough-and-tumble play and fewer competitive games than neighbouring farmer children.

242.content: In Marlowe's cross-cultural sample of foragers, the median residential group size was 27 people (mean 41.4, range 13 to 250, across 263 societies).

243.content: In a cross-cultural study of bereavement, women cried more often than men during bereavement, and where final ceremonies for the dead were held, prolonged grief was less common.

244.content: Late Pleistocene social organization was probably more varied than the nomadic-egalitarian model, with some forager groups showing inequality and seasonal hierarchy.

245.content: A meta-analysis found that the sex differences people state in mate preferences for looks and earning prospects barely predict whom they actually like in face-to-face meetings or relationships.

246.content: A review argued that the sex difference in jealousy appears mainly in hypothetical forced-choice questions and weakens or disappears in reports of real infidelity and other measures.

247.content: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends room-sharing without bed-sharing, saying room-sharing on a separate surface can cut SIDS risk by up to half and avoids the suffocation risks of adult beds.

248.content: A reanalysis argued that women's hunting in forager societies was occasional and that a sexual division of labor in hunting was real.

249.content: Data from the Alyawara showed that once food processing is counted, foragers spent far more time on getting food than the original affluent society figures suggested.

250.content: A review found weak and inconsistent evidence that pretend play causes the developmental gains often credited to it.

251.content: Forager diets varied so widely with habitat and season that they fit no single standard pattern that modern people could copy for better health.

252.content: A meta-analysis of 148 studies of children and adolescents found that boys showed more direct aggression than girls, while the sex difference in indirect aggression was trivial.

253.content: A rival account holds that music evolved as a credible signal, of coalition strength in group song and of parental attention in infant song, and that it signals existing social bonds rather than creating them.

254.content: A simulation model found that grandmothering alone was not enough to select for the long human post-reproductive lifespan.

255.content: Among foragers in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, societies where men contributed more to subsistence were more monogamous.

256.content: Across societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, closer father-infant care and higher male contribution to subsistence go with less polygyny, and foragers tend to show closer father-infant relationships than pastoralists.

257.content: About 85 percent of societies in the anthropological record permitted a man to have more than one wife. Normative monogamy spread from classical Greece and Rome and, in recent centuries, worldwide, with laws against polygyny arriving in Japan in 1880, China in 1953, India in 1955 and Nepal in 1963.

Henrich and colleagues state that in relatively egalitarian societies, including most foragers, few men gain enough status to attract a second wife, usually no more than one extra, and very successful men rarely obtain three or at most four. Among tropical African foragers, rates of polygyny range from 3 to 20 percent.

258.content: In five societies with detailed data (Ache, Hadza, !Kung, Lamalera and Meriam), better hunters had higher age-corrected reproductive success than other men in their group.

259.content: Among Hadza men, upper-body strength predicted their reputation as hunters and their reproductive success.

260.content: Among 49 Hadza men from nine camps, those with lower-pitched voices had more living children and more children born, controlling for age; pitch did not predict child mortality. In 52 Hadza women, pitch did not predict any reproductive outcome.

261.content: Hadza participants preferred symmetric faces, as UK participants did, and the preference was stronger among the Hadza.

262.content: Hadza and British participants both preferred averaged faces, but the Hadza did not prefer averaged faces made from European faces.
