438.content: In 60 healthy men randomised to 1.5 mg alprazolam a day, etifoxine or placebo for five days, alprazolam did not change the startle response to unpredictable threat on day 1 or day 5, and neither drug changed self-reported anxiety. The authors note this conflicts with earlier benzodiazepine studies that used higher single doses.

439.content: Leshner, then director of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, argued that research of the previous 20 years showed drug addiction to be a chronic, relapsing brain disease that results from the prolonged effects of drugs on the brain. He held that behavioural and social-context aspects are part of the condition itself, so the most effective treatment combines biological, behavioural and social-context components.

440.content: The review states that all known addictive drugs activate brain reward regions through sharp rises in dopamine release. With repeated use, dopamine cells come to fire to the cues that signal the drug (places, people, the person's own prior mental state), and these conditioned dopamine surges trigger craving and drug seeking. The authors report that such cue responses can trigger strong craving long after use has stopped, for example after incarceration or treatment.

The authors state that repeated exposure to most drugs adapts the stress circuitry of the extended amygdala (corticotropin-releasing factor, dynorphin), so stress reactivity and negative mood rise when the drug wears off or is withdrawn. The person then takes the drug mainly to get transient relief from this dysphoria, and each binge deepens the dysphoria of the next withdrawal. The circuit-level evidence they cite comes mainly from animal studies.

The authors state that only a minority of people who use drugs become addicted, and estimate that the most severe features develop in about 10% of people exposed to addictive drugs, so long-term exposure is necessary but by no means sufficient. Factors they list as raising vulnerability are family history, exposure in adolescence, socially stressful surroundings with poor family and social support and few behavioural alternatives, easy access to drugs, and other mental health conditions.

441.content: Robinson and Berridge propose that addictive drugs share the ability to enhance mesotelencephalic dopamine transmission, which attributes incentive salience ('wanting') to drug-related stimuli. In some individuals repeated drug use makes this system increasingly, and perhaps permanently, hypersensitive. They propose that this sensitized 'wanting' can grow independently of drug 'liking' and of withdrawal, so compulsive seeking can continue when pleasure and withdrawal have faded and despite loss of reputation, job, home and family.

In the review's section on persistence, the authors report that in rats a single injection of amphetamine, cocaine or morphine produced behavioural sensitization lasting weeks to months, and rats given escalating amphetamine doses were as sensitized a year after the last dose as at 2 to 4 weeks. Sensitization was reported to last over 3 months after cocaine and over 8 months after morphine. They note it was not known whether sensitization of drug 'wanting' lasts as long as sensitization of movement responses.

442.content: Kreek and colleagues review evidence that genetic variation may partly underlie impulsivity, risk taking and stress responsivity, and a substantial proportion of vulnerability to addiction. They propose that these traits may act differently at each stage: starting drug use, regular use, addiction, and relapse.

443.content: A meta-analysis of 12 twin and 5 adoption studies estimated the heritability of being diagnosed with alcohol use disorder at 0.49 (95% CI 0.43 to 0.53), with shared environment accounting for 0.10 (0.03 to 0.16). Estimates did not differ by sex, by design (twin versus adoption) or by assessment method (personal interview versus hospital or population records). The authors read the modest shared-environment share as evidence that environment also contributes to family clustering.

444.content: Hall, Carter and Forlini argue that the brain disease model of addiction promoted by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse since 1997 is not supported by animal and neuroimaging evidence to the extent its advocates suggest, has not delivered more effective treatments, and has had a modest effect on drug policy. They argue its focus on a minority of severely addicted people undermines population-level policies that discourage smoking and heavy drinking.

445.content: Heilig and colleagues summarise animal choice studies: rats extensively trained to self-administer cocaine readily gave up the drug when a sweet solution was offered as an alternative, and the same was later found for heroin, methamphetamine and alcohol. They also cite contingency management, which pays people for abstinence, as evidence that drug use in people with addiction stays sensitive to rewards.
The review cites Spragg's 1940 finding that chimpanzees normally chose a banana over morphine, but when they were physically dependent and in withdrawal their preference reversed to morphine.

The authors report that, over the long term, people with opioid addiction die at about 15 times the rate of the general population, and that among those still alive stable abstinence after 10 to 30 years of observation is under 30%. They state that return to controlled use is rare with opioids, and that outcomes improve markedly when opioid addiction is treated as a chronic relapsing condition with retention in treatment.

The authors acknowledge that brain-centred accounts long gave too little attention to social inputs, and summarise animal findings: in rats, lack of social play early in life raises the motivation to take addictive drugs in adulthood, and the opportunity to interact with another rat reduces addiction-like behaviour. In monkeys, changes in social hierarchy altered dopamine D2 receptor availability and the motivation to obtain cocaine.

446.content: Schuckit reports that alcohol, like benzodiazepines and barbiturates, increases GABA effects and inhibits NMDA glutamate activity; with repeated exposure the brain adapts, and when blood alcohol falls the symptoms are roughly the opposite of the drug's effects (insomnia, anxiety, raised pulse, breathing rate, temperature and blood pressure, hand tremor). About half of people diagnosed with alcohol use disorder have withdrawal symptoms when they cut down or stop, and in 3 to 5% of these grand mal convulsions, delirium or both develop. Symptoms usually begin within 8 hours of falling blood alcohol, peak at about 72 hours and are much reduced by days 5 to 7.

Schuckit reports that about 1 to 4% of hospitalised patients with alcohol withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens, diagnosed by DSM-5 criteria) die, and that timely diagnosis and adequate treatment could lower this rate. Death usually comes from hyperthermia, heart rhythm disturbances, complications of withdrawal seizures or accompanying medical illness. Delirium usually begins about 3 days after withdrawal symptoms start and lasts 1 to 8 days or more; benzodiazepines are the mainstay of treatment, best given in an intensive care unit.

447.content: Petursson describes the symptoms reported in the benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome: sleep disturbance, irritability, tension and anxiety, panic attacks, hand tremor, sweating, nausea, palpitations, headache, muscle pain and perceptual changes, with seizures and psychotic reactions reported mainly after high doses. After normal therapeutic doses three symptom patterns are reported: short rebound anxiety and insomnia within 1 to 4 days, a full withdrawal syndrome usually lasting 10 to 14 days, and a return of the original anxiety. Physical dependence can follow prolonged treatment at therapeutic doses; withdrawal is more severe after high doses or short-acting drugs.

448.content: Brett and Murnion state that anyone who has taken a benzodiazepine for longer than 3 to 4 weeks is likely to have withdrawal symptoms if it is stopped abruptly, and that abrupt cessation after 1 to 6 months of use can bring life-threatening seizures, so the dose should be reduced gradually. Their list of withdrawal features includes grand mal seizures 1 to 12 days after stopping. Gradual withdrawal over at least 10 weeks has been successful in most primary care studies.

449.content: Kosten and Baxter report that after abrupt cessation of short-acting opioids (heroin, hydrocodone, oxycodone) withdrawal usually begins within 12 hours of a missed dose, peaks at 36 to 72 hours and eases over the following 4 to 7 days; methadone withdrawal is milder but may last 2 weeks or more. They trace much of it to the locus coeruleus, whose noradrenaline neurons raise their activity to offset the opioid and overshoot when it is removed. With prolonged use, avoiding withdrawal often becomes the strongest force keeping use going.

The authors state that opioid withdrawal is generally not fatal; death can occur when rehydration is poorly managed, which has happened in criminal justice settings. They stress the high risk of untreated withdrawal from dehydration through vomiting and diarrhoea, and from overdose soon after people drop out of residential treatment, and note that lowered tolerance raises overdose risk when opioids are restarted.

The review reports, from cited studies of patients on long-term opioid analgesics for non-cancer pain, that one study found 45% showed aberrant drug-taking behaviours and another found a lifetime rate of opioid use disorder, as defined by DSM-5, of 35%, while most such patients do not meet the criteria.

450.content: A meta-analysis of six studies from six prison systems (69,093 person-years; 1,033 deaths in the first 12 weeks after release, 612 of them drug-related) found a three- to eightfold increased risk of drug-related death in the first 2 weeks after release compared with weeks 3 to 12, and a pooled relative risk of 1.7 for weeks 3 and 4 compared with weeks 5 to 12. The authors attribute the excess mainly to tolerance lost during imprisonment.

451.content: Ducci and Goldman report weighted mean heritabilities of addictions from large twin cohorts ranging from 0.39 for hallucinogens to 0.72 for cocaine, with alcohol, opioids, nicotine and cannabis in between (their Figure 1). Heritability is usually higher for addiction than for use, but starting use is heritable as well. Specific gene variants found so far account for only a small part of the genetic variance; one nicotinic receptor variant accounts for about 0.5% of the variance in cigarettes smoked per day.

452.content: A meta-analysis of twin studies (28 on starting cannabis use, 24 on problematic use) estimated that genes accounted for 48% of the variance in starting use in males and 40% in females, with shared environment 25% and 39%. For problematic cannabis use, genes accounted for 51% in males and 59% in females, and shared environment 20% and 15%.

453.content: A meta-analysis of six twin studies of starting smoking and ten of persistent smoking estimated heritability of starting at 0.37 in men and 0.55 in women, with shared environment 0.49 and 0.24. For persistence of smoking, heritability was 0.59 in men and 0.46 in women, with shared environment 0.08 and 0.28.

454.content: In 1,196 male twin pairs from the Virginia Twin Registry, interviewed about lifetime use and abuse or dependence (as the authors measured it) of cannabis, cocaine, hallucinogens, sedatives, stimulants and opiates, one common genetic factor strongly influenced use and abuse or dependence for all six classes. Substance-specific genetic factors had a modest influence on use and none was detected for abuse or dependence. The authors conclude that experiences unique to the person largely determine which class a predisposed person uses or misuses.

455.content: In 1951 a postal survey of all UK doctors whose addresses the BMA held gave smoking histories for 34,439 male doctors (two thirds responded); only 17% of them were lifelong non-smokers. In the discussion the authors add that 70% of all UK men born around 1920 were smoking manufactured cigarettes in 1950, at ages 25 to 34.

A high proportion of the doctors who smoked in 1951 stopped during the following decades, after the British medical profession accepted the evidence linking cigarettes to lung cancer. Men born 1900 to 1930 who kept smoking cigarettes died on average about 10 years younger than lifelong non-smokers; stopping at about age 60, 50, 40 or 30 gained about 3, 6, 9 or 10 years of life expectancy.

456.content: Using smoking histories rebuilt from National Health Interview Surveys of 1965 to 2009, the authors estimate that about 80 percent of US men born in 1920 had smoked at least 100 cigarettes by age 30, the highest of any male birth cohort. Male smoking began to decline before 1964, which they suggest may reflect awareness of the early 1950s research linking smoking to lung cancer.

457.content: In five forager populations with full life tables, total fertility rate (births per woman surviving the reproductive years) was 8.2 among the Ache, 6.9 Agta, 6.2 Hadza, 5.5 Hiwi and 4.3 Ju/'hoansi, a forager mean of 6.2. Across 75 small-scale natural-fertility societies the mean was 5.98 (SD 1.40), and only 7 (9 percent) were below 4; of the 11 hunter-gatherers in that sample, two were below 4 (Batak, and Efe at 2.6, which the authors attribute to infertility from sexually transmitted infection). The average interval between births among hunter-gatherers was 3.7 years.

458.content: Across 18 human populations with lifetime data on men's and women's numbers of children, variance in men's reproductive success was higher than women's on average, with the male to female variance ratio ranging from 0.79 (historical Finland) to 4.75 (Dogon, Mali). In the forager populations in the table the ratio was 1.66 among the Aka, 1.77 among the Dobe !Kung, 1.93 among the Hadza and 4.22 among the Ache.

Brown and colleagues found that the ratio of men's to women's variance in reproductive success depends on the marriage system: in the six monogamous populations it was not different from 1 (Pitcairn Islanders' distributions overlap completely), while polygynous populations had higher ratios, and serially monogamous ones (Dobe !Kung, Ache, Pimbwe) resembled polygynous ones. They argue this variation is inconsistent with universal sex roles of the kind Bateman described and that sex roles in humans are better treated as varying with ecology and culture.

459.content: Schacht and Kramer report that although polygynous marriage is permitted in nearly 85 percent of societies in the Standard Cross-Cultural Sample, most marriages within those societies are monogamous. Among Savanna Pume hunter-gatherers of Venezuela, 20 percent of women and 11 percent of men are married polygynously at some point in their lives, and most marriages are monogamous, as in other foraging groups.

Schacht and Kramer summarise genetic estimates of nonpaternity in humans as ranging from 0 to 11 percent across societies, with median values of 1.7 to 3.3 percent, against rates that regularly exceed 20 percent in socially monogamous birds.

The review sets out the dispute over when the human pair bond arose: some researchers read modest body size dimorphism in australopithecines about 4 million years ago as evidence of early monogamy and male provisioning, others read the same fossils as highly dimorphic and place monogamy later, and the fragmentary fossil record may be an unreliable guide to mating systems at all.

Schacht and Kramer review marriage across societies and report that, although most marriages are monogamous at any one time, people often re-enter the marriage market: among hunter-gatherers, industrialising societies and many Western populations, remarriage after a spouse's death or after divorce is common, so that men and women have several partners over their reproductive years. They judge that serial monogamy was probably the norm through human history.

460.content: In 22 natural-fertility societies, mostly tropical foragers, horticulturalists and pastoralists, mean age at menarche ranged from 12.6 to 18.4 years. Age at menarche correlated with age at first reproduction (r = 0.76), and first reproduction followed menarche by four years on average. Menarche age was not related to total fertility or reproductive fitness.

461.content: Among the Dogon of Mali, a natural-fertility farming population with a mean of 8.6 live births per woman, hormone profiles of 93 women and a census of menstrual-hut visits showed that fertile women aged 20 to 34 had a median of only two menses each over two years. The median number of menses per lifetime was about 100, roughly a third of the number for an American woman with three live births.

462.content: Gluckman and Hanson argue that as age at menarche has fallen with better child health, biological maturation now comes well before psychosocial maturation, which they describe as happening for the first time in human evolutionary history. They add that contemporary early puberty should not be medicalised.

463.content: In two studies (3,177 online participants in 10 nations, and a re-analysis of Buss's 1989 data from 8,953 people in 31 nations), the sex differences in mate preferences presumed to have evolutionary roots were smaller in nations with greater gender parity on the Global Gender Gap Index.

464.content: A survey of 67 studies reporting nonpaternity found that for men with high paternity confidence the rate is typically 1.9 percent (excluding studies of unknown method), well below the 10 percent or more often cited. Cross-culturally, men's confidence of paternity goes with more involvement with children and more investment from paternal kin.

465.content: In two nationally representative US surveys (How Couples Meet and Stay Together, 2009 and 2017; 5,421 heterosexual couples), the share of heterosexual couples who met online rose from 2% of couples who met in 1995 to 39% of couples who met in 2017, while meeting through friends fell from 33% to 20%, through family from 15% to 7%, and through coworkers, neighbours, school and church also fell. The authors date the point where meeting online overtook meeting through friends to about 2013.

Among US heterosexual couples who met online, 89% in the 2017 survey had no personal connection before meeting online, and the share brought together online by a friend or other third person fell from 11.2% in the 2009 survey to 3.7% in 2017.

466.content: On one large free US dating site (New York, Boston, Chicago, Seattle, January 2014), attention was very unequal: most users received a handful of first messages at most while a small fraction received far more; the most contacted user, a 30-year-old woman in New York, received 1504 messages in the month. Desirability, measured from who messages whom, formed a clear hierarchy that was consistent across the four cities.

Men and women on the same US dating site mostly wrote to people ranked about 25% more desirable than themselves. Reply rates fell as the gap grew: men were more than twice as likely to get a reply from women less desirable than themselves, and for messages to more desirable women the reply rate never rose above 21%.

467.content: In the US General Social Survey, the share of men aged 18 to 24 who said they had no sexual activity in the past year rose from 18.9% in 2000 to 2002 to 30.9% in 2016 to 2018; among women of that age the change (15.1% to 19.1%) was not significant. Sexual inactivity also rose among men aged 25 to 34 (7.0% to 14.1%) and women aged 25 to 34 (7.0% to 12.6%), and weekly sex fell among married men and women. Men with lower income and part-time or no work were more likely to be sexually inactive.

468.content: In the US National Survey of Family Growth (in-person interviews; 10,590 women aged 15 to 44 in 2013 to 2017), the median age at first menstrual period fell from 12.1 in 1995 to 11.9 in 2013 to 2017, and the share of girls who had reached menarche by each age from 8 to 12 was higher in the later period.

469.content: An expert panel weighed US puberty data from 1940 to 1994. Most panellists judged the data enough to suggest a trend toward earlier breast development and earlier menarche in girls; a minority judged the data on girls insufficient for any marker, and almost all judged the data on boys insufficient to assess a trend.

470.content: From US birth certificates (all births), the average age of first-time mothers rose 3.6 years, from 21.4 in 1970 to 25.0 in 2006. In 2006 the average age at first birth in the selected rich countries compared ranged from 25.0 in the United States to 29.4 in Switzerland; every country shown rose since 1970, by 2.9 years in Sweden up to 4.6 years in Denmark.

471.content: From all US birth records, the mean age of mothers at first birth rose from 26.6 in 2016 to 27.5 in 2023, and rose in every racial and ethnic group and at every level of urbanicity; in 2023 it was 28.5 in large metropolitan counties and 24.8 in the most rural (noncore) counties.

472.content: The GBD 2021 estimates put the global total fertility rate (births per woman) at 4.84 in 1950 and 2.23 in 2021. Fertility fell in every country and territory since 1950, and in 2021 it was above the replacement level of 2.1 in 94 of 204 countries and territories (46.1%), 44 of them in sub-Saharan Africa.

473.content: From census data on European women born 1916 to 1965 (13 countries), the share of women who never had a child fell steeply until about the 1940 birth cohort in both Western and state-socialist Europe, then rose again in the West: in the 1960 cohort it ranged from 10% in Greece and Spain to 20% in Germany. The authors report that women born around 1900 in Northern and Western Europe and Italy had childlessness of up to 25 to 30%, and that the rise in women's education explained only a small part of the later trends.

474.content: In an experiment, women who saw highly attractive women rated their own desirability as a marriage partner lower, while seeing socially dominant women had little effect; for men the pattern reversed, with dominant men lowering men's self-rated desirability as a marriage partner more than attractive men did. The authors read the effect as a change in the perceived pool of competitors.

475.content: A meta-analysis of 77 experimental and correlational studies (141 effect sizes) found small to moderate links between exposure to media images of thin-ideal bodies and women's body dissatisfaction (d = -0.28), internalisation of the thin ideal (d = -0.39) and eating behaviours and beliefs (d = -0.30).

476.content: In a nationally representative sample of US adult internet users (N = 2,075), 1,461 people (about 70%) had viewed pornography at some point and 1,056 (just over half) had used it in the past year. Roughly 11% of men and 3% of women agreed at least somewhat with the statement "I am addicted to pornography".

In the same US national sample, agreeing with "I am addicted to pornography" went with being male, younger, more religious, more morally opposed to one's own pornography use (moral incongruence) and using more pornography. The authors conclude that feeling addicted reflects both how much a person uses and how they judge that use morally.

477.content: Grubbs and colleagues propose a model in which many pornography-related problems, especially feeling addicted, are better understood as a clash between a person's beliefs about pornography and their own use (moral incongruence), and test it with a systematic review and meta-analysis. They note that researchers remain divided on whether internet pornography use is addictive.

478.content: A meta-analysis of 50 studies (more than 50,000 participants, 10 countries) found pornography use associated with lower sexual and relationship satisfaction, in cross-sectional surveys, longitudinal surveys and experiments, with significant results for men only. Pornography use was not related to body satisfaction or self satisfaction.

479.content: In two experiments with US students, viewing centerfold nudes lowered how sexually attractive a nude stranger was rated. In the second experiment the drop appeared only for men shown female nudes, and men who found the centerfolds more pleasant rated themselves as less in love with their wives.

480.content: Three preregistered, high-powered close replications of Kenrick, Gutierres and Goldberg 1989 Study 2 exposed men and women in committed relationships to opposite-sex erotica or abstract art. Pooled with the original in a meta-analysis, they found no support for the original finding that such exposure lowers men's ratings of their partner's sexual attractiveness (original d = 0.91) or their love for the partner (original d = 0.69).

481.content: In a US probability survey of adults aged 18 to 60, most respondents had used pornography at some point. Among women, 21.4% had been choked during sex, 32.3% had had a partner ejaculate on their face and 34.0% had received aggressive fellatio. After adjusting for age, age at first exposure and relationship status, pornography use was significantly associated with these rough sexual behaviours.

482.content: From 1,162 population surveys in 204 countries and territories, 51.9% of all women aged 15 to 49 were using some contraception in 2019 and 47.7% a modern method, up 20.1 percentage points since 1970. Modern method use ranged from 1.9% of women in South Sudan to 87.9% in Norway.

483.content: Using old US state laws that banned the sale of contraceptives (in force until the 1965 Griswold decision) as a natural experiment, Bailey finds that birth rates fell more slowly in states with sales bans after the pill arrived in 1957; by 1965 the gap was about 8 births per 1,000 women of childbearing age. Without the bans, marital fertility would have been 8% lower in those states and 4% lower in the US as a whole. A simple counterfactual attributes about 40% of the fall in US marital fertility from 1955 to 1965 to the pill.

484.content: In Ton'tumsi, a Tsimane village of 57 adult men, peers rated four forms of status: winning fights, getting one's way in group disputes, community-wide influence and respect. The four forms and most of their predictors were held by the same few men; there was little sign of different men holding standing in different domains.

In the same village, men rated as good hunters were rated as more respected (r .47), but skill in food production did not predict community-wide influence once other factors were controlled; influence came mainly from allies and kin support and from market skills such as Spanish and wage work.

485.content: Among the Tsimane, leading a task and holding political standing were different things. Organising a group barbasco fishing trip rotated across households (organisers as young as 8, many of them women, and only 7 of 31 regular households never organised one), and organisers took no more fish than others. The elected village post went to few men: five in one village since 1989, and never a woman.

486.content: Across 21 small-scale populations, wealth inequality depended on how people made a living. Weighted Gini coefficients were 0.25 for hunter-gatherers and 0.27 for horticulturalists, against 0.42 for pastoralists and 0.48 for farmers, where land and livestock can be owned and passed on. The authors compare the forager figure to income Gini in Denmark, Norway and Finland (0.24) and note that pastoral and farming populations were more unequal than the US (income Gini 0.37).

487.content: In hunter-gatherer populations (Ache, Hadza, Tsimane, Lamalera, Meriam, Ju/'hoansi), Gini coefficients for eleven kinds of wealth (hunting and foraging returns, grip strength, body weight, reproductive success, Lamalera boat shares and housing, exchange and sharing partners) mostly fell between 0.2 and 0.5 when body weight is left out; the weighted average was 0.25, and the two material measures (Lamalera boats and housing) averaged 0.36. The authors call this moderate: very low by current world standards, and far from complete equality.

488.content: Using house size as a stand-in for household wealth at 63 archaeological sites, hunter-gatherer sites had a median Gini of 0.17, horticultural sites 0.27 and agricultural sites 0.35. Old World societies later reached about 0.48 to 0.60. The authors set these beside modern wealth Ginis cited from other studies: 0.80 for the USA in 2000 and 0.73 for China.

489.content: In four studies of US participants (college groups such as sororities and ROTC units, a broader national sample, an experiment, and a longitudinal study across graduation), respect and admiration in one's face-to-face groups went with life satisfaction and positive feeling more strongly than income or education did. When a person's standing in their group rose or fell, their well-being rose or fell with it.

490.content: Asked to name a famous person they were fond of, 151 US early adolescents (mean age 14.8) mostly chose actors, singers and athletes, and 61.1% thought of that figure as a relationship partner: girls mostly as a friend, boys more often as a mentor or authority. Those who did reported more involvement and stronger feelings toward the figure.

491.content: In a quota sample of 2,028 Hungarian adults aged 18 to 64, matched to the population by sex, age and region, 800 (39%) said they had a favourite celebrity. On a 7-item admiration scale with a cut-off of 26, the authors estimate that 4.53% of adults and 8.51% of 18 to 34 year olds have a high level of admiration for a celebrity.

492.content: In a survey of 838 people and interviews with 103, age was a strong predictor of interest in celebrity gossip, and media exposure predicted it while social isolation did not. The authors read this as celebrities serving first as models to learn from and, later in life, as people misperceived as part of one's own social network.

493.content: In memory-confusion experiments with University of California, Santa Barbara undergraduates, participants watched a dispute between two teams of mixed race. When team membership was marked by a visible cue that cut across race (shirt colour), participants confused people by team more and by race much less. Categorisation by sex dropped only slightly (effect size 0.91 to 0.84) and stayed stronger than categorisation by team. Less than 4 minutes of exposure was enough.

Kurzban, Tooby and Cosmides argue that ancestral foragers travelled on foot, rarely moved home more than about 40 miles, and so almost never met people from populations genetically distant enough to look like a different race. On this reading the mind has no built-in race category; it tracks alliances, and race is used when it signals alliance.

494.content: In further memory-confusion studies with UC Santa Barbara undergraduates, two groups that cooperated peacefully (for example volunteers of two charities) were enough for participants to sort people into alliances, with no rival or enemy needed and no team colours. When race did not predict who was cooperating with whom, categorisation by race fell, sometimes to zero, while categorisation by sex was unaffected.

495.content: A preregistered replication of Kurzban et al 2001 with 463 US adults on Mechanical Turk, powered at 95%, found that encoding of race fell and encoding of team rose when a visual team cue was added. The drop in race encoding was smaller than in the original, and race was not erased.

496.content: Tajfel and colleagues divided schoolboys into groups on a trivial basis and had them allocate real money between anonymous others. Participants favoured their own group, and the strongest pattern was maximising the difference between ingroup and outgroup even when that cost both groups absolute reward.

497.content: Across experimental studies of cooperation, people cooperated more with ingroup than outgroup members (d = 0.32). The effect was small with bare categorisation and no mutual dependence (dictator games, d = 0.19) and larger when outcomes were interdependent (social dilemmas, d = 0.42), and larger when group membership was common knowledge. The gap came from favouring the ingroup rather than derogating the outgroup.

498.content: In third-party punishment experiments with indigenous groups in Papua New Guinea, observers who could pay to punish a person who broke a sharing norm protected victims from their own group much more than victims from other groups, whatever the violator's group. Violators expected leniency from punishers of their own group, and norm violations were more frequent when punisher and violator shared a group.

499.content: In a game-theoretic model and agent-based simulations, Choi and Bowles find that under conditions they take as typical of late Pleistocene and early Holocene humans, neither altruism toward one's own group nor hostility toward other groups could spread alone, while the two could spread together if hostility produced conflicts that groups with more altruists won.

500.content: In the American National Election Study, the gap between how US partisans rated their own party and the other party on a 0 to 100 feeling thermometer grew from 22.64 degrees in 1978 to 40.87 degrees in 2016. The rise came from colder feelings toward the other party, not warmer feelings toward one's own, and the gap fell slightly between 2012 and 2016.

In US surveys, about 4 to 5% said in 1960 that they would be upset if their child married someone from the other party; by 2010 about one third of Democrats and one half of Republicans said so. Klar and colleagues (2018) found that much of this opposition falls away when the potential spouse is described as rarely talking about politics.

501.content: In 563,312 tweets about gun control, same-sex marriage and climate change, each additional moral-emotional word was associated with about 20% more retweets. The association was stronger for retweets within liberal or conservative networks than between them.

502.content: Burton, Cruz and Hahn re-tested the moral contagion model on six Twitter corpora (for example COVID-19, #MeToo, #MuellerReport). Out-of-sample prediction gave inconsistent results, and with Brady et al's covariates the association held in the #MuellerReport tweets and not in the COVID-19 tweets. A deliberately absurd measure, the count of the letters X, Y and Z, was associated with more sharing in four of six corpora.

503.content: In 2,730,215 Facebook and Twitter posts from US news media and members of Congress, each word referring to the political out-group was associated with about 67% higher odds of a share or retweet (meta-analysed across eight datasets). Words about the political in-group showed no significant association. The out-group association was about 4.8 times that of negative-emotion words and 6.7 times that of moral-emotional words, and out-group words went with "angry" reactions on Facebook.

504.content: In a preregistered field experiment, US Republicans (n = 542) and Democrats (n = 697) who used Twitter were paid to follow for one month a bot retweeting elected officials and opinion leaders of the other side. Treated Republicans became more conservative on a seven-point policy scale (0.12 points in the most cautious estimate, 0.60 for full compliers, 0.11 to 0.59 standard deviations). Treated Democrats became slightly more liberal, not statistically significant.

505.content: At seven US universities with strong football teams in the 1973 season, students wore more school-identifying clothing on the Monday after a win than after a loss or tie. In a phone study, students described a win with "we" nearly twice as often as a loss (26% vs 13.5%). The tendency to claim the link was strongest when the student had just been told they did poorly on a test.

506.content: In two small studies of male fans (8 at a college basketball game, 21 watching a televised World Cup match), mean salivary testosterone rose in fans of the winning team and fell in fans of the losing team.

507.content: Smith argues that evolutionary psychology cannot work as currently understood. To explain a present-day mental mechanism by evolution, one must show that it corresponds to a mechanism selected for in the ancestral environment, that it descends from that mechanism, and that it still has the same function. She calls the task of showing this the matching problem and argues that evolutionary psychology has no means to solve it.

508.content: Egeland and colleagues reply that the matching problem proves too much. The two routes biologists use to support vertical homology in animals are equally open to evolutionary psychology. If evolutionary psychology cannot use them, then neither can animal behaviour research, so the objection would sink well-regarded biology along with it.

Egeland and colleagues reply that a mechanism needs environmental continuity only in its own input conditions. To test a hypothesis about its evolved function, the present environment must contain variation in the cues the mechanism responds to. The rest of the environment can differ completely from the ancestral one. Their worked case: if disgust is tuned to infection risk, people should react more to someone else's blood than to their own, and this can be tested today.

Egeland and colleagues reply with two cases they say meet the evidential standard Smith accepts for the corneal reflex. The amygdala is conserved across mammals, reptiles and birds, works as a fast automatic relevance detector, and lesions impair detection of fitness-relevant information. Disgust has a conserved structure-function mapping (insula), a pathogen-avoidance function, lesion evidence, and automatic processing.

Egeland and colleagues concede that the matching problem points at a real underdetermination: the evidence evolutionary psychologists gather does not prove which of the competing hypotheses is correct. Learned mechanisms such as reading show that design can appear without satisfying the homology condition. They answer that underdetermination affects all sciences and calls for testing rival hypotheses against each other.

Egeland and colleagues charge Narvaez and colleagues with the moralistic fallacy. Narvaez et al. say evolutionary psychology leaves out thriving, which they say natural selection requires. Egeland et al. answer that unless thriving just means differential fitness, it has no bearing on natural selection. Evolution is amoral, so building ideas of the good into it reads values into a fact.

509.content: Heyes argues that distinctively human cognitive mechanisms, such as imitation, mindreading, language and selective social learning, get their adaptive design from cultural evolution. They are built in each lifetime by general learning mechanisms from information supplied by other people, and passed on through social interaction, without genetic programs for them.

Heyes's view implies human nature changes over historical, not geological, time. Humans are not stuck with Stone Age minds: culture keeps building new cognitive mechanisms, and new technologies supply the stimulus for further cultural evolution of the mind.

Heyes limits her own attack: genetic evolution gave humans a starter kit that differs only slightly from that of other apes. It made humans friendlier and more socially motivated, sharpened attention to other people, and expanded general learning and executive control. It did not provide programs for powerful domain-specific mechanisms such as mindreading and language.

What Heyes says would settle it: compare how much usable information the developmental environment supplies. If the environment supplies too little to explain a mechanism's properties (poverty of the stimulus), genes are indicated. If it supplies enough (wealth of the stimulus), learning or culture is indicated. She adds that she looked for evidence of genetic assimilation of gadgets, such as faster learning in natural conditions or greater identical-twin similarity, and did not find it.

510.content: Maung applies Smith's matching problem to evolutionary psychiatry, including mismatch accounts of mental disorder. To support any breakdown, mismatch or persistence hypothesis, one must show that the mechanisms in a disorder resemble ancestral ones, descend from them, and were selected for their effects. For many disorders psychiatry lacks the methods to show this, so these hypotheses are untestable and stay underdetermined by data.

Maung argues the evidence cannot separate adaptationist accounts of disorder from two rivals: disorders as neutral byproducts of evolved structures, and disorders as products of development in the modern environment. He says the developmental account may be more plausible and easier to test, citing higher depression and psychosis rates in cities.

Maung charges evolutionary psychiatry with circular reasoning, which Sleutels calls the Flintstones fallacy. Properties of modern minds are assumed to have belonged to ancient minds, and those assumed ancient properties are then used to explain modern minds, with no independent evidence about the ancient minds.

Maung answers the shared-mechanism defence. Anxiety involves the sympathetic nervous system and depression involves inflammation, both conserved across vertebrates. He replies that a conserved system's involvement in a disorder does not show whether that involvement is a breakdown, a mismatch or a persisting adaptation. That would need evidence that the system acted in the same contexts in our ancestors and was adaptive there, which the missing fossil record and comparative data cannot supply.

511.content: Genome scans show substantial human genetic change in the last 50,000 years, and field studies in many species show selection can shift a trait by one standard deviation in about 25 generations. If humans evolve at comparable rates, significant genetic change could occur within a few hundred years. The adaptive-lag (mismatch) idea rests on gradualism, and this evidence undercuts gradualism.

The idea of stable selection pressures in an environment of evolutionary adaptedness is contradicted by paleoecology and paleoanthropology. The Pleistocene climate was variable and its pattern of variation kept changing, and early Homo, early Homo sapiens and Upper Paleolithic people lived very different lives. There is no single stable ancestral environment to serve as the baseline.

Niche construction theory predicts that humans build environments to suit their adaptations and solve self-made problems through learning and culture, so humans should show much less adaptive lag than evolutionary psychology expects. Large Holocene population growth in culturally built environments is consistent with this.

Brain wiring is too complex to be specified in detail by genes; developmental processes, epigenetic influences and learning in constructed physical and social environments build the mind. The mind is built through constant interplay between the individual and its environment and does not consist of pre-specified programmes.

There is no uniform human genetic programme. Human populations differ genetically partly through recent selection, and gene-culture coevolution has probably shaped selection on the brain, so cognitive biases may differ between populations as well as within them.

Comparative psychology shows domain-general mechanisms exist: associative learning works across many kinds of events in many species, and one learning rule explains hundreds of experiments from honeybees to humans. Most animal data fit a general-process account better than adaptively specialised modules, and massive modularity is not supported by neuroscience.

Instead of asserting whether modern behaviour is adaptive, researchers should measure, trait by trait and population by population, when and to what extent current behaviour is adaptive, using behavioural-ecology optimality models and gene-culture coevolution models where optimality fails.

512.content: All traits, evolved or not, are constructed during individual development from entangled factors such as DNA, epigenetic marks, nutrition and social environment. Human capacities are specified neither by genes nor by environment; they emerge in development. Evolutionary psychology's assumption that evolved traits are prespecified in the genome is inconsistent with current biology.

The Extended Evolutionary Synthesis rejects the idea that Pleistocene selection pressures account for the traits of contemporary humans, given that people today emerged in swiftly changing environments. Organisms construct their environments and development produces the variants selection acts on.

Separating causal factors into genes, which are fixed and formative, and environment, which is variable and supportive, cannot be defended. Gene activity is regulated by systemic factors, many from outside the organism, so genetic and environmental factors cannot be meaningfully partitioned.

Mainstream cognitive science now takes embodied, embedded, extended and enactive accounts seriously, and even the moderate versions reject the Pleistocene-programme computationalism of narrow evolutionary psychology, which treats the brain as a computer running evolved programs on ancestral content.

The evolved developmental niche (soothing perinatal experience, extended breastfeeding, responsive multiple caregivers, affectionate touch, social support, free play in nature with mixed-age peers) has been part of the social mammal line for 20 to 40 million years. It can provide a baseline for species-typical development, so researchers should stop treating people with niche-inconsistent childhoods in industrialised societies as typical of the species.

513.content: Using the 3.9 million SNP HapMap data, the authors find that the age distribution of recently selected variants rules out a constant rate of adaptive evolution. Human adaptive evolution has accelerated in the past 80,000 years, and the recent rate must be ten to a hundred times the long-term rate. The implication for a mismatch account is that the ancestral design may have been revised since the Pleistocene.

If adaptive mutations kept pace with population growth, the Neolithic and later periods saw adaptive evolution more than 100 times faster than most of human evolution. Selection examples named are disease resistance, which became more important with farming epidemics, and diet, such as lactase.

The claim that human genetic evolution slowed once cultural adaptation took over is refuted by the large number of recent adaptive variants. Rapid cultural change in the Late Pleistocene created more opportunities for genetic change.

514.content: The forty-year debate over whether the mind is modular, massively modular or general-purpose is ill-posed. Fodor's modules are defined at the intentional level (what lies outside the control of a central 'you'), while evolutionary psychology's modules are functional-level descriptions of mechanisms by input and output. The two sides use one word for different things, and the question 'how modular is the mind' has no coherent answer until the level is marked.

Framing evolved systems as the inflexible, automatic part of the mind, set against a flexible, deliberating, rational part, is always an intentional-level mistake. At the functional level every process, including slow, deliberate and conscious ones, is produced by evolved mechanisms, so evolution cannot be opposed to flexibility.

Because 'modularity' has caused so much confusion, nobody should use the term unmarked. Encapsulation- or automaticity-based modules should be called intentional modules and mechanisms defined by function should be called functional modules. Evolutionary psychologists should drop the term and speak of functional mechanisms or systems.

515.content: Gould and Lewontin argue that the adaptationist programme cannot be refuted in practice: when one adaptive story fails it is replaced by another, and when none is available the researcher pleads temporary ignorance. Because a new adaptive story can always be invented, failing a test never leads to considering a non-adaptive explanation.

The authors say evolutionists often accept an adaptive explanation once it is consistent with natural selection and plausible. Plausibility is no test, because plausible stories can always be told; the task is to find criteria that pick the right explanation among many plausible pathways.

The paper lists alternatives to adaptation (genetic drift, developmental by-products, multiple adaptive peaks, later use of parts that arose for other reasons) and says a good fit between organism and environment does not by itself show that natural selection produced it. Present use of a trait says nothing about why it exists.

Gould and Lewontin say they would object much less if an adaptive explanation could, in a given case, be rejected for lack of evidence after failing an explicit test, so that alternatives get a chance.

516.content: Buller argues the adaptive problems that shaped the human mind cannot be specified. Stated abstractly they say nothing about psychology; stated precisely they are speculation, because the fossil record says little about ancestral social life and living hunter-gatherer groups vary too much to stand in for ancestors.

Buller says the claim that modern humans carry a Pleistocene-adapted mind ignores how fast selection can act. Selection has altered life-history traits within about 18 generations in studied populations, and agriculture and industry changed selection pressures on human psychology since the Pleistocene.

Buller argues that even with little genetic change since the Pleistocene, psychological traits develop through gene-environment interaction, so the same genes in new environments can produce different psychological traits. There is therefore no good reason to assume all evolved psychological characteristics stay adapted to forager life.

In his closing section Buller says the evidence needed to support specific accounts of human psychological adaptation over the last couple of million years is scarce and probably lost for good, so much about the evolution of the mind can only be speculated on.

517.content: Buller argues that the main evidence for three celebrated evolutionary psychology findings (cheater detection, a sex difference in jealousy, and greater abuse of stepchildren) does not establish them, and that this failure comes from the framework itself: reverse engineering the mind from the Pleistocene, assuming massive modularity, and assuming a universal human nature.

Buller argues that the two main results cited for a cheater-detection module in Wason selection tasks are also explained by a mind that applies general logical principles, because social-contract rules have a different logical form from plain indicative conditionals.

518.content: Foley says the hunter-gatherer lifestyle has in practice been assumed to be the human EEA, with departures from it treated as leading to maladaptation. His chronology of hominin social evolution shows the EEA is not a single environment: different traits arose at different times over some 35 million years, with different mechanisms.

Foley says hunting and gathering is only one part of the human evolutionary environment, and that later conditions, including denser settled agricultural communities, may be significant parts of human evolutionary history rather than mere aberrations.

519.content: Foley says the EEA is a new concept that needs scrutiny for its usefulness, and that reconstructions of ancestral human environments must rest on sound palaeobiological inference and the phylogenetic context of primate evolution.

520.content: Kendler argues that sorting psychiatric conditions into organic (a visible brain finding) and functional (no visible finding) is a leftover of nineteenth-century neuropathology and Cartesian dualism. Whether a change shows up in a scan, under an electron microscope, or only as altered physiology is a fact about current technology, not about the kind of condition.

Kendler tests whether individual cases of major depression can be sorted into psychogenic (reactive, situational) and biological forms. They cannot: cases with a clear adverse trigger carry the same familial or genetic risk as cases without one, and genetic and environmental risks are positively and developmentally intertwined.

Kendler reports that for schizophrenia, major depression and alcohol dependence, causes are spread across biological, psychological and social-cultural levels, and causes at one level often act through and modify causes at other levels. Psychiatric disorders do not sort into hardware and software problems.

521.content: RDoC treats psychopathology as deviation along normal-to-abnormal dimensions of basic functional systems, each implemented by an identified brain circuit, and asks what accounts for dysregulation or dysfunction in those systems.
Cuthbert says that if psychiatry is ever to have a neuroscience-based diagnostic system, complex symptoms will have to be explained as dysregulation in basic brain operations.
Cuthbert names the central task of RDoC as establishing mechanisms by which disruptions in one or more functional constructs produce specific symptoms or impairments.

522.content: Under active inference, mood is a hyperprior: the brain's long-run expectation about how predictable the consequences of its actions are. Depression is the brain predicting with high confidence that outcomes will be uncertain and uncontrollable, which yields a chronic negative state that maintains itself and resists revision by new evidence.

The authors propose that hyperpriors may be genetically encoded or changed by chronic intense stress, after which neuromodulator set-points lock into an aberrant tonic drive that no longer responds to error signals, producing a self-reinforcing loop of action and perception.

The authors argue that if mood disorders are computational pathologies, the same faulty computation can arise from different neuromodulator faults in different patients, which may explain treatment resistance and the failure to find a consistent biomarker. They propose replacing the search for a biomarker with a computational signature.

The authors say their account predicts that a volatile environment with persistently large prediction errors should lower mood by lowering estimated precision, and that this could be tested with a mood-induction paradigm built on experimentally induced prediction errors.

523.content: LeDoux describes defensive survival circuits as present in all complex animals, with core components highly conserved across vertebrates. He also says invertebrates do not have the same conserved circuits as vertebrates, and that comparative work on non-mammalian vertebrates is still a pressing need.

The amygdala nuclei that handle learned threats in rats work similarly in rabbits and non-human primates. LeDoux cites evidence for homologous amygdala circuitry in reptiles and birds, and human imaging and lesion results show the amygdala has a key role in defense conditioning in humans too.

524.content: Developmental gene expression, connections and neurochemistry show that the amygdala of reptiles, birds and mammals shares one basic plan, and frogs (anuran amphibians) have most of the same parts. The authors conclude a basic amygdala was present at least in the ancestral tetrapods.

In ray-finned fish the region matching the pallial amygdala (part of the teleost pallium) is involved in emotional learning, so the authors suggest the amygdala area used in emotional memory evolved before the first amphibians. Fish lack a vomeronasal amygdala.

525.content: In goldfish, removing the medial pallium (the proposed homologue of the mammalian pallial amygdala) impaired retention of a learned avoidance response, much as amygdala lesions do in mammals. The authors note that ray-finned fishes and land vertebrates share a common ancestor that lived some 400 million years ago.

526.content: Tract tracing, immunohistochemistry and in situ hybridisation in 32 adult river lampreys found a midbrain cell group with the location, inputs (pallium, hypothalamus, raphe, substantia nigra) and outputs (pretectum, substantia nigra) of the mammalian periaqueductal gray, the command centre for freezing, flight and defensive fighting. The authors conclude a PAG homologue was present very early in vertebrate evolution.

527.content: The lamprey griseum centrale has practically the same connections as the zebrafish griseum centrale and the mammalian PAG. The mammalian PAG also receives input from the amygdala, which has not yet been identified in the lamprey; homologous areas have been suggested in zebrafish.

In lamprey, dopamine neurons in a caudal diencephalic nucleus (the lamprey substantia nigra pars compacta) most likely share their developmental origin with the SNc and VTA of amniotes. Their connections are practically identical to those of the mammalian SNc, they burst in response to salient stimuli as in mammals, and a lateral habenula circuit that evaluates action outcomes and controls dopamine neurons is conserved across vertebrates.
In the lamprey striatum no strict division into dorsal and ventral striatum can be made; it may be more like the dorsal striatum of mammals.

528.content: The basic circuit diagram of the basal ganglia is virtually identical in lamprey and mammals, including the dopamine neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta projecting to the striatum and to downstream motor centres. The authors place the split of the lamprey and mammal lines about 500 million years ago.

529.content: Teleost fish and lampreys have no midbrain dopamine cells; their dopamine neurons sit in the posterior tuberculum of the diencephalon, and it is uncertain whether these are homologous to the mammalian SNc and VTA. The authors judge the role of dopamine in basal ganglia motor control likely conserved in tetrapods.

The mesolimbic pathway (midbrain dopamine to the nucleus accumbens, critical for reward behaviour) is less clearly conserved than the motor pathway. Amphibians have midbrain dopamine input to a proposed accumbens, but its receptor distribution is unknown, and the D3 receptor pattern of the mammalian accumbens is not seen in birds.

530.content: Panksepp says the evidence shows that all mammals have positive and negative emotional networks, including SEEKING, RAGE and FEAR, in homologous subcortical brain regions. He dates them only by clade (all mammals) and calls them ancient; the paper gives no figure in millions of years.

Panksepp reviews brain stimulation studies in which electrical stimulation of specific subcortical sites evokes the same seven kinds of emotional arousal, PANIC/GRIEF (separation distress) among them, in every mammal species tested so far. He states that these subcortical structures are homologous across the mammals that have been tested.

531.content: Panksepp says primary-process emotional systems sit in subcortical regions that are anatomically, neurochemically and functionally homologous in all mammals studied.
Panksepp dates the GRIEF (separation distress) system to well over a hundred million years ago, citing a homologous system in birds.

532.content: Mammals and fruit flies build their clocks from orthologous proteins (CLOCK with CYCLE or BMAL1, and PERIOD), so a similar basic clock mechanism was present in their common ancestor, before insects and mammals separated more than 500 million years ago.

No relationship has been found between the key clock proteins of cyanobacteria and those of mammals, so circadian rhythms have probably arisen at least twice, once in an ancestor of cyanobacteria and again in an ancestor of animals (plants may be a third origin).

533.content: The sea anemone Nematostella vectensis has orthologs of Clock and Cycle whose proteins pair up as in mammals and insects, light-responsive cryptochromes, and E-box motifs near rhythmically expressed genes. Core clock parts were therefore in place in the last common ancestor of cnidarians and bilaterians. Nematostella has no Period ortholog.

534.content: A phylogenetic and molecular-clock analysis of about 70 prokaryote genomes dates the cyanobacterial clock genes separately. The double-domain kaiC formed about 3,500 to 3,800 million years ago, kaiB and the kaiBC pair arose between about 2,320 and 3,500 million years ago, and kaiA, which the Synechococcus clock needs along with the other two, is the youngest, estimated at 944 and 1,051 million years ago by two methods. The three-gene cluster therefore dates to about 1,000 million years ago.

535.content: Beginning around two million years ago, human ancestors moved from a fairly sedentary ape-like life to hunting and gathering, which needed more physical activity than earlier hominins had. The authors argue that human physiology evolved under high daily aerobic activity, so our reliance on exercise for health upkeep is likely a legacy of that shift.

536.content: Circulating endocannabinoids rose after high-intensity treadmill running in humans and dogs (a running-adapted mammal), but not after slow walking, and not in ferrets (a non-running mammal) at any intensity. The authors suggest a brain reward for endurance exercise helps explain why humans and other running-adapted mammals exercise habitually.

537.content: Leptin has been found in all vertebrate groups examined. Injected leptin reduces food intake in goldfish, rainbow trout, grass carp, Atlantic salmon and striped bass, as it does in mammals.

Teleost leptins share several regulatory effects with mammalian leptin, but current evidence suggests leptin does not act as a fat-store signal (adipostat) in teleosts. Teleost leptin is mostly made in the liver, not fat, and fasting often raises it rather than lowering it as in mammals.

538.content: River lamprey has two melanocortin receptors, one orthologous to MC1 and one to MC4, the receptor that regulates food intake in mammals, teleost fish and probably birds. Neither lamprey receptor was found in the brain, while sharks and teleosts express melanocortin receptors centrally. The authors suggest the brain functions of melanocortin receptors arose after jawless vertebrates split off and before the jawed vertebrates diversified. They cite 564 (molecular) and 525 (fossil) million years for the jawless split.

539.content: Doubly labelled water measurements in 141 humans, 27 chimpanzees, 8 bonobos, 10 gorillas and 11 orangutans showed that, controlling for body size and activity, human daily energy expenditure exceeded that of chimpanzees and bonobos, gorillas and orangutans by about 400, 635 and 820 kcal per day. Humans also had the highest body fat percentage. The authors conclude the human line evolved a faster metabolism.

540.content: Comparing the genomes of 35 vertebrate species and 4 invertebrate outgroups, the authors find the vasotocin (vasopressin) gene in all vertebrates and a structurally similar gene in three of the four invertebrate relatives, while oxytocin is a tandem duplicate of vasotocin that arose after jawed vertebrates split from lampreys and hagfish.

The receptor analysis supports a single vasotocin receptor gene shared with an invertebrate ancestor, represented today in the sea squirt, which later duplicated into the vertebrate receptor families.

541.content: In African elephants, gelada and hamadryas baboons, each layer of the multi-level society is about 3 times the size of the layer below, close to the ratio reported for human social networks; in orcas the ratio is 3.8. The authors leave the origin of this layered pattern open.

542.content: Dunbar reviews the layered human network (about 5, 15, 50, 150 and beyond) and reports that mammals living in multi-level societies, mainly baboons, chimpanzees, elephants and dolphins, show the same inner layers, but stable animal groups stop at the 50 layer. Only humans add the 150 layer and the layers beyond it.

543.content: The review describes the maternal care circuit worked out in rats: pregnancy hormones prime the medial preoptic area, which at birth switches pup stimuli from aversive to attractive and drives the dopamine pathway from the ventral tegmental area to the nucleus accumbens, with oxytocin and prolactin acting on it. The authors conclude that human parenting shares many of these subcortical mechanisms, with more cortical control added in humans.

The same hormone and brain systems that drive maternal care are shaped in the infant by the care it receives, so parenting and attachment styles pass to the next generation without genetic change; the authors report this in rodents and parallel findings in humans.

544.content: Lactation is part of the life history of all living mammals: monotremes, marsupials and placentals. Oftedal argues that milk began as a skin-gland secretion in synapsids perhaps about 310 million years ago, and that by about 210 million years ago small, fast-growing mammal ancestors already depended on milk.

545.content: Using his five criteria for play, Burghardt lists play-like behaviour well outside mammals and birds: Nile softshell turtles batting balls, juvenile red-bellied cooters in play-fight-like courtship, monitor lizards, a saltwater crocodile, dart poison frogs in rough-and-tumble play, cichlid and mormyrid fish, stingrays, octopuses, wasps and spiders.
Every nonhuman primate species plays in all three ways (locomotor, object and social play) as juveniles, which is why comparative tests of play origins inside primates are hard.

546.content: The leading play researchers state that play is a mixed category that seems to have evolved independently several times, in animals whose nervous systems are organised differently, so there is no single neural mechanism of play across animals.

The same review lists as an open question whether rough-and-tumble play (play fighting) shares common mechanisms across mammals such as rodents, canids, cetaceans, bears and primates, and whether these extend to birds.

547.content: An overview of original observations, published reports and anecdotes describes locomotor, object and social play in crocodilians, including social play with other crocodilians and with mammals.

548.content: A phylogenetically controlled comparison of play across 15 mammalian orders found play in marsupials, rodents and primates, with larger-brained orders having more playful species; within orders the brain size link weakened or vanished.

549.content: In the same food-giving test run on 24 groups of 15 primate species including humans, the extent of allomaternal care (care of infants by individuals other than the mother) was by far the best predictor of how readily a species helps others unasked. Humans fit the general primate pattern.

Among the apes only humans became cooperative breeders, perhaps after moving into savannah habitats; in the authors' scenario shared childcare added a proactive helping motive convergently, as in other primate lineages that breed cooperatively such as marmosets and tamarins.

550.content: The authors weigh three possible starting points for the human package of helpless newborns, big slow-growing brains and fast reproduction (bipedality, selection for early birth, a better diet) against cooperative breeding, and conclude that extensive allomaternal care came first: only help from others lets mothers wean early and reproduce fast while raising slow, big-brained young.

The review places the setting for cooperative breeding in early Homo about 2 million years ago, living in arid savannas with strongly seasonal food, in large mixed-sex groups with shared defence and food sharing.

In the same account, body size dimorphism between the sexes in early Homo was reduced relative to earlier hominins such as Australopithecus afarensis, which the authors tie to male cooperation, food sharing and the start of a sexual division of labour.

551.content: Sea lampreys, a jawless vertebrate, already have the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis: three hypothalamic GnRH peptides and GnRH receptors acting on the pituitary and gonads. The authors treat the lamprey as showing the reproductive hormone system of the first vertebrates, whose lineage they date to over 550 million years.

552.content: Pair bonding is rare in fish, amphibians and reptiles, common in birds, and found in 9% of mammal species. In the prairie vole the pair bond runs on oxytocin, vasopressin and dopamine acting on circuits for individual recognition, social reward, territory and maternal care, which the authors propose were re-tuned into a pair bond.

553.content: Classifying 2,543 mammal species and reconstructing their history on a mammal supertree, the authors find that the ancestral state for all non-human mammal groups is solitary females, and that social monogamy arose about 60 separate times, from solitary ancestors where females lived far apart.

Of the classified species, 68% were solitary, 9% socially monogamous, 5% in unstable groups and 17% in stable groups; social monogamy is more common in primates (29%) and carnivores (16%) than in rodents (6%).

554.content: Using the Lucy skeleton and the A.L. 333 fossil assemblage, with simulations on humans, chimpanzees and gorillas, the authors estimate that skeletal size dimorphism in Australopithecus afarensis was most similar to that of modern humans, which they read as raising the probability that the species was mainly monogamous.

555.content: Using two new resampling methods on eight limb-bone measurements, the authors find postcranial size dimorphism in Australopithecus afarensis similar to gorillas and orangutans and significantly greater than in modern humans and chimpanzees, suggesting its mating strategy differed from that of modern humans.

556.content: Plavcan reviews dimorphism across primates and finds the causes of human size dimorphism uncertain; a phylogenetic reconstruction including fossil hominins shows the modern human condition is derived, so some similarities with chimpanzees may have arisen independently.

557.content: Unmyelinated low-threshold touch fibres (C-LTMRs) in hairy skin were first recorded in other mammals in 1939; the studies cited are in cats and monkeys. Humans were long assumed to lack them until microneurography found them in the face, arm and leg, where they are called C-tactile (CT) afferents; their response properties so far look similar across species.

558.content: In mice, a rare set of unmyelinated sensory neurons marked by the receptor MRGPRB4 innervates only hairy skin, responds to massage-like stroking of the back but not to pinching, and its chemogenetic activation makes mice prefer the place where it happened, suggesting the stroking signal is rewarding.

559.content: In the African cichlid fish Astatotilapia burtoni, males switch rapidly and reversibly between dominant and subordinate states depending on the social setting. A subordinate male given a chance to rise changes colour and behaviour within minutes, and within 20 minutes a gene switch (egr-1) turns on in the brain cells that run the reproductive axis; social descent produces fleeing and loss of colour within minutes.

The review states that social behaviour in vertebrates is run by conserved brain networks. The social behaviour network (lateral septum, medial amygdala and bed nucleus of the stria terminalis, preoptic area, anterior and ventromedial hypothalamus, midbrain periaqueductal grey) was first described in mammals, and homologous regions have been found in reptiles, fish and birds. In the cichlid, a chance to rise in rank switches on genes across all six nodes of this network.

560.content: Long-term studies of wild social mammals show that social integration and, to a lesser extent, social status predict life span in at least four mammalian orders. The link between status and survival has been tested in at least 12 species including humans (among them wild rabbits, meerkats, baboons, rhesus and long-tailed macaques), and these species represent several separate transitions from solitary to social living.

561.content: In crayfish, injecting serotonin into subordinate animals made them willing to fight the dominants again, mainly by lowering the chance that they retreat and lengthening fights.

562.content: Laubach and colleagues state that rodent prefrontal cortex is agranular in most species and that cytoarchitecture supports homologies among medial frontal areas, especially the anterior cingulate cortex, in rodents, monkeys and humans. The granular lateral prefrontal areas that dominate human research do not exist in rodents.

563.content: In fruit flies (Drosophila), three days of repeated vibration stress reduced voluntary activity; the state was reversed by lithium and by raising serotonin signalling to the mushroom bodies.

564.content: Innate immune pattern-recognition receptors, including Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors and scavenger receptors, are found throughout the animal kingdom; some invertebrates such as the sea urchin, and many plants, have greatly expanded families of these receptors.

The antibody, T cell receptor and MHC based adaptive immune system is first found in cartilaginous fish and is thought to have arisen in the first jawed vertebrates; complete RAG genes occur in every jawed vertebrate studied and not in jawless fish. The system has been remarkably uniform over 500 million years.

Lampreys and hagfish have their own adaptive immune system built on variable lymphocyte receptors assembled from leucine-rich repeat modules; these genes show no structural similarity to antibodies or T cell receptors and do not use RAG. The authors conclude that jawed and jawless vertebrates developed their antigen receptors independently, while B-like and T-like lymphocyte lineages probably already existed in the common ancestor of all vertebrates.

565.content: A meta-analysis of 48 social groups from 22 primate species in 12 genera found that female primates groom most those group mates that groom them most (weighted average r = 0.583), and the effect held after controlling for maternal kinship (r = 0.468). The authors read this as a general pattern across the primate order, and note similar exchanges in coatis.

566.content: In an experiment, dominant chimpanzees punished individuals who stole their own food but did not punish thieves who stole from third parties, even related ones. The authors suggest that third-party punishment to enforce cooperation may be a trait derived in the human lineage.

567.content: This theme-issue overview reviews parasite avoidance behaviour across animals, from the nematode C. elegans and social insects to aquatic animals, birds and mammals including rodents, ruminants, primates and humans. The authors note that parasite avoidance is a task every living thing must solve, so commonalities across animals are expected; they argue the word disgust can be used for animal parasite avoidance as fear is for predator avoidance, while noting that whether animal avoidance is continuous with human disgust has long been debated.

Primates avoid contaminated food: bonobos given food contaminated with conspecific faeces balance their feeding to reduce infection risk using several senses, and free-ranging macaques that kept away from food contaminated with faeces and soil had fewer gut parasites; chimpanzees and mandrills also use sight, smell or touch to avoid contaminants or parasitized group mates.

568.content: Benton and colleagues give fossil-based age limits for 88 nodes of the animal tree, from the origin of animals to the split of modern humans and Neanderthals. For each node they name the oldest fossil that securely belongs to the living group (this sets a hard minimum age) and the oldest rich fossil beds that lack the group (this sets a soft maximum age). The true split lies above the minimum and probably below the soft maximum.

Crown animals and crown bilaterians (the last common ancestor of protostomes and deuterostomes, which includes humans and insects) have a fossil minimum of 550.25 million years, set by the Ediacaran fossil Kimberella, read as a bilaterian, from the White Sea biota dated to about 552.85 million years. The soft maximum is 636.1 million years for bilaterians (Lantian biota) and 833 million years for all animals (Bitter Springs Formation).

Crown vertebrates (the last common ancestor of lampreys and hagfishes on one side and jawed vertebrates including humans on the other) have a fossil minimum of 457.5 million years, set by the armoured jawless fish Arandaspis from the Stairway Sandstone of Australia. The soft maximum is 636.1 million years. The authors keep the maximum wide because early Cambrian soft-bodied fossils such as Haikouichthys and Myllokunmingia from Chengjiang may be early vertebrates; they judged that evidence too weak to set the minimum.

Crown jawed vertebrates (the human-shark split) and crown bony vertebrates (the human-zebrafish split, ray-finned versus lobe-finned fishes) share a fossil minimum of 420.7 million years, set by the lobe-finned fish Guiyu oneiros from the Kuanti Formation of Yunnan, China. Soft maxima are 468.4 million years for jawed vertebrates and 444.9 million years for bony vertebrates.

Crown tetrapods (amphibians versus the line to reptiles, birds and mammals) have a fossil minimum of 337 million years and a soft maximum of 351 million years. Crown amniotes (the bird-mammal split, that is, humans versus reptiles and birds) have a minimum of 318 million years, from the Joggins Formation of Nova Scotia, and a soft maximum of 332.9 million years. The authors note the bird-mammal split has often been given as 310 to 315 million years and the 2012 timescale makes it older.

Crown mammals (humans versus the platypus and echidnas) have a fossil minimum of 164.9 million years, from the Middle Jurassic Ambondro of Madagascar, and a soft maximum of 201.5 million years. Crown therians (marsupials versus placentals) have a minimum of 156.3 million years from the eutherian Juramaia of China and a soft maximum of 169.6 million years. Crown placentals have a minimum of 61.6 million years (earliest Paleocene, Ravenscrag Formation) and a soft maximum of 164.6 million years.

Crown primates have a fossil minimum of 56 million years (Altiatlasius, latest Paleocene, Morocco) and a soft maximum of 66 million years. Crown catarrhines (Old World monkeys versus apes) have a minimum of 24.44 million years (Rukwapithecus, Tanzania) and a soft maximum of 34.0 million years. Crown hominoids (humans versus gibbons) and crown great apes (humans versus orangutans) both have a minimum of 11.6 million years, set by the orangutan-line ape Sivapithecus from the Chinji Formation of Pakistan, and a soft maximum of 33.9 million years. Gibbons have no definite fossil record before the Pleistocene, so the gibbon split takes the same minimum as the orangutan split.

The human-chimpanzee split has a fossil minimum of 6.5 million years, set by the skull of Sahelanthropus tchadensis from Chad, accepted by the authors as an early hominin, with an indirect biostratigraphic age of about 7.5 to 6.5 million years. The soft maximum is 10 million years, from late Miocene ape sites with no chimpanzee or human line fossils. The authors note that early molecular studies put the split near 5 million years and some as recent as 2.7 million years.
