About 24 percent of the whales had major to extreme wear of the lower-jaw tooth crowns, more than 60 percent of lower teeth 2 and 3 were fractured, and more than 61 percent of those teeth had been drilled (bore holes). Four of the five whales with the highest age-adjusted damage scores were captive-born. The authors attribute the damage largely to oral stereotypies, the whales biting and chewing concrete tank surfaces and steel gates; the study scored photographs and did not observe or count that behaviour.

820.content: A database of official reports, local media articles and private communications, compiled by authors who conclude that keeping killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) in oceanaria is ethically indefensible, counts 29 of the 65 killer whales owned by SeaWorld since 1964 (45 percent) as involved in one or more published aggressive incidents. A small number of whales account for most incidents and about 55 percent have none on record. The paper also describes the authors' own unstructured contact with juvenile killer whales at SeaWorld San Diego in 1979 and 1980. It gives no rate for wild killer whales to compare with.

821.content: In two populations of resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) off British Columbia and Washington State, yearly census records from 1973 to 2016 for 378 whales with a known maternal grandmother (4,578 whale-years, 123 deaths) show that a whale whose maternal grandmother had died within the previous two years had a mortality hazard 4.5 times that of a whale with a living grandmother, at average salmon abundance. Where the grandmother who died had stopped reproducing, the hazard rose by a further factor of 1.5, to 6.7 in total. The benefit of a living grandmother showed in years of low to moderate salmon abundance. The model also carried a term for a mother's death in the previous two years, which applied to sons only.

822.content: Using multigenerational records for two populations of killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca), the authors report that mothers who have stopped reproducing increase the survival of their offspring, most of all their older sons. The abstract gives no figures.

823.content: In the southern resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca), a closed population of 71 to 98 animals censused yearly from 1976 to 2010, a male's position in the social network was tied to his survival: males in the most central positions had about one third of the mortality risk of the least central males (hazard ratio 0.33 for community closeness, 41 male deaths), and the link held only in years of low salmon abundance. For females, social position was unrelated to survival (hazard ratio 1.06, 40 deaths). The authors suggest that well-connected males have better access to shared food and to information when salmon is scarce.

824.content: Using a towed hydrophone array and visual tracking of photo-identified animals, the authors assigned calls to single free-ranging resident killer whales (orcas, Orcinus orca) that were more than 35 m from the other members of their matrilineal group and out of sight of them. Focal whales gave 36 percent of their calls within 5 seconds of a call from another group member, four times more than expected by chance, and consecutive calls by different whales matched in call type more often than chance. The authors say the function of these matched exchanges remains to be explored.

825.content: A Cochrane review pooled 15 randomised trials of a single session of psychological debriefing given within one month of an event (road accidents, burns, assaults, miscarriage, childbirth, soldiers on a peacekeeping mission; most trials in the United Kingdom, Ireland and Australia). Compared with no intervention, people who were debriefed were no less often diagnosed with PTSD at up to 3 months (Peto odds ratio 0.58, 95% CI 0.10 to 3.26, 1 trial, 40 people), at 3 to 6 months (1.17, 0.70 to 1.98, 3 trials, 278 people) or at 6 to 12 months (0.93, 0.35 to 2.46, 1 trial, 105 people). Self-reported symptom scores did not differ at 1 to 4 months (SMD 0.11, 95% CI -0.10 to 0.32, 5 trials, 356 people) and were slightly worse in the debriefed at 6 to 13 months (SMD 0.26, 0.01 to 0.50, 3 trials, 265 people). The authors found no benefit on scores for low mood, anxiety or general functioning either.

In the same review, the one trial that measured diagnosis at 12 months or more (133 burn patients, assessed at 13 months) found more debriefed people diagnosed with PTSD than controls (Peto odds ratio 2.51, 95% CI 1.24 to 5.09). The two trials with the longest follow-up, the burn trial at 13 months and a road accident trial at 3 years, both reported worse outcomes in the debriefed. The authors add that in the burn trial the debriefed group started with larger burns and more perceived threat to life, and that more people were lost to follow-up in one arm than the other, so they call the exact size of the adverse effect open to question.

The review authors conclude that compulsory debriefing should cease and that routine single-session debriefing after individual trauma cannot be recommended in military or civilian life. They offer explanations they did not test: one session makes the person go through the event again without time for the distress to subside, it may turn ordinary distress into a medical matter and raise the expectation of symptoms, and trying to forget or keep one's distance may be an adaptive response that the session interferes with. They also suggest that family and friends may already give people an informal version of the same thing, which would leave a formal session little to add.

826.content: Three-year follow-up of a randomised trial in Oxford: 106 people admitted to hospital after a road traffic accident were allocated to about one hour of psychological debriefing, mostly within 24 to 48 hours, or to no intervention, and 61 of them (30 debriefed, 31 controls) answered at 3 years. The debriefed group scored worse at 3 years on general psychiatric symptoms (Brief Symptom Inventory, difference 0.08, 95% CI 0.009 to 0.15), enjoyment of travel as a passenger, pain, physical recovery, everyday functioning and financial problems. Intrusion and avoidance scores on the Impact of Event Scale did not differ between the groups overall (F(1,58) = 2.03, P = 0.16).

In the same trial the result differed by how people scored at the start. Among those in the top quarter of initial Impact of Event Scale scores (24 or above, about 17 people), the debriefed still scored high at 3 years (mean 25.9) while the controls had dropped to 11.8, the level of people who started low (t(14) = 2.56, P = 0.023). The gap was already present at 4 months. The debriefed high scorers had more severe injuries, and the difference stayed at least marginally significant after adjusting for injury severity (all P below 0.07).

827.content: Abstract only. 133 adult burn patients were randomly allocated to one session of individual or couple psychological debriefing or to no intervention, and 110 (83%) were interviewed 3 and 13 months later by an assessor who did not know the allocation. At 13 months 16 of the debriefed (26%) and 4 of the controls (9%) were diagnosed with PTSD. The authors report that the debriefed group had higher questionnaire scores at the start and more severe burns, and both went with a worse outcome.

828.content: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 114 randomised trials with 8,171 adults, at least 70 percent of whom in each trial were diagnosed with PTSD lasting 3 months or more. Against waiting list or usual care, trauma-focused cognitive behavioural therapy lowered post-treatment symptom scores by a pooled SMD of -1.32 (95% CI -1.57 to -1.08, 51 comparisons, evidence rated moderate quality), prolonged exposure by -1.59 (-2.05 to -1.13, 12 comparisons), cognitive therapy by -1.33 (4 comparisons), cognitive processing therapy by -1.03 (4 comparisons) and EMDR by -1.23 (-1.69 to -0.76, 11 comparisons). The authors call the evidence for trauma-focused CBT and EMDR robust and recommend them as first-line treatments.

In the same review, treatments without a trauma focus and a guided internet version also beat waiting list or usual care on post-treatment symptom scores: CBT without a trauma focus (SMD -1.06, 95% CI -1.39 to -0.73, 7 comparisons), present-centred therapy (-0.97, -1.33 to -0.62, 2 comparisons) and guided internet-based trauma-focused CBT (-1.08, -1.80 to -0.37, 3 comparisons, 145 people). Supportive counselling (-0.43, -0.90 to 0.04, 2 comparisons), psychodynamic therapy and relaxation training showed no clear benefit over waiting list, and trauma-focused CBT did better than supportive counselling head to head (-0.63, -1.04 to -0.21, 8 comparisons). The authors note that supportive counselling was often run as a control in which talking about the event was barred, that a funnel plot points to publication bias in the main comparison, and that most trials left out people with substance dependence, psychosis diagnoses or severe depression scores.

829.content: Network meta-analysis done for the NICE guideline on PTSD: 90 randomised trials, 6,560 adults with a PTSD diagnosis or clinically important symptoms, 22 interventions, evidence rated moderate to low quality by the authors. Against waiting list, the drop in symptom scores at the end of treatment was largest for EMDR (SMD -2.07, 95% credible interval -2.70 to -1.44), trauma-focused CBT (-1.46, -1.87 to -1.05) and self-help with support (-1.46, -2.33 to -0.59), followed by CBT without a trauma focus (-1.22, -1.95 to -0.49), self-help without support (-0.91, -1.67 to -0.15) and counselling (-0.73, -1.41 to -0.05). EMDR and trauma-focused CBT still showed lower symptom scores than waiting list at 1 to 4 months after treatment (-1.12 and -0.73).

The authors state that every treatment found effective was a structured therapy delivered by healthcare professionals with specialist training and regular supervision. All but one of the trials of self-help with support used computerised trauma-focused CBT, and only 4 of the 13 trials of self-help without support did. Counselling was among the least effective, and the authors add that in 10 of the 11 counselling trials it served as the control arm for another therapy, so its benefit may be underestimated through researcher allegiance.

830.content: Cochrane review of 70 randomised trials with 4,761 adults treated for chronic PTSD as diagnosed in the trials. On clinician-rated symptom scores, individual trauma-focused CBT (SMD -1.62, 95% CI -2.03 to -1.21, 28 trials, 1,256 people) and EMDR (-1.17, -2.04 to -0.30, 6 trials, 183 people) did better than waiting list or usual care. CBT without a trauma focus and group trauma-focused CBT also did better than waiting list or usual care. More people dropped out of the active treatments. The authors rated the evidence for every comparison as very low quality, citing small samples, unexplained heterogeneity, high or unclear risk of bias in many trials and little follow-up data on long-term effects.

831.content: Meta-analysis of the experiments on trigger warnings, content warnings and content notes (12 manuscripts in the 2022 preprint, all from 2018 or later, most of them single-session experiments that randomised people to a warning or none). The published abstract states that warnings had no effect on affective responses to negative material or on educational outcomes, that they reliably increased anticipatory affect, and that findings on avoidance were mixed. The preprint gives these pooled estimates: affect after the material d = 0.02 (95% CI -0.05 to 0.10, 86 effect sizes, 9 manuscripts), distress after the warning and before the material d = 0.43 (0.09 to 0.77, 5 manuscripts), avoidance d = 0.06 (-0.09 to 0.21, 5 manuscripts) and comprehension d = 0.06 (-0.02 to 0.14, 3 manuscripts).

832.content: Review of extinction research, mostly in rats (Rattus norvegicus) and mice (Mus musculus), with pigeons and humans for some effects. When a cue that predicted shock is presented again and again without shock, the fear response drops, and four findings show the original learning is kept: the response returns when the cue is met outside the place where extinction happened (renewal), when time passes (spontaneous recovery), after the shock is given again on its own (reinstatement), and it can be relearned fast. The authors conclude that extinction is mainly new inhibitory learning laid over the old memory and expressed mostly in the context where it was learned, while the first-learned fear carries over to new contexts more readily.

At the neural level the review reports that extinction of fear in rodents (rats, Rattus norvegicus, and mice, Mus musculus) needs three connected regions: plasticity in the amygdala is needed to learn extinction, inhibition of amygdala neurons by the medial prefrontal cortex is involved in retrieving it, and hippocampal-prefrontal circuits carry the return of fear when the context changes. The synaptic changes of extinction are added to those of the original fear learning and do not reverse them. In humans, imaging studies show activity in the homologous prefrontal area when extinction is retrieved.

833.content: Two experiments in healthy adults measured fear by skin conductance. In the first (34 people), a picture paired with a mild wrist shock was shown repeatedly without shock straight after learning until the response was gone; after unsignalled shocks the response to the picture came back, in the same room (t(15) = 5.42, P < 0.001) and in a different room (t(17) = 2.52, P < 0.05). In the second (14 people), a response extinguished on day 1 had returned 24 hours later with no further shock (t(13) = 2.31, P < 0.05), and only to the picture that had gone with shock. The authors conclude that extinction, even when done at once, leaves the original fear memory in place and that the timing gives no support for intervening very soon after a traumatic event.

In the same paper, male Sprague-Dawley rats (Rattus norvegicus) that had learned to freeze to a tone paired with footshock were given 20 tone-alone trials in a different box either about 12 minutes or 3 days after learning. Freezing to the tone came back after unsignalled shocks and, in a separate experiment, 21 days later without any shock. It came back as much after immediate extinction as after delayed extinction (group by time F(1,14) = 0.3, P = 0.63 for spontaneous recovery).

834.content: Fourteen pairs of identical male twins, one of whom had served in combat in Vietnam while the other had not (in 7 pairs the combat twin was diagnosed with PTSD), went through fear conditioning and extinction on day 1 and a recall test on day 2, with skin conductance as the measure. The groups did not differ in learning the fear or in extinguishing it on day 1. On day 2 the combat veterans diagnosed with PTSD responded more than their own twins and more than the veterans without the diagnosis (diagnosis by exposure interaction F(1,12.1) = 4.3, P = 0.03). The authors read the weaker recall of extinction as acquired with the combat and the diagnosis, since the identical twin who stayed home did not show it.

835.content: Sixteen people diagnosed with PTSD and 15 trauma-exposed people without the diagnosis did a two-day conditioning and extinction procedure in an fMRI scanner. Skin conductance did not differ between the groups while fear was learned and extinguished on day 1. On day 2 the exposed people without the diagnosis responded less to the extinguished cue than to an unextinguished one (0.12 against 0.30 microsiemens), and the group diagnosed with PTSD did not (0.40 against 0.37; group by stimulus F = 4.99, P = 0.03). During recall the diagnosed group showed less activation in hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex and more in dorsal anterior cingulate, and across all 31 people better extinction recall went with more hippocampal and ventromedial prefrontal activation.

836.content: 106 trauma-exposed adults from a primarily African American, low-income inner-city population in the United States (53 with no diagnosis, 14 who met criteria for PTSD only, 17 for major depression only, 22 for both) learned that one pair of shapes came with an airblast to the throat (danger) and another pair never did (safety). Startle to a noise probe was the measure. People with no diagnosis and people who met criteria for depression only startled less to the safety cue than to the danger cue, and less again when a safety shape was shown together with a danger shape. The two groups who met criteria for PTSD showed no such drop, and a higher startle on the combined cue went with higher scores on hyper-arousal symptoms only.

837.content: Twenty university students in Los Angeles (15 women) each named the person who gives them the most support day to day and supplied a photo. Neutral pictures were then paired with an electric shock while either that photo or a photo of a matched stranger was on screen, with skin conductance as the measure. Fear was acquired for pictures shown with the stranger (t(19) = 4.86, P < 0.001) and was not acquired for pictures shown with the support figure (t(19) = 0.63, P = 0.54), and the difference between the two conditions was significant (t(19) = -3.80, P = 0.001).

838.content: Thirty university students in Los Angeles (22 women) first learned to fear two pictures paired with shock. During extinction one picture was shown with a photo of the person who supports them most and the other with a photo of a stranger. With the photos on screen, a fear response remained for the stranger-paired picture (t(29) = 3.88, P = 0.001) and none for the support-paired one. With the photos taken away the same held (stranger-paired t(29) = 2.85, P = 0.01; support-paired t(29) = 0.84, P = 0.41; difference between the conditions t(29) = 2.21, P = 0.04). After reminder shocks 24 hours later, fear came back for the stranger-paired picture (t(29) = 2.40, P = 0.02) and did not come back for the support-paired one (t(29) = 0.30, P = 0.77), though the size of the return did not differ significantly between the two conditions (P = 0.06). At 2 weeks neither picture brought fear back, which the authors put down to conditioning that was too weak.

839.content: Peer-reviewed commentary by a psychiatrist at Tulane University who examined 122 claims in the book The Body Keeps the Score (42 on neurobiology, 51 on treatment, 29 on other topics; the full analysis is in his own self-published book). He reports that the brain differences seen in people diagnosed with PTSD come from cross-sectional studies, which cannot show cause and do not replicate consistently, and that three reviews of studies measuring the brain or body before the event all concluded that the differences likely came first. He reports that the book's ten body-based treatments have not been shown to beat trauma-focused talking therapies, with EMDR the one that matches CBT without beating it. He concludes that the claims of trauma-caused brain damage and of unique efficacy for body-based treatments are not supported by the weight of research.

840.content: Qualitative review of 25 prospective studies (5,675 people) that measured brain or body variables before a traumatic event and followed people afterwards; 21 of the studies were of young adults in the military, police or fire services, and the 15 largest were 86 to 100 percent male. In 19 of the 25, a difference linked to later posttraumatic stress symptoms was already there before the event. Of the 10 studies able to test whether the event changed the measure, 3 found that it did and 7 found that it did not. The author concludes that most of the differences found in people diagnosed with PTSD are better read as there beforehand than as damage done by the event.

841.content: Review of the claim that people can block out a traumatic event and later recover the memory intact, which the authors tie to what they call the body-keeps-the-score hypothesis (van der Kolk and Fisler 1995): trauma held on an implicit level with no story of what happened. They report that the central parts of traumatic events tend to be remembered well, that complete loss of memory is rare among groups such as concentration camp survivors, and that in suggestive interview studies about 30 percent of participants come to remember an event that never happened.

Pooling the published surveys, the authors report that on average 58 percent of those surveyed (4,745 people) indicated some degree of belief in repressed memories. Among surveys they cite, 69.6 percent of a sample of clinical psychologists strongly endorsed that the mind can unconsciously block out memories of traumatic events, and 93 percent of a sample of EMDR practitioners answered that access to traumatic memories can be blocked. In a survey of 2,326 United States adults, 9 percent reported that a therapist had raised the possibility that they had repressed memories of childhood abuse.

842.content: Short review of three disputes about memory for trauma. On the claim that such memories are fragmented, it reports a study of 60 trauma-exposed adults, half of them diagnosed with PTSD, whose recorded accounts were scored on 28 measures of coherence: memories of the event were about as coherent as very positive and very important memories, and those diagnosed with PTSD gave no less coherent accounts than those without the diagnosis. In a treatment study it reports, fragmentation did not change reliably over treatment and was unrelated to who improved. The authors note that one researcher has challenged the first study's conclusion and judge the rebuttal convincing.

843.content: Altman, who studied the Kuninjku of western Arnhem Land from 1979, reports that direct demanding is one of several ways food and goods move. Most everyday sharing happens at the time of production, where game is divided among everyone in the hunt whoever made the kill, and unsolicited gifts are also made. By rule, direct claims are limited to close kin and people who share everyday space. He states that most sharing occurs within the household. He gives no counts.

Altman reports that Peterson's 1993 article looks more at the ways people avoid demands than at instances of demanding, and that Peterson himself noted there is no measure of how frequent demand sharing is compared with unsolicited giving. Altman questions the article's words 'much' and 'often' on that ground, and adds that later writers turned 'much sharing is by demand' into 'all sharing is by demand'.

844.content: Among the Batek of Peninsular Malaysia, 25 men and 19 women observed for an average of 39.7 days in 1975 to 1976 were followed for reproductive outcomes up to 2016. Foraging return rate, the number of people a person gave food to or received it from, cooperative foraging and the presence of kin were all unrelated to lifetime fertility and to number of surviving children, in men and in women. Fertility ranged from 0 to 17 (mean 7.4) and surviving children from 0 to 12 (mean 6.2).

The same paper gives the authors' power analysis: with the average effect that von Rueden and Jaeggi's meta-analysis reports for foragers (0.18), about 200 people are needed for 80% power, against the 44 in this study. With the largest forager effect in that meta-analysis (0.46) the number needed is 34.

Batek camps on the Lebir River in 1975 to 1976 held 34.2 people on average (11.3 men, 8.6 women, 14.4 children under 14) and stayed 8.2 days in one place. Food was shared at once and never stored. Almost nothing was eaten during foraging trips. A hunter usually came into camp quietly and gave the carcass to someone else to butcher and hand out, and gatherers passed surplus tubers to other families without display. Bragging was frowned on. On an average day a Batek adult gave food to or received it from between one and two other people (mean total sharing degree 1.7 for men, 1.58 for women).

845.content: Among the Aka of Linganga-Makaou in northeastern Congo (one residential group of about 80 people followed for 92 days in 1991 to 1992 and one of 43 people for 11 days in 1995), women stewed meat and plants in front of or inside their huts and served it out in plain view of the camp. A cook and her children ate only about 20% of the stew she cooked, and about 75% of the stew a woman ate had been cooked by other women. Adult men usually ate together at the men's shelter, where plates were carried to them, and sometimes ate with wife and children.

In the same Aka study, camp size set how far a meal reached. In the small camps every woman shared stew with, and received it from, every other woman, and being present was the only condition for getting a portion. In the large camps a cook could no longer serve everyone and gave mostly within her own cluster of huts; closer kin received more often, and women without close kin ties to the cook also received. Partners changed when the camp changed size.

Kitanishi reports that every food among these Aka had a named owner (konja) who led its sharing, and who was sometimes someone other than the hunter, collector or cook: for game, the owner of the tool that stopped the animal. An owner with more than 20 kg of meat always shared it. Camp members seldom pressed an owner to share with them and avoided showing that they wanted a share. Sharing waited for an absent owner.

846.content: Among the Hadza, 67 of 89 interviewed men and women from 13 camps gave usable rankings of the hunters they knew (72 hunters from nine camps, shown as photographs). Split-half agreement between raters averaged 0.89 over 10,000 random splits, and 87% of the pairwise correlations between raters were positive; eight raters (12%) disagreed with the rest. Agreement was somewhat higher for the best hunters than for middling ones.

In the same Hadza study, measured bow draw strength, recognition of animal calls and archery aim together accounted for 44% of the variation in hunting reputation; eyesight did not relate to it. The authors conclude that reputation reflects real skill in aggregate and that it is too noisy an index of skill for hunting to work as an honest signal of hidden qualities.

847.content: Among the Great Andamanese, as Radcliffe-Brown recorded them in 1906 to 1908, a pig brought home whole was roasted and cut up at the camp's public cooking place, which the bachelors tended, and the meat was given out among the community. Each woman then cooked the family meal at the fire in her own hut. The evening meal was the main meal and a family one; bachelors cooked and ate together and unmarried women ate by themselves. He states that custom spread nearly all food evenly through the camp, with younger men faring a little worse than their elders, and that refusing a request was bad manners.

Radcliffe-Brown reports that when an adult died among the Great Andamanese, the news spread through the camp, all the women gathered round the body and wept until exhausted, the men then wept over it, and all adult members of the community covered themselves with clay. If burial waited until morning, everyone in the camp stayed awake. After the burial the whole camp moved away until mourning ended. Near relatives mourned for several months, with clay, food rules and no dancing, and friends wept with them at the dance that closed it. For a very young child there was no general mourning of the whole camp.

On anger, Radcliffe-Brown reports that when an Andamanese man worked himself into a rage, shooting an arrow near his opponent or breaking property, the women and children fled into the jungle and, if he was formidable, sometimes the men as well; a man of influence could usually end the scene, and anger was short-lived. A man given to violent anger was feared and never gained esteem. A man who shirked getting food was still fed and nothing was said to him, yet he lost the esteem of the camp.

848.content: In a UK poll of 2000 adults in April 2016, people who more often ate their evening meal with others rated their life satisfaction higher and named more people they could count on for support: about five on average across the sample, and as few as half that among those who mostly ate alone. Nearly 70% had never had a meal with a neighbour, and 15% had not eaten with another family member in six months. The survey was taken once, so it cannot order the variables; the author's path analysis points from eating together to feeling close, and he says the reverse cannot be excluded.

849.content: In the American Time Use Survey (about 235,000 adults, 2003 to 2023, weighted to the US population), the share who ate all of the previous day's meals alone rose to 26% in 2023, more than half again above its 2003 level. Among people living alone about 70% ate all meals alone, against roughly 20% of those living with others, and the rise was steepest under age 35.

Gallup World Poll data from 142 countries (2022 to 2023) show that shared meals vary widely today: people in Senegal reported 11.7 lunches and dinners a week eaten with someone they knew, people in Bangladesh and Estonia 2.7, with the United States ranked 69th and the United Kingdom 81st. People who shared one meal in the past week rated their lives 5.2 on the 0 to 10 ladder against 4.9 for those who ate every meal alone. The authors state that they do not settle which way the link runs.

850.content: In the 2015 European Working Conditions Survey (29,784 employees in the EU28), 4.8% answered that they rarely or never had the feeling of doing useful work, down from 7.8% in 2005 and 5.5% in 2010. The share was 1.7% among teachers and 9.7% among refuse collectors, and no occupation had a majority who felt their work was of no use. The answer went most strongly with whether the employee felt respected by management (rho 0.324).

In the same survey, UK employees in 2015 who said their job was not useful scored a mean of 49.3 (SD 28.3) on the WHO-5 wellbeing scale, against 64.5 (SD 21.7) for those who said it was useful, and the authors report a similar gap across the EU28. They state that the one-wave design cannot rule out the reverse path, in which people who already feel low rate their job as less useful.

851.content: In the US Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey (577,268 establishment-month observations, 2001 to 2006, with published data to 2011), employers filled 5.2% of open posts per working day on average, and the mean time a vacancy stayed open ranged from 14 to 25 working days over the business cycle. The daily fill rate was about 12% in construction and 3% in information, finance, health, education and government, and ran from 1.1% in establishments with the lowest staff turnover to 11.4% in those with the highest.

852.content: A meta-analysis of 97 studies of adults diagnosed with borderline personality disorder by DSM or ICD criteria (11,366 diagnosed participants, 3,732 non-clinical and 13,128 psychiatric controls; 92 of the 97 studies were case-control). In the 42 studies that gave the figure, a pooled 71.1 percent of diagnosed participants reported at least one adverse childhood experience: physical neglect 48.9 percent, emotional abuse 42.5, physical abuse 36.4, sexual abuse 32.1 and emotional neglect 25.3. Adversity was reported by the participants themselves, mostly looking back as adults.

In the same meta-analysis the size of the link depended on the design. In case-control studies, people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder were 13.91 times as likely as non-clinical controls to report childhood adversity (95% CI 11.11-17.43, after trim-and-fill; 16.86 in the 29 studies left after outliers were removed). In the two general-population studies the pooled odds ratio was 2.56 (1.24-5.30). In the only two prospective studies it was 2.59 (0.93-7.30, p = .070), which the authors call non-significant; the two single-study odds ratios were 4.99 and 1.70. Against other psychiatric groups the odds ratio was 3.15. The authors name selection of more severe trauma histories into clinics, 'healthy' control groups, and retrospective reporting as possible reasons for the gap.

853.content: The McLean Study of Adult Development followed 290 inpatients aged 18 to 35 who met both Revised Diagnostic Interview for Borderlines and DSM-III-R criteria for borderline personality disorder, plus 72 patients who met criteria for other personality disorders, with interviews every two years for 16 years. By 16 years the estimated cumulative share of the borderline group who had stopped meeting the criteria for at least two years was 99 percent, and for at least eight years 78 percent. About 30 percent reached remission at the first possible follow-up, against about 85 percent of the comparison group. After a two-year remission 36 percent met the criteria again; after an eight-year remission 10 percent did. Of the surviving borderline group 87.5 percent (231 of 264) were interviewed at all eight waves; 13 had died by suicide and 13 in other ways.

In the same 16-year follow-up, recovery was much less common than remission. Recovery required a Global Assessment of Functioning score of 61 or more, which the authors operationalised as remission of the primary diagnosis plus at least one emotionally sustaining relationship with a close friend or partner plus full-time, competent work or school (being a houseperson counted). The estimated cumulative share of the borderline group with a recovery lasting two years was 60 percent and lasting eight years 40 percent, against 85 and 75 percent in the comparison group. Of those who recovered for two years, 44 percent later lost the recovery. The authors report that work problems are the main reason patients fail to reach or keep recovery.

854.content: An opinion piece whose two authors, both psychiatrists, report that they were members of the World Health Organization group for the ICD-11 revision of the classification of personality disorders. They argue that the borderline personality disorder diagnosis is no personality disorder, since its criteria are oscillating symptoms and behaviour where a personality disorder needs stable traits; that it entered DSM-III in 1980 as a compromise to satisfy psychoanalysts; that all attempts to find a borderline factor have failed; and that the ICD-10 and ICD-11 work groups rejected the label, which was then 'forced in by powerful lobbies', with a 'borderline pattern specifier' added to ICD-11. They also state, without a reference, that chronic sleep disturbance creates the same symptoms. They conclude the label should be abandoned.

In the same opinion piece the authors write that the borderline label is a major source of stigma among health professionals, that patients so labelled are seen as harder to manage even when their behaviour is no worse than that of other patients, that other complaints are waved away as part of the diagnosis, and that a mention of emotional instability in a referral letter is now used to exclude patients from a range of mental health services. They report no data of their own; one cited study covers staff attitudes in community mental health teams.

855.content: In the summary of his 1938 paper the psychoanalyst Adolph Stern labelled a group of his patients 'border line': in his words, their material ran in two directions, towards the psychotic and towards the psychoneurotic. He reported that these patients had not been adequately reached by the methods that worked with the average psychoneurotic patient. He did not present them as untreatable: the stated aim of the paper is to show that their narcissism is open to psychoanalytic therapy when the technique is varied, though he calls therapy more difficult and the prognosis more grave than in psychoneurotic patients. The summary reports no patient numbers.

856.content: The introduction of this paper states that 256 possible combinations of the nine DSM criteria yield the same borderline personality disorder diagnosis, so that two patients with the diagnosis may share only one criterion; the authors cite Lewis and colleagues 2012 for it. The figure is a count that follows from the rule of five or more out of nine (126 + 84 + 36 + 9 + 1). It is not a finding of this study.

A cluster analysis of 187 patients in the Netherlands who met SCID-II interview criteria for borderline personality disorder and were referred for mentalization-based treatment found three clusters. The largest, 145 patients (78 percent), scored as 'core' borderline with no marked elevation on other personality disorder dimensions; 27 showed histrionic, narcissistic and antisocial features; 15 showed schizotypal and paranoid features. The authors report that differences between the clusters were small and that the clusters did not differ on attachment or on childhood trauma scores, and they read this as a strong common factor under the diagnosis.

857.content: The review states the DSM-5 rule for a borderline personality disorder diagnosis as five or more of nine criteria and notes that this gives 256 possible ways to meet the criteria, which the authors read as considerable heterogeneity among diagnosed patients. They add that a patient with four severe criteria (emptiness, unstable relationships, identity disturbance and self-harm) gets no diagnosis for want of a fifth. They report that no medication has been approved by regulatory agencies for the diagnosis.

The same review holds positions that cut against a simple reading of the borderline personality disorder label as empty. The authors state that the diagnosis can be made reliably by semi-structured interview and told apart from other diagnoses, though elsewhere they ask for more reliable measures of the phenotype. On causes they state there is convincing evidence that genetic factors and adverse childhood experiences interact and play a central role, while noting that the reported links with maltreatment do not seem specific to this diagnosis, that no single nucleotide polymorphism has been identified, and that the neurobiology remains to be clarified. The review does not discuss the discordant-twin studies of abuse and borderline traits.

On treatment the review reports that psychotherapy outperforms treatment as usual on the core symptoms of the borderline personality disorder diagnosis with effect sizes of 0.50 to 0.65, that no approach has proved superior to the others, and that almost half of patients do not respond sufficiently: mean non-response was 48.8 percent across psychotherapies (dialectical behaviour therapy 47 percent, schema therapy 42, psychodynamic therapies 42) and 64 percent for treatment as usual. It also reports that no class of psychoactive medication has consistently proven efficacious for the diagnosis, that no medication is approved for it by the US Food and Drug Administration, and that almost 19 percent of patients report taking four or more psychotropic drugs.

858.content: A Cochrane review of 46 randomised trials (2,769 participants diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, mostly women, 29 different medications, searches to February 2022) found no difference between any medication and placebo on any primary outcome at the end of treatment: severity of the diagnosed symptoms, self-harm, suicide-related outcomes and psychosocial functioning. The evidence was mostly of very low certainty. For symptom severity scores the standardised mean difference was -0.18 for antipsychotics (8 trials, 951 participants), -0.27 for antidepressants (2 trials, 87) and -0.07 for mood stabilisers (4 trials, 265), all with intervals that include zero. Low-certainty evidence suggested antipsychotics may slightly reduce scores for interpersonal problems (SMD -0.21) and mood stabilisers may reduce them (SMD -0.58). Seventeen trials were funded or partly funded by industry. The authors conclude that no pharmacological therapy seems effective in specifically treating the diagnosed pathology.

859.content: In New Zealand's national records, among people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder in public specialist mental health services who were dispensed any psychotropic medication, 49.9 percent of 1,468 people were dispensed three or more different psychotropic medications during 2014 and 55.9 percent of 1,915 people during 2019; 8.4 and 10.7 percent were dispensed seven or more. A medication counted when it was dispensed at least twice in the calendar year. In 2019, the authors report, antidepressants went to 80.2 percent, antipsychotics to 67.3, benzodiazepines to 58.6, opioids to 46.1 and mood stabilisers to 33.7 percent; quetiapine alone went to 53.8 percent. Of all diagnosed people, 24.0 percent (2014) and 19.1 percent (2019) were dispensed no psychotropic medication. The authors state that no psychotropic drug is licensed for the diagnosis.

The same New Zealand study describes who is in the records and what the records cannot show. The data cover 1,932 people diagnosed with borderline personality disorder in 2009 to 2014 and 2,368 in 2015 to 2019, all in publicly funded specialist services; among those dispensed psychotropic medication 82.6 and 85.4 percent were female. The authors say diagnoses made in primary care or by private psychiatrists were not captured, so the study captured the most severe cases, and that they had no data on other diagnoses, so the share of the dispensing that was aimed at other diagnosed conditions is unknown.

860.content: In face-to-face interviews with 34,653 US adults in the 2004-2005 Wave 2 National Epidemiologic Survey on Alcohol and Related Conditions, 5.9 percent met lifetime DSM-IV criteria for borderline personality disorder on the survey's structured interview (99% CI 5.4 to 6.4): 5.6 percent of men and 6.2 percent of women, which the authors report as no difference. Meeting the criteria was more common in younger adults, in separated, divorced or widowed adults and in people with lower income and education.

861.content: A Swedish register study followed 1,851,755 people born 1973 to 1993, of whom 11,665 were diagnosed with borderline personality disorder in specialist care between 1997 and 2013 (85.4 percent of them female). The rate of diagnosis in relatives of a diagnosed person, against relatives of undiagnosed people, fell with genetic distance: hazard ratio 11.5 for monozygotic twins (95% CI 1.6-83.8), 7.4 for dizygotic twins (1.0-55.3), 4.7 for full siblings (3.9-5.6), 2.1 for maternal half-siblings (1.5-3.0) and 1.3 for paternal half-siblings (0.9-2.1). In the best-fitting liability model, additive genetic factors accounted for 46 percent of the variance in who was diagnosed (95% CI 39-53) and non-shared environment for 54 percent (47-61).

In the same Swedish study the environment shared by siblings accounted for little or none of the variance in who was diagnosed with borderline personality disorder. The model with a shared-environment term estimated it at 3 percent (95% CI 0-14) and the full model at 4 percent (0-16); dropping the term did not worsen the fit, and the best-fitting model has no shared-environment term at all. The authors conclude that shared familial factors such as socioeconomic conditions are unlikely to contribute substantially. They add that the abuse and other traumatic events reported by diagnosed people may be unique environmental risks to one child in a family, may act through gene-by-environment interaction, or may reflect gene-environment correlation.

862.content: A self-report questionnaire went to 706 mental health clinicians (psychiatrists, psychiatry residents, social workers, nurses and psychologists) at nine US academic centres. Most said they consider borderline personality disorder a valid diagnosis, and nearly half reported that they preferred to avoid these patients. Staff nurses gave the lowest self-ratings on caring attitudes, empathy and treatment optimism, and social workers the highest on caring. Self-rated caring attitudes, empathy and treatment optimism were all reported as higher among clinicians who had cared for more patients with the diagnosis in the past 12 months.

863.content: Bruene proposes that the pattern diagnosed as borderline personality disorder is an extreme of a 'fast' life history strategy: early cues of danger and unreliable care, he argues, set expectations that resources and partners will not last, which favours immediate use of what is at hand, high stress reactivity, vigilance about being left, impulsive risk and unstable pair bonds. He lists as consistent the reported findings on delay discounting, low agreeableness and conscientiousness scores, trust-game behaviour, earlier first intercourse and more partners in diagnosed women, and decline of impulsive symptoms with age. He states that the full diagnosed condition is not adaptive, that milder forms might pay off reproductively in unpredictable settings, and that brain-imaging differences may be adaptations to early stress and not damage. He calls for data on survival and reproduction, which do not yet exist.

Bruene reports evidence against his own life history reading of the borderline personality disorder label: the two studies he cites found no earlier physical maturation, such as age at first period, in diagnosed women, although a fast strategy would lead one to expect it. He writes that this is a serious drawback for the theory. He also notes that high harm-avoidance scores and strong disgust reported in diagnosed patients fit a slow strategy better, and that, since five of nine criteria suffice, two patients may overlap in only one symptom, so the model may not fit all who carry the diagnosis.

864.content: A single-blind randomised trial (first author at the Centre for Addiction and Mental Health, Toronto) assigned 180 patients diagnosed with borderline personality disorder, all with at least two suicidal or self-injurious episodes in the past five years, to one year of dialectical behaviour therapy or one year of general psychiatric management, which combined psychodynamically informed therapy with symptom-targeted medication management. Both groups improved on most measures, including the frequency and severity of suicidal and self-injurious episodes, emergency visits, hospital days, and scores for borderline symptoms, depression, anger and interpersonal functioning. The authors report no significant differences between the groups on any outcome.

865.content: A prospective cohort study followed 500 children with documented cases of physical abuse, sexual abuse or neglect and 396 demographically similar control children into adulthood. The authors report that significantly more of the abused or neglected group met criteria for borderline personality disorder as adults; taken by type, this held for the physically abused and for the neglected children, and the abstract does not list sexual abuse among them. Having a parent with alcohol or drug problems, not working full-time, not finishing high school, and diagnoses of drug abuse, major depressive disorder and posttraumatic stress disorder were associated with meeting the criteria and, in the authors' analysis, mediated the link between the childhood maltreatment and the adult diagnosis. The abstract gives no percentages or odds ratios.

866.content: Reviewing field studies of Congo Basin foragers (Aka, Baka, Bofi, Efe, Mbuti), Hewlett reports that forager parents rarely if ever use corporal punishment, while it is common among the neighbouring farmers, citing work on the Aka and the Baka. In an observational study of Bofi toddlers that he summarises, conflicts in which an older child hit the toddler never occurred among the foragers and did occur among the farmers. Children stayed in sight of adults: Aka children aged 4 to 16 were within visual range of an adult for 64 percent of the day and within six metres of a parent or other adult for 45 percent, and Bofi forager children aged 4 to 5 were within arm's reach of a parent or adult for 33 percent of the day against 6 percent for farmer children.

Hewlett reports that losing a parent to death or divorce was common for Congo Basin forager children and that a child had other places to go. Among the Aka, 42 percent of children aged 11 to 15 lived with a stepparent or a single parent, and at the time an Aka chose a spouse he or she was living with both natural parents only 29 percent of the time. Children decided which parent to live with and often visited the other. Among the Efe, 27 percent of children had no parent in camp, through death, divorce or temporary absence. Turnbull's account of the Mbuti, which Hewlett summarises, has many people giving a child food and support and children calling several people mother and father.

867.content: A short review of cooperation in small-scale societies states that social norms are enforced on children through punishment and gives the Aka foragers of Central Africa as the example: Aka children report that if they refuse to babysit, their parents will withhold food, hit them, insult them or gossip about them. The review cites Boyette's interview study of Aka children for this. In the same passage it reports that Batek parents tease children who act aggressively, and that severe sanctions are rare in small-scale societies.

868.content: In 1,382 same-sex twin pairs from the Minnesota Twin Family Study (896 identical, 486 fraternal; over 95% Caucasian), 27.5% of twins reported emotional, physical or sexual abuse before age 18, and each kind of abuse went with a higher score on a 19-item self-report borderline trait scale at age 24 (correlations .12 to .24). Within identical pairs in which one twin reported abuse and the other did not (197 pairs for any abuse, 94 emotional, 131 physical, 65 sexual), the two twins' trait scores did not differ significantly for any kind of abuse. Within fraternal pairs the twin who reported abuse scored higher for any, emotional and physical abuse. The authors read the pattern as shared genes carrying the link between reported abuse and the trait score.

In the same Minnesota twin sample, model fitting put the heritability of the borderline trait score at .35, shared environment at .10 (not significant) and non-shared environment at .56. Reported abuse was only slightly heritable (.05 to .13) and was mostly shared family environment (.43 to .65). The overlap between reported abuse and the trait score was mainly genetic (genetic correlations .31 to .97), and the non-shared environmental correlations were small: .08 for any abuse, .18 for emotional abuse, .10 for physical abuse and -.06 for sexual abuse. The authors state that the small positive values suggest there might be small causal effects of abuse on the trait score.

869.content: In 2,808 Norwegian twins aged 17 to 23 (Oslo University Adolescent and Young Adult Twin Project), childhood trauma (emotional abuse, physical abuse, sexual abuse or witnessing violence) was assessed with the Childhood Trauma Interview and borderline traits with the Structured Interview for DSM-IV Personality. The trait score was about 50% heritable and reported trauma 33% to 69% heritable. Trauma and trait scores were weakly but significantly associated in the whole sample. Within twin pairs discordant for trauma the authors found little to no evidence for a causal effect of trauma on the trait score, and they attribute the association to common genetic influences.

870.content: A pre-registered meta-analysis pooled 34 quasi-experimental studies of childhood maltreatment and mental health problems, measured as diagnoses or symptom scores (twin and sibling difference, adoption, fixed-effects, natural-experiment and propensity-score designs; 29 cohorts, 54,646 participants, mean age 28 at assessment). Before the quasi-experimental adjustment the association was moderate (Cohen's d = 0.56, 95% CI 0.41 to 0.71, from the 20 studies that gave an unadjusted figure); after it a small association remained (d = 0.31, 0.24 to 0.37), which is 45% smaller. Restricted to the same 20 studies the adjusted figure was 0.26. The authors conclude that a large part of the usual association is confounded by pre-existing genetic and environmental risk and that the rest is consistent with a small causal contribution.

In the same meta-analysis the adjusted association did not differ significantly by type of quasi-experimental design, by sex, by age at assessment, by prospective against retrospective measurement of maltreatment (d = 0.29 against 0.32) or by whether one person rated both exposure and outcome (0.32 against 0.28). It was present for internalising, externalising and psychosis-type outcomes, each as measured by the included studies' diagnoses or symptom scores. It differed by type of maltreatment: emotional abuse (3 studies) and institutional neglect (one cohort of Romanian adoptees) showed the largest values. Only 4 of 84 effect sizes from twin and sibling studies used anything other than self-report for both maltreatment and outcome.

871.content: In a US Midwest cohort (908 children with court-substantiated abuse or neglect before age 12 in 1967 to 1971 and 667 matched comparison children; 1,196 interviewed at mean age 28.7), court records and the adults' own recall of maltreatment picked out largely different people (kappa = 0.25). Adults with a court record who did not recall maltreatment had no raised rate of any lifetime DSM-III-R diagnosis on the Diagnostic Interview Schedule compared with adults who had neither a record nor recall (risk ratio 0.92, 95% CI 0.78 to 1.08). Adults who recalled maltreatment had raised rates whether a court record existed (1.35, 1.21 to 1.50) or did not exist (1.29, 1.15 to 1.45).

The same pattern held for internalising and externalising diagnoses as classified from that interview (court record only 0.87 and 0.96; record plus recall 2.08 and 1.32; recall only 1.73 and 1.27), across physical abuse, sexual abuse and neglect, in men and women, in Black and White participants, and among adults with no diagnosis in the year of the interview. The authors conclude that the rate of psychopathology linked to court-documented maltreatment, even severe cases, is minimal without the person's own report, and high with that report whether or not the records agree. They list the limits: court records miss cases, severity and duration were not measured, and it is one cohort.

872.content: In a population-based sample of 1,411 adult female twins, 30.4% reported some childhood sexual abuse and 8.4% reported intercourse. Self-reported abuse was associated with every psychiatric and substance dependence diagnosis assessed by interview, most strongly bulimia and alcohol and other drug dependence; odds ratios were modest and often non-significant for non-genital abuse and mostly above 3.0 for intercourse. Controlling for family background and parental psychopathology, as reported in interviews with twins and parents, reduced the odds ratios by a small to modest amount. In twin pairs discordant for abuse the exposed twin was at consistently higher risk, and the authors conclude that the results are consistent with a causal link.

873.content: In 40 pairs of male identical twins of the Vietnam era in which one twin saw combat and the other did not (17 pairs where the combat twin was diagnosed with chronic PTSD on the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale, 23 where he was not), hippocampal volume was measured by MRI. Among the 12 pairs with severe PTSD scores (above 65), both the combat-exposed twin and his unexposed identical brother had smaller hippocampi than the 23 non-PTSD pairs as classified by that scale (6.66 and 6.75 ml against 7.41 and 7.25 ml), and brothers within a pair did not differ. The combat veteran's symptom score correlated with his own hippocampal volume (r = -0.64) and with his unexposed twin's (r = -0.70). Combat severity was unrelated to hippocampal volume.

The authors conclude that a smaller hippocampus in people diagnosed with chronic PTSD is a pre-existing familial trait that goes with vulnerability, and that the data speak against the reading that combat stress or the years of symptoms shrink it: the veterans with the diagnosis had no smaller hippocampi than their own twins who never saw combat. Limits they state: the group difference appeared only for severe, long-lasting PTSD cases, the lack of fraternal twins means heredity could not be separated from shared environment, and childhood abuse was reported somewhat more often in the PTSD pairs (29% and 24% against 13% and 9%, not significant) although removing those subjects left the result in place.

874.content: In 222 identical and 184 fraternal pairs of nonveteran volunteer twins, scores on a traumatic events inventory and on a DSM-IV PTSD symptom inventory were fitted with biometric models. Exposure to assaultive trauma (such as robbery or sexual assault) was best explained by additive genetic, shared and unique environmental effects, while exposure to non-assaultive trauma (such as a motor vehicle accident or a natural disaster) was best explained by shared and unique environment only. PTSD symptom scores were moderately heritable with the rest unique environment, and the genetic effects on assaultive trauma exposure and on the symptom scores were highly correlated.

875.content: In 4,042 male twin pairs from the Vietnam era, genetic factors accounted for 13% to 30% of the variance in liability for self-reported re-experiencing symptoms, 30% to 34% for avoidance symptoms and 28% to 32% for arousal symptoms, after adjusting for differences in combat exposure. Identical pairs were more alike in combat exposure than fraternal pairs. The authors found no evidence that shared environment contributes to these posttraumatic stress symptoms.

876.content: Among 4,029 male twin pairs who served in the US military during the Vietnam era, identical twins were more alike than fraternal twins in volunteering for service in Vietnam (correlations 0.40 and 0.22), in serving in Southeast Asia (0.41 and 0.24) and, among 820 pairs where both served there, in self-reported combat experiences (0.53 and 0.30). Heritability estimates ranged from 35% to 47%, family environment had no significant effect on any of these, and military records of combat decorations gave very similar results.

877.content: In 3,304 members of male twin pairs from the Vietnam Era Twin Registry, interviewed by telephone in 1992 with the Diagnostic Interview Schedule, model fitting for lifetime DSM-III-R diagnoses attributed liability for the PTSD diagnosis partly to a 15.3% genetic contribution shared with alcohol and drug dependence and a 20.0% genetic contribution specific to it. A family-environment component was reported only for drug dependence (33.9% of the variance). The remaining variance for all three was unique environment.

878.content: In 25,252 adult twins of the Swedish Twin Registry (born 1959 to 1998), 38.6% reported at least one of 7 adverse childhood experiences in a web survey, and psychiatric diagnoses after age 19 were taken from the national patient register. In the full cohort each additional reported experience went with 52% higher odds of any diagnosed psychiatric disorder (odds ratio 1.52, 95% CI 1.48 to 1.57). Within twin pairs who differed in what they reported, the odds ratio per additional experience was 1.29 (1.14 to 1.47) in fraternal pairs and 1.20 (1.02 to 1.40) in identical pairs, an attenuation of 39.1% and 57.5%. Identical twins who reported 3 or more experiences had 2.11 times the odds of a diagnosed disorder of co-twins who reported none (1.13 to 3.94), against 4.57 in the full cohort; for any against no experience the identical-pair odds ratio was 1.19 (0.84 to 1.70).

By type of experience in the same Swedish twin cohort, within-pair estimates were considerably attenuated for every type except sexual abuse: twins who reported childhood sexual abuse had odds of any diagnosed psychiatric disorder of 3.09 (95% CI 2.68 to 3.56) in the full cohort, 2.10 (1.33 to 3.32) within fraternal pairs and 1.80 (1.04 to 3.11) within identical pairs. Per additional experience, associations with diagnosed depressive, anxiety and stress-related disorders were seen in the cohort and within pairs, and for the substance use disorder diagnosis within identical pairs but not within fraternal pairs.

In the same Swedish twin sample a univariate twin model attributed variation in the number of adverse childhood experiences a person reported to additive genetic factors (34.6%, 95% CI 25.2 to 44.0), shared environment (22.1%, 14.3 to 29.9) and non-shared environment (43.3%, 40.1 to 46.5). The authors read the attenuation within twin pairs as showing that familial confounding, genetic and environmental, contributes to the link between these experiences and adult diagnoses. They note that the experiences were reported in retrospect and that register diagnoses capture only cases seen in inpatient or specialist outpatient care.

879.content: A genome-wide meta-analysis of reported childhood maltreatment in 185,414 people of European ancestry (UK Biobank, Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, ALSPAC, ABCD, Generation R) found 14 associated loci and a SNP heritability of 0.079. With those variants as instruments, two-sample Mendelian randomisation gave evidence for a one-way effect of maltreatment on the major depressive disorder diagnosis and two-way effects with the ADHD and schizophrenia diagnoses, each as defined in the outcome genome-wide studies. The authors note that the instruments explain little of the variance in maltreatment and that the study does not separate maltreatment as an event from maltreatment as a person's own report.

The same Mendelian randomisation analysis found no significant effect of childhood maltreatment on coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes or C-reactive protein concentration, and none in the reverse direction, although reported maltreatment was genetically correlated with coronary artery disease. The authors give two possible reasons: the genetic instruments explained little variance in maltreatment, or the associations with physical health seen in observational studies are correlational.

In a UK Biobank hold-out sample of 12,855 people that included 2,849 sibling pairs, a polygenic score for reported childhood maltreatment predicted which sibling reported more maltreatment: the between-sibling effect was 0.053, about 58% of the total between-family effect of 0.095. The authors read this as the child's own genetically influenced traits evoking or selecting exposure (active and reactive gene-environment correlation); a passive route through the parents' genes and home was not significant (0.039, p = 0.13) and could not be excluded. The polygenic score explained at most 0.91% of the variance in reported maltreatment.

880.content: In 90 female twin pairs (65 identical; mean age 29) from the University of Washington Twin Registry, a higher count on a modified 5-category Adverse Childhood Experiences questionnaire (physical and sexual abuse were asked separately) went with worse self-rated general health (p = .01) and vitality (p = .04) on the SF-36. Within twin pairs neither association remained: the general health estimate was 1.56 points per category (95% CI -3.02 to 6.15) against -2.67 (-4.72 to -0.61) in the whole sample. The sample was young, healthy and small, the outcome is a self-rating, and no disease was measured.

881.content: Using Swedish medical records and registers, the authors followed 525 young adults (aged 20 to 37) with prospectively documented severe childhood maltreatment, 1,979 unexposed former child and adolescent psychiatry patients, 1,388 matched healthy controls, and their siblings and cousins. Maltreatment went with a higher rate of being diagnosed with a substance use disorder (crude hazard ratio 6.61; 3.50 after adjustment for sex, birth year, externalising problems, parents' substance use disorder as recorded, and socioeconomic factors). Compared with their own unexposed siblings, exposed individuals still had about three times the rate of being diagnosed (adjusted hazard ratio 3.12, 95% CI 2.21 to 4.42).

882.content: In 1,991 same-sex pairs from a young adult Australian volunteer twin panel (mean age 29.9) interviewed by telephone, 16.7% of the women and 5.4% of the men reported childhood sexual abuse. Twins who denied abuse and whose co-twin reported it had raised rates of many adverse outcomes compared with other twins who denied abuse, which the authors read as correlated family background risk. Within discordant pairs the twin who reported abuse still had significantly greater risk than the co-twin for all 8 outcomes examined: major depression as diagnosed in the structured interview, suicide attempt, conduct disorder, alcohol dependence, nicotine dependence, social anxiety, rape after age 18 and divorce, all as reported in the interview.

883.content: In structured telephone interviews with 5,995 Australian twins, 5.9% of the women and 2.5% of the men reported childhood sexual abuse. In the whole sample those who reported abuse were more likely to receive lifetime diagnoses of major depression, conduct disorder, panic disorder and alcoholism, and to report suicidal ideation and a suicide attempt. When twins who reported abuse were compared with their own co-twins who did not, no differences in the interview diagnoses were seen. Rates of the major depression and conduct disorder diagnoses and of reported suicidal ideation were higher when both twins reported abuse than when one did. The authors conclude that the association arises at least in part through shared familial factors.

884.content: In a Registered Report using DNA from 11,407 children in two cohorts from the UK and the USA, children with higher polygenic scores for mental health problems had a small increase in the odds of adverse childhood experiences. The authors report that the raised level of mental health problems in children exposed to these experiences was at least partly due to pre-existing genetic risk, and that some experiences, such as maltreatment and parental mental illness, remained associated with mental health problems independent of that genetic confounding.

885.content: In the World Mental Health surveys (26 surveys in 24 countries, 2001 to 2012; 68,894 adults in the part II sample), 70.4% of respondents reported at least one lifetime event from a list of 29 event types built on the DSM-IV definition of a traumatic event. The share ranged from 28.6% in Bulgaria to 84.6% in Ukraine. 18.2% reported exactly one event and 30.5% reported four or more different events. The mean number of reported exposures was 3.2 in the total sample and 4.6 among those with any. The most common event was the unexpected death of a loved one (reported by 31.4%), followed by witnessing death, a dead body or serious injury (23.7%), being mugged (14.5%) and a life-threatening car accident (14.0%); the five most common types made up 51.9% of all exposures.

In the same surveys, the authors used the ages at which respondents said each event happened to model which earlier events went with later ones. Earlier events of nearly every kind were associated with later events. The strongest links were from interpersonal violence to further interpersonal violence (odds ratio 2.6) and to sexual or partner violence, and from collective violence to later man-made disaster (odds ratio 2.1). Being married was the most consistent correlate of lower exposure. Women were more likely than men to report intimate partner or sexual violence (odds ratio 2.3) and less likely to report events in the other four groups (odds ratios 0.4 to 0.8). Married respondents had lower odds than the never married in every group except accidents and injuries (odds ratios 0.5 to 0.9). The authors state that the design is observational and cannot settle causality.

886.content: In the World Mental Health surveys (24 countries, n = 68,894), the interview scored PTSD once for the worst event and once for a randomly chosen event, so risk could be given per event. Across all events, 4.0% of exposures were followed by an episode that met DSM-IV/CIDI criteria for PTSD, which with 3.2 exposures per person gives 12.9 lifetime episodes per 100 people. Risk was highest after rape (19.0%), physical abuse by a romantic partner (11.7%), kidnapping (11.0%) and sexual assault other than rape (10.5%); for combat it was 3.6% and for the unexpected death of a loved one 5.4%. Intimate partner and sexual violence made up 9.8% of exposures and carried nearly 42.7% of all person-years with PTSD symptoms as reported.

Respondents whose reports met DSM-IV/CIDI criteria for PTSD after the randomly chosen event were asked how long any symptoms had lasted. Mean reported duration was about six years (72.3 months), from over 13 years after combat to about one year after a natural disaster. The means are pulled up by long tails: 25 to 40% of cases reported recovery within one year, many within six months, and median duration was five years for war-related events, three years for physical or intimate partner and sexual violence, and one to two years for the other categories. The authors state that their durations are biased upward, since recovery was defined as having no symptoms at all.

887.content: In 26 World Mental Health surveys (71,083 adults in the part II sample), 3.9% of all respondents and 5.6% of respondents who reported a listed event met DSM-IV criteria for PTSD at some time in their lives, as scored by the CIDI interview. Among the exposed the lifetime figure was 6.9% in high-income countries, 3.9% in upper-middle-income and 3.0% in low and lower-middle-income countries, and ranged from 0.5% to 14.5% across countries. Among the exposed, 2.8% met criteria in the past 12 months and 1.4% in the past 30 days.

The authors used symptoms in the past 12 months among lifetime cases as their indicator of persistence. Of the 4,103 respondents who had ever met the DSM-IV/CIDI criteria for PTSD, 50.5% reported symptoms in the 12 months before the interview, and 49.8% of those reported symptoms in the past 30 days. The 12-month share among lifetime cases ranged from 23.1% to 82.1% across surveys, some with very few cases (Belgium 28.0%, Lebanon 58.2%). The authors add that some respondents will have had symptoms that came and went, and that the DSM does not separate full remission from symptoms that flare up on reminders.

Among respondents who reported a listed event, those who were younger, female, not employed, not currently married, less educated and on lower household income were more likely to have met DSM-IV/CIDI criteria for PTSD in their lifetime. For persistence (symptoms in the past 12 months among lifetime cases) only the lowest income category and an employment status of "other" were associated in the pooled sample, and in the low and middle-income country groups no sociodemographic variable was associated with persistence. The authors state that they cannot tell whether marital status or socioeconomic status came before the PTSD classification or followed from it.

888.content: The authors pooled 54 longitudinal studies (67 analyses, each with more than 100 people and at least three measurements) that sorted people into symptom trajectories after a potentially traumatic event or major life stressor: military deployment, civilian injury and accidents, disaster, illness such as heart attack and cancer, bereavement, job loss, divorce and others. In random-effects pooling the "resilient" trajectory (stable low scores) averaged 65.7% (95% CI 61.6 to 69.8), recovery 20.8% (16.2 to 25.8), chronic high scores 10.6% (8.6 to 12.7) and delayed onset 8.9% (5.3 to 13.3). Each figure is pooled only over the analyses that found that trajectory (63, 49, 47 and 22 of the 67), so the four do not sum to 100. Between-study heterogeneity was above 98% for every trajectory.

Across the same 67 analyses the share in the "resilient" (stable low score) trajectory varied with who was studied and how. It was highest in studies of military deployment (mean 75.3%) and lowest in studies of children (52.0%); the chronic trajectory was largest in studies of refugees and war-exposed civilians (mean 23.8%). Studies with a measurement from before the event found more people in the resilient trajectory (mean 73.7%) than studies that began after it, and events lasting a long time went with more chronic and recovery trajectories than single acute events. The authors found no relation between sample size and trajectory shares. They suggest that training before and support after the event may explain the high share among soldiers, police and firefighters, which they did not test.

889.content: The authors reanalysed the German Socio-Economic Panel data (1984 to 2011) that earlier papers had used to report that most people are resilient: yearly life-satisfaction ratings of 1,214 people who lost a spouse, 1,579 who divorced and 2,461 who became unemployed. With the same model settings as the earlier papers a stable-high "resilient" class was the largest (75%, 85% and 81%). When classes were allowed to differ in how much people varied, and people within a class were allowed to differ in their rate of change, the resilient class was the smaller one: the authors report 47% for spousal loss, 36% for divorce and 48% for unemployment, against 59%, 72% and 69% in the earlier papers.

890.content: Abstract only. The authors ran meta-analyses on 14 risk factors for PTSD among adults exposed to trauma. Gender, age at trauma and race were associated with PTSD in some populations and not in others; education, previous trauma and general childhood adversity were associated more consistently but to varying degrees; psychiatric history, reported childhood abuse and family psychiatric history had more uniform associations. Every factor had a modest effect size taken alone, and factors operating during or after the event (trauma severity, lack of social support, additional life stress) had somewhat stronger effects than factors from before it.

891.content: This meta-analysis pooled studies of trauma-exposed adults outside clinical settings that related self-reported social support to scores on self-report PTSD symptom scales, taken at least one month after the event: 139 studies with 145 cross-sectional effect sizes (62,803 people) and 37 studies with 38 longitudinal effect sizes in which support was measured first (25,792 people). More support and fewer negative social reactions went with lower scores, r = -.27 cross-sectionally (95% CI -.30 to -.24) and r = -.25 longitudinally (95% CI -.28 to -.21). Heterogeneity was high (I2 = 91.6 and 86.5). In the longitudinal studies, support measured after the event was more strongly associated than support measured before it, a difference that rested on four effect sizes and was marginal after adjustment.

In the same meta-analysis the size of the association depended on what was measured and where. Negative social reactions (blame, disbelief, being treated differently) had the largest association with self-report PTSD symptom scores (r = -.40 cross-sectionally), then perceived support (-.27), then structural support such as network size (-.19) and enacted, practical support (-.15). Studies from Western countries showed a larger association (r = -.30) than studies from non-Western countries (r = -.12) in cross-sectional data. Associations were weaker after natural disasters (longitudinal r = -.13) than after combat or war (-.33) and interpersonal violence (-.30), and larger in veteran than in civilian samples (-.31 against -.22). Who gave the support made no difference.

892.content: Among the Turkana of northern Kenya, semi-nomadic herders who raid and are raided for cattle, the authors interviewed 218 men who had each taken part in at least one violent raid, using the PCL-5 checklist translated into Turkana. 62 of the 218 (28%) scored 33 or higher, the threshold used in Western samples for a provisional diagnosis of PTSD. In this area about half of adult male deaths come from combat (about 54% of those on offensive raids and 46% while defending), raiding is at least 200 years old, and firearms replaced spears from the late 1970s. The authors state that the scores show the symptoms are experienced there and do not show a clinically recognised condition, since the checklist is not validated among the Turkana.

The authors sorted the 20 PCL-5 symptoms by proposed function before collecting data. Among Turkana men who scored high, the symptoms they call learning-and-reacting (intrusive memories, nightmares, flashbacks, distress and bodily reactions on reminders, hypervigilance, startle) were as common as among treatment-seeking United States service members who scored high. Five of the seven symptoms the authors class as depressive (the text names low concentration, detachment, irritability, loss of interest and negative feelings), plus avoiding reminders and avoiding memories, were less common among the Turkana; the remaining depressive symptoms (negative beliefs and emotional numbing) were about as common. In models of the Turkana scores, combat exposure and losing animals were positively associated with the learning-and-reacting symptoms and carried more model weight there than for the depressive symptoms, while exposure to moral violations, wider moral concern and exposure to social sanctions were positively associated with the depressive symptoms and carried more weight there. Killing an enemy carried little weight in the models.

The paper records what Turkana communities do after a raid. A successful party is celebrated; the men recount the events to age mates, family and settlement members; men are praised by name for bravery, and those judged cowards are criticised and may be beaten or fined a bull after collective deliberation. Three rituals exist for men who have killed: akiger (scarring that marks and honours the killer, optional), akipur (a purification seen as mandatory, to keep the killer from wasting away) and ngitebus (protection from the ghosts of the slain, done with akipur or after a haunting). One man said he had undergone ngitebus 11 times over 20 years after repeated hauntings. The authors report little or no stigma in talking about combat. In this same population 28% scored at or above the US PCL-5 screening threshold, and the authors suggest, without testing it, that community support may explain the lower depressive symptoms.

893.content: In a preregistered study of 60 Turkana men who had taken part in at least one cattle raid (northern Kenya), 21 scored 33 or higher on the PCL-5 checklist and 39 scored lower. Saliva was taken at about 5:40, 8:00 and 11:00 in the morning. The authors found little evidence that the morning fall in cortisol or in testosterone differed between men with high and low PTSD symptom scores, contrary to reports from Western samples of a blunted daily rhythm in people diagnosed with PTSD. In an earlier sample from the same population, 72% of men reported having killed an enemy in combat and 26% had at least one visible bullet wound.

894.content: Abstract only. Using a binomial equation on the published criteria, the authors report that the DSM-IV criteria for PTSD can be met by 79,794 different combinations of symptoms and the DSM-5 criteria by 636,120 combinations, an eightfold rise. The authors use this to argue that the DSM classification is too heterogeneous for research on reactions to potentially traumatic events.

895.content: Abstract only.
