Haslam proposes that concepts in psychology that refer to negative experience and behaviour have widened in recent decades, outward to new kinds of event and downward to less extreme ones, and illustrates this with abuse, bullying, trauma, mental disorder, addiction and prejudice. He attributes the widening mainly to rising sensitivity to harm and warns that it risks treating everyday experience as pathology.

896.content: The authors tested whether the word "trauma" has come to be used for less severe things in psychology writing. In 825,628 English-language psychology article abstracts from 1970 to 2017 they took the words that appear near "trauma" each year and scored each for severity using published ratings of how negative and how arousing a word is. From 1974 to 2017 the average severity of those neighbouring words fell with year (regression beta -.30 for all words, p = .048; -.37 for nouns, p = .013), and in years when "trauma" was used more often its neighbours were less severe (r = -.32 for all words, -.40 for nouns). The slopes explain 7% and 12% of the year-to-year variance.

897.content: The authors read 1,856 medical files of British servicemen with post-combat disorders from 1854 to 1991 and rated each for flashbacks and ten other signs of PTSD. Flashbacks were recorded in 0 of 28 files from Victorian campaigns, 0 of 400 from the Boer War, 3 of 640 (0.5%) from the First World War, 5 of 367 (1.4%) from the Second World War, 0 of 21 from Malaya and Korea, and 36 of 400 (9.0%) Gulf War veterans. Three of the eight World War cases with flashbacks did not meet DSM-IV criteria for PTSD when their other symptoms were scored. Earlier files recorded bodily symptoms far more often.

On why flashbacks became more common, the authors reject the cinema as the turning point: films were part of popular culture through both World Wars, when flashbacks were recorded in 0.5% and 1.4% of their files. They suggest the change may be tied to television sets in the home from the 1950s and 1960s and later to video recorders, on the ground that television brings sudden disturbing images into a familiar and apparently safe place, and they note that some patients describe flashbacks as like a video recording being played back. The authors offer this as a hypothesis; the files contain no test of it, and they could not study veterans of the Vietnam war, where they think the rise may have begun.

The paper states that PTSD was codified with diagnostic criteria in the third edition of the DSM in 1980, and that the 1980 checklist did not use the word flashback: it described re-experiencing of the trauma through recurrent intrusive recollections, recurrent dreams, or suddenly acting or feeling as if the event were happening again. The word flashback entered the criteria in the 1987 revision. Since the word did not exist during the World Wars, the authors rated old descriptions themselves and counted visual hallucinations in men who were not psychotic.

898.content: Abstract only. Among the Ju/'hoansi of the Kalahari, the authors translated the DSM-IV symptoms of PTSD into the local language and interviewed 10 men and 10 women whom village elders had nominated as affected by domestic violence in the past year. All 20 reported the re-experiencing and arousal symptoms, and 35% met the full DSM-IV criteria for PTSD for incidents in the past year; many who were otherwise distressed did not meet the avoidance criterion.

899.content: Abstract only. Among Samburu warriors, herders of northern Kenya who raid and are raided, the authors related raiding history to DNA methylation at two candidate genes and to PTSD symptom scores. Methylation was associated with overall raiding activity and with reportedly showing mercy to enemies. PTSD symptom scores were not associated with the methylation measures, and the only combat variable associated with the symptom scores was losing one's own livestock in a raid.

900.content: Abstract only. Among 120 Agta of the Philippines interviewed when they still lived as hunter-gatherers, 26% of adult men had survived an attack by a reticulated python (Malayopython reticulatus, synonym Python reticulatus), and six fatal attacks were recorded between 1934 and 1973. The Agta also hunted and ate pythons.

901.content: A scoping review searched four databases to 1 August 2025 and found 134 studies (151,134 participants) whose samples were defined as neurodivergent or neurodiverse. Its Table 2 lists 24 different clinical labels that the studies reported under the word. The most common were autism (92 studies, 68.7%) and ADHD (86, 64.2%), then dyslexia (44), dyspraxia (21), anxiety disorder (20) and dyscalculia (17), and the reported labels also included depression (15), bipolar disorder (8), borderline personality disorder (3) and posttraumatic stress disorder (3). 29 studies (21.6%) reported no clinical label for their sample at all.

In the same review, most studies identified their participants without a clinical assessment. 56 studies (41.8%) reported asking participants which diagnoses they had been given, and 50 studies (37.3%) reported asking only whether participants self-identify as neurodivergent or neurodiverse, without naming any diagnosis. 18 studies (13.4%) used reports from parents, teachers or others, 12 (9.0%) used health records and 10 (7.5%) used screening questionnaires or tests. 56 of the 134 studies (41.8%) used the terms without a formal definition.

The authors state that neither neurodiversity nor neurodivergence is a specific clinical or diagnostic entity. They recommend precise diagnostic descriptors for clinical practice and for research on clinically defined conditions, and they propose keeping the word neurodivergent for studies of self-identification and identity. Co-authors with lived experience of ADHD raised the concern, as the authors report it, that reliance on self-identification may play down functional impairment or hide routes to clinical support.

902.content: In an online survey of 93 Austrian clinical psychologists who each run at least one assessment a week (mean 16.3 years in practice; surveyed 15 June to 5 July 2025), 73.1% reported that emerging-adult patients arrive with a self-diagnosis more often or much more often than before, and 75.3% reported the same for patients who want one specific diagnosis, with none reporting a decrease in wanted diagnoses. The diagnoses the psychologists reported as most often wanted were ADHD (83 psychologists, printed as 88.2%) and autism spectrum disorder (62, 66.7%), and as most often self-diagnosed ADHD (74, 79.6%) and autism spectrum disorder (63, 67.7%). These figures are the clinicians impressions, and the study counted no patients.

The psychologists reported that patients who want a specific diagnosis most often seek relief from guilt or responsibility, formal inclusion in an identity group, and attention or social recognition, and they reported access to treatment less often. For patients who come for confirmation after a self-diagnosis, the psychologists most often reported relief from guilt or responsibility and validation of the patient self-understanding, again ahead of treatment. 55.9% of the psychologists reported that they always or often ask about motives when they suspect a wanted diagnosis. The text gives no percentages for the motives, which are shown in figures 3 and 4.

In open answers (359 coded statements) the psychologists most often reported patients rejecting a result that did not match the diagnosis they expected (57 statements), emotional reactions such as disappointment or anger (42), criticism of the clinician (33), pressure such as threats of legal action or of non-payment (24) and moving on to further psychologists until the wanted diagnosis is given (6). Three anecdotes report a personality disorder or bipolar diagnosis given in place of the ADHD diagnosis the patient wanted, each met with distress or anger. The authors report that answers shaped by the wanted diagnosis made it hard to tell actual symptoms from malingering, and they give no count of either.

903.content: In an editorial from Scotland's National Autism Implementation Team, the authors define neurodivergent as describing individuals whose neurocognitive functions or neurodevelopmental differences fall outside prevalent societal norms, and they state that such individuals do not necessarily have a neurodevelopmental disorder. The authors write that neurodiversity, neurodiverse, neurodivergent and neurotypical describe subsets of the normal population marked off by the limits of current societal norms, and they reserve the word disorder for function at an extreme with significant functional impairment.

The authors state that DSM-5 and ICD-11 both describe the ADHD and autism spectrum diagnoses as lifelong traits that vary across the population, with no separation between normality and diagnosis, and that a diagnosis is given when traits outside the limits of normal variation go with significant functional impairment. They report that a small number of diagnosed people have symptoms from a specific pathology such as fragile-X syndrome, while the majority have traits at one end of, and probably within, normal variation with no specific aetiology. They state that people with extreme traits and no functional impairment do not have a diagnosis, and that all the viewpoints they review put environmental adjustment first.

904.content: Abstract only. Mothers and newborns from maternity hospital wards were assigned to a supplementary carrying group, a group advised to increase responsive parenting, or a control group (59, 57 and 94 infants at 6 weeks). Diaries confirmed that the carrying group carried more, up to the target level, while the responsiveness advice brought only limited increases in carrying, a modest increase in feeding frequency and no change in parental interaction or play. Audio recordings, parent diaries and parent ratings found no difference in crying or fussing between the three groups at 2, 6 or 12 weeks, and carrying while settled was not significantly correlated with fussing and crying. The authors conclude that neither intervention can at present be recommended as a way to prevent infant crying.

905.content: Using the public dataset of the 522 acute antidepressant trials collected by Cipriani and others, the authors pooled the placebo-controlled trials that reported continuous scores: 109 trials (32,399 patients) on the 17-item Hamilton scale and 28 trials (11,705 patients) on the Montgomery-Asberg scale, in adults diagnosed with major depression, mostly over 8 weeks. The mean drug-placebo gap was 2.07 points (95% CI 1.76 to 2.37) on the Hamilton scale, which runs from 0 to 52, and 2.99 points (2.24 to 3.74) on the Montgomery-Asberg scale, which runs from 0 to 60, that is 4% and 5% of the top of each scale. The authors set this against published thresholds of about 7 and 8 points for a clinician to notice a minimal improvement, and about 4 and 5 points for a minimal important difference by patient-oriented ratings.

The same analysis tested the claim that the Hamilton scale hides the benefit of the drugs. The pooled standardised difference was 0.27 (0.23 to 0.30) on the 17-item Hamilton scale and 0.30 (0.22 to 0.38) on the Montgomery-Asberg scale, a gap of 0.03 that was not significant (p = 0.47 by subgroup analysis). The authors add that most trials were industry-sponsored and at high or unclear risk of bias for allocation concealment and blinding, and they call the reported sizes upper-bound estimates. The analysis was post hoc, had no protocol, and used the trial search of Cipriani and others.

906.content: A review of visual cliff and real drop-off experiments argues that there is no compelling evidence for fear of heights in human infants. Infants avoid a drop-off only after several weeks of crawling or walking experience, and the avoidance does not carry over to a new posture: infants who refuse a gap while sitting go over the edge when newly crawling, and new walkers walk over slopes and cliffs they refused as experienced crawlers. Infants who avoid show positive or neutral faces and voices, stay at the edge and look for other ways down, and treat a 71 cm drop and a 17 cm drop alike. The authors read the avoidance as learned perception of what the body can do, and they report that there are no longitudinal data on when and how fear of heights later develops.

The same review reports the evidence on the other side: crawling infants show a faster heart rate when placed on the deep side of the visual cliff and infants who cannot yet crawl do not, and kittens, goats and other animals freeze or back away when placed there. The authors answer that two weeks of crawling is enough for the faster heart rate and not for avoidance, so the heart rate may reflect arousal. They also report that studies of adults find fear of heights does not need a conditioning event such as a traumatic fall, and that about 30% of adults report height fear and about 5% a height phobia in the surveys they cite.

907.content: A review of the stranger-approach studies concludes that fear of strangers is no universal stage of infancy. Small early studies reported it in nearly every infant (18 of 19, 36 of 36, 14 of 14). In one later study at most 33% of infants showed any distress in any phase of the session; across studies smiling, looking and offering toys were the most common responses; and one laboratory reported that among more than 500 infants aged 10 and 12 months only the rare baby showed anything like fear of the stranger. The authors conclude that some infants do fear strangers, with negative affect, attempts to get away and physiological change, and that this subset tends to have an inhibited temperament.

The same review reports what raises and lowers infants negative reactions to a stranger across studies. Almost no infants react negatively when tested at home and some do in the laboratory, and reactions are fewer when the mother is present, when the infant sits on her lap, and when the infant has had time to get used to the room. A slow approach that stops a few feet away draws few negative responses, while a rapid approach, a touch or an attempt to pick the infant up draws more; a child stranger draws almost none and a full-sized adult the most. With the mother holding a 9-month-old no infant cried and under 10% looked uneasy; seated on the floor about 10% cried and about 45% looked uneasy; when the stranger picked the infant up 60% cried or looked uneasy.

908.content: In laboratory house mice (Mus musculus, strain C57BL6/J), a dark disc expanding overhead on a ceiling monitor, the optical pattern of an object approaching from above, set off either flight to a nest within a second or prolonged freezing, on the animal first exposure to it. In the first test of 10 animals, 3 began to flee less than 250 ms after the disc appeared, and the animals that did not flee froze. A white expanding disc, a dimming disc of constant size and a receding disc did not produce the sub-second flight, and the same disc shown from below produced no escape. The authors call the response innate and read it as defence against aerial predators.

909.content: Abstract only. 24 infants aged 2 to 11 weeks responded to a symmetrically expanding shadow, the optical pattern of an object on a collision course, with an integrated avoidance response and upset. They did not respond this way to asymmetrically expanding shadows (an object on a miss path) or to contracting shadows (a receding object). The response was observed in all the infants regardless of age. In a second experiment 7 infants reacted defensively to the approach of a real object, except when it was on a miss path.

910.content: Abstract only. Infant and adult rhesus monkeys (Macaca mulatta) showed persistent avoidance responses to a symmetrically expanding closed contour in the field of view, the optical equivalent of an impending collision, and showed none to the same sequence run in reverse. The authors state that this visual stimulus alone is a strong exciter of avoidance and that the response appears early in life.

911.content: Abstract only. In two laboratory studies with 25 adults each, acoustic startle stimuli were delivered in alternating periods of complete darkness and light. In both studies darkness significantly increased the size of the startle reflex and left prepulse inhibition unchanged, which the authors read as a change in affect and not in attention. The size of the increase in the dark correlated significantly with how strongly participants rated their own fear of the dark as children, on retrospective rating scales.

912.content: In rural southern Tanzania, where lions (Panthera leo) attacked more than 1,000 people between 1988 and 2009 and over two-thirds of the attacks were fatal, the authors analysed 474 victims with known attack times. The vast majority were attacked after dark, nearly 60% between 18:00 and 21:45, and hourly attack rates were 2 to 4 times higher in the 10 days after the full moon, when the early evening is moonless, than in the 10 days before it. In Serengeti and Ngorongoro lions, food intake was also highest on the darkest nights (belly-size records, 7,683 sightings of females). The authors state that before this study no empirical data existed on how darkness changes the risk of predation on humans.

913.content: Abstract only. In a large New Zealand birth cohort followed from childhood (authors at Dunedin Medical School), a history of falls with injury (fracture, dislocation, intracranial injury or laceration) before age 9 showed no positive relationship with fear of heights at age 11 or at 18. Injurious falls between ages 5 and 9 were more frequent among those without a fear of heights at 18 (P < 0.01), the opposite of what a conditioning account expects. The authors read this as support for non-associative accounts, in which height fear needs no frightening event to start.

914.content: 110 adults aged 23 to 26 (51 women; pairs of friends, dating, cohabiting and married partners) lay in an fMRI scanner under threat of electric shock while alone, while holding the hand of a stranger, and while holding the hand of their partner. Threat-related activity in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and posterior cingulate was lower with the partner hand than alone, and activity in four regions was lower with the partner hand than with the stranger hand. Holding the hand of a stranger gave no reduction compared with being alone, and participants rated the stranger condition as more negative than both others. Rated negativity alone against partner was a non-significant trend (P = .08), and the kind of relationship made no difference.

915.content: A systematic review of longitudinal studies that followed people from unemployment into work, each with a comparison group, found 18 studies, one of them a randomised trial. In 15 of the 18, returning to work went with better health: either health improved after re-employment or it declined in those who stayed unemployed. Most outcomes were mental health measures such as depression and distress scores; in 541 middle-aged US women, for example, depressive symptoms scored on the Beck inventory fell among the newly employed and rose among the others over 3 years. The studies were too varied to pool, and the search ended in 2005.

The same review found selection running the other way: poor health, high distress included, made people less likely to get back into work, and the authors conclude that only a portion of the link between re-employment and health is causal. They could not determine whether returning to work fully or only partly reverses the health decline that goes with job loss. They found some evidence that re-employment within 6 months of job loss goes with better health than later re-employment.

916.content: In Singapore, 196 low-income adults with chronic debt were surveyed before and 3 months after a charity paid off up to 5,000 Singapore dollars of their debts (about three months of household income). The share who met the DSM-IV symptom criteria for generalised anxiety, which the authors used as a measure of the response to poverty and debt and not as a diagnosis, fell from 78% to 53%, and 38% of those with the symptoms before no longer had them after. Each additional debt account cleared went with an 11% lower likelihood of the anxiety symptoms, while the amount of money alone showed no association. Error rates on an attention task fell from 17% to 4%. There was no untreated comparison group, and the authors call their evidence quasi-experimental.

917.content: Read in the 2018 working-paper version. 3,362 Swedish lottery players were surveyed 5 to 22 years after a draw (69% response), and the analysis compared players within groups where prize size was random, following a pre-registered plan. Per 100,000 US dollars won, overall life satisfaction was higher by 0.037 SD and satisfaction with finances by 0.067 SD, while happiness (0.016 SD) and a mental health score from the 12-item General Health Questionnaire (0.013 SD) did not differ significantly from zero. The authors calculate that the three earlier lottery studies that reported mental health gains had about 5 to 7% statistical power.

918.content: Read in the accepted-manuscript version. In the British Household Panel Survey, 137 reports of lottery or pools wins of 1,000 to 120,000 pounds were compared with people who reported no win or a small win. Two years after the win, the winners score on the 12-item General Health Questionnaire, a self-rated measure of mental strain on a 36-point scale, had improved by 1.4 points relative to the comparison groups. In the year of the win itself, mental strain went up on average.

919.content: Abstract only. In a longitudinal community study, half of the cases that the authors classified as neurotic disorder at first interview had remitted one month later. Remission was significantly related to a recent onset, a recent peak, a recent threatening life event and a later "neutralizing" event, defined in advance as an event that cancelled the impact of an earlier threatening event or difficulty. The authors attribute one third of all remissions to such an event. Remission was not significantly related to demographic variables, severity, syndrome type, medical consultation or psychotropic drug prescription.

920.content: Abstract only. 86 Dutch primary care patients diagnosed as depressed with the Present State Examination (69% women, mean age 36.6) were followed for 3.5 years, with life changes rated on the Life Events and Difficulties Schedule. In Cox regression, positive life change shortened the time to remission in women and not in men, and its association with remission was stronger in people scoring high on neuroticism. Low severity of earlier difficulties, high self-esteem and a tension-reducing coping style also went with faster remission.

921.content: Fisher and colleagues scanned 10 women and 5 men (mean age 19.8) who had been rejected by a partner an average of 63 days earlier and said they were still intensely in love. Looking at a photo of the person who left them, compared with a photo of a familiar neutral person, went with activity in the ventral tegmental area on both sides, the ventral striatum, medial and lateral orbitofrontal and prefrontal cortex and the cingulate gyrus, areas the authors tie to gains and losses, craving and emotion regulation. The more days since the break-up, the less activity in the right ventral putamen and pallidum. Activity in the anterior ventral pallidum was not predicted; the authors speculate that it reflects attachment, on the strength of prairie vole work.

Fisher and colleagues report the result of Jankowiak and Fischer's survey of the ethnographic record: of 166 societies, evidence of romantic love was found in 147. They add that the other 19 held no evidence against it and that the gap was ethnographic oversight. This is a second-hand report; the 1992 paper itself was not read.

922.content: Acevedo and colleagues scanned 10 women and 7 men from the New York area, aged 39 to 67 and married 10 to 29 years (mean 21.4), who said they were still intensely in love with their spouse. Looking at the spouse's face, compared with a close friend and a familiar acquaintance, went with activity in the ventral tegmental area and dorsal striatum, as in studies of new love, and in regions tied to maternal attachment in other studies (globus pallidus, substantia nigra, raphe nucleus, thalamus, insula, anterior and posterior cingulate). The sample was picked for intense love: recruitment asked 'Are you still madly in love with your long-term partner?' and about 40 percent of callers were screened out.

923.content: Aron and colleagues scanned 10 women and 7 men who had been intensely in love for 1 to 17 months. Looking at a photo of the loved person, compared with a photo of a familiar person, went with activity in the right ventral tegmental area and the right caudate nucleus, dopamine-rich areas tied to reward and motivation in mammals. Activity in the right anteromedial caudate rose with scores on a passionate love scale. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

924.content: Xu and colleagues repeated the Aron 2005 procedure in Beijing with 18 Chinese participants in early-stage romantic love. Looking at the loved person's face, compared with a familiar acquaintance, went with activity in the ventral tegmental area and the caudate, as in the earlier US and UK studies. The authors also found activity that varied with how traditional or modern a participant's attitudes were, and activity in two areas that went with relationship happiness 18 months later. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

925.content: In a random sample of 274 married people in the United States, 40 percent of those married more than 10 years rated themselves 'very intensely in love'. In a second random sample of 322 people in New York State married more than 10 years, 29 percent did. Intense love went with thinking positively about the partner, affection and sex, shared novel and challenging activities and general happiness. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

926.content: Finkel and colleagues argue that Americans now ask their marriage for different things than in the past: less for food, shelter and safety, and more for esteem and personal growth, on top of friendship, emotional intimacy and sexual fulfilment. Meeting those needs takes time and attention, and the authors hold that spouses on average invest less of both than before, so that average marital quality falls while the best marriages do better than marriages of earlier eras. They call this the suffocation model. It is a model built from historical and survey work and is not itself a tested result.

Finkel and colleagues review US survey findings on married people's ties outside the marriage. In one analysis, never-married adults were 62 percent more likely than married adults to see their parents and 81 percent more likely to see their siblings at least weekly, 77 percent more likely to spend social evenings with neighbours and 133 percent more likely to do so with friends several times a month (Gerstel and Sarkisian 2006, model values with controls). Time that married Americans spent with friends or relatives without the spouse on a weekend day fell between 1975 and 2003, by 24 percent for those without children at home and 53 percent for those with children (Dew 2009). Spouses reported 6.0 close friends in 1980 and 5.4 in 2000 (Amato and colleagues 2009).

The same review reports that time spouses spent alone together also fell in US time diaries between 1975 and 2003: by 30 percent on weekdays and 17 percent on weekend days for couples without children at home, and by 40 percent on weekdays for couples with children at home, whose weekend time together did not change (Dew 2009). Averaged over the two years, couples without children at home had 3.77 hours together on a weekday and 6.00 on a weekend day; couples with children had 1.54 and 1.76.

927.content: Across two studies, people who spread their needs for emotional support over several different relationships, each used for a particular emotion, had higher well-being than people with as many close relationships who leaned on fewer of them for everything. Paraphrased from the abstract only; the abstract gives no sample sizes or effect sizes.

928.content: In two US national surveys (National Survey of Families and Households 1992 to 1994; General Social Survey 2000, 2004, 2006 and 2012), single adults were more likely than married adults to stay in frequent touch with, give help to and get help from parents, siblings, neighbours and friends. The gap was larger for the never married than for the previously married and held for women and men, and much of it remained after controls for life stage and income. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

929.content: Hewlett and colleagues bring together divorce figures from ten hunter-gatherer and forager-farmer populations. Reported rates: Agta 18 percent, Tsimane 20, Aka 27 (4 of 15 couples over five years), Paliyan 35, Chabu 46, Bofi 54, Ache 61 (by the end of the first year of marriage, in the forest period), Hadza 24 to 39 and !Kung 8 to 37 depending on how long the marriage had lasted, and north Alaskan Inuit close to 100 (nearly every couple separated at least once). The authors' summary is that at least a quarter to a third of hunter-gatherer marriages end in divorce, that divorce is informal, and that remarriage is common. The rates are not measured the same way across populations.

The same review tabulates how many mates or marriages adults had over their reproductive years: Ache men 10.8 and women 11.7; Hadza men 3.3 and women 1.6; !Kung women 2.5; Bofi women 2.2; Aka women 1.9; Hiwi women 1.7; BaYaka men 1.6 and women 1.1; Paliyan 2.4 for both sexes. It also reports Marlowe's estimate that perhaps 20 percent of Hadza stay married to the same person for life, that every Efe man over 40 had married at least twice, and that among the Chabu 47 percent of adults had divorced at least once and 22 percent at least twice.

930.content: Winking and Gurven describe marriage in five populations from the original demographic studies. Ache women (pre-contact forest period) averaged 12.1 husbands in a lifetime, and about 63 percent of children had a secondary father. Hiwi women averaged 1.7 husbands, and marriages were mostly monogamous and long-lasting. !Kung women reported an average of 2.45 husbands; first marriages were typically arranged by parents and often ended within weeks or months. Tsimane women average about 1.4 spouses, and divorce is very rare after the first years of marriage.

Using mortality and fertility schedules for the Ache, Hadza, Hiwi, !Kung and Tsimane, Winking and Gurven calculate how many children a man would lose through lower child survival if he left his wife, and how much younger a second wife would have to be to make up the loss. Children without a father died at 1 (Hadza) to 2.54 (Tsimane) times the rate of children with one before age five, and because child deaths fall quickly with age, the loss from leaving was small in all five populations; a second wife only modestly younger made up for it. The authors conclude that higher child survival is too small a return to explain why men stay, and point to women's choice of partner instead.

931.content: Among the Tsimane of lowland Bolivia, forager-horticulturalists living in villages of related families, young people have some say in whom they marry and parents often arrange a match. The preferred partner is a cross-cousin (the child of a mother's brother or a father's sister), and brothers and sisters often pair off their children with each other, though the children can and do choose someone else. In data on 622 marriages, a father helped his son or daughter get a spouse in 36 percent. Parents weigh in more on daughters' marriages than on sons'. A man with no partner in sight looks in other villages and courts for a few weeks while the woman and her family judge him. About 20 percent of marriages end in divorce.

The same study tested whether Tsimane adults whose father died while they were children did worse. Of five outcomes (adult height, body mass index, age at first child, number of children for age, surviving children for age), only the body mass index of adult daughters was lower. The authors conclude there is no substantial evidence that Tsimane fathers have a large effect on how their children do as adults, although Tsimane men provide a lot and rarely divorce.

932.content: Among the Hadza of Tanzania, 159 married adults (83 men, 76 women) answered a shortened love scale by interview, with intimacy, passion and commitment each rated on three steps, and reported the children born in their current marriage. Commitment went with more children in both sexes. Among women, passion went with more children and intimacy with fewer. The authors note that the order cannot be settled: having children may raise commitment.

Sorokowski and colleagues describe Hadza marriage, citing Marlowe's ethnography: marriages are typically not arranged, divorce is common, about 4 percent of men have two wives and nearly all adults are married. They describe the Hadza as a society where individuals, and not their parents, were responsible for choosing a partner.

933.content: Apostolou coded 40 variables from historians' accounts of 16 historical societies spanning about 5,000 years, from Pharaonic Egypt and Babylon through Classical Greece and Imperial Rome to later states. In 15 of the 16, the main way to marry was arrangement, with parents choosing the spouse; the record for the Incas was inconclusive. Fathers made the decision in 10 societies. In 9 societies parents controlled daughters' marriages more than sons'. A daughter's opinion was recorded as not considered in 6 societies and considered in 2. Divorce existed in 14 and extramarital relationships were reported in 11. The author notes that the sources were written by men and mostly describe the upper class.

In this paper Apostolou restates the result of his 2007 study: across 190 contemporary hunting and gathering societies the main way of mating is arranged marriage, and marriage by free courtship prevails in only a small minority. He calls the step from present-day foragers to ancestral ones 'inferential'.

934.content: Rosenfeld followed a nationally representative US panel of 3,009 adults with partners from 2009 to 2015 (How Couples Meet and Stay Together). Couples who met online broke up no more often than couples who met offline once the length of the relationship was taken into account: among couples who met after 1995, the offline group broke up at 7.3 percent a year, and the online group, set to the same profile, at 7.0 percent, a difference too small to tell from zero. Heterosexual couples who met online, and most of all on dating sites, married sooner. The author says he measures no causal effect of the internet.

935.content: In a US sample of 19,131 people who married between 2005 and 2012, described by the authors as nationally representative, more than a third of marriages began online. Marriages that began online were slightly less likely to have ended in separation or divorce, and those still married rated their marriage slightly higher, than marriages that began offline; both differences held after controls for demographic differences. The survey was commissioned by the dating company eHarmony, and two authors had ties to it. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

936.content: Sinclair and colleagues repeated a 1972 study that had found love growing when parents interfered (the 'Romeo and Juliet effect'). They followed 396 people in relationships for 3 to 4 months and found no such effect: people who reported more interference or less approval from family and friends reported lower love, commitment and trust on every measure. The authors report that a meta-analysis showed the same. Paraphrased from the abstract only.

937.content: A meta-analysis of 137 studies with 37,761 participants, collected over 33 years, looked at what comes before the break-up of dating relationships. Commitment, love and closeness were among the strongest signs of a couple staying together; satisfaction, alternatives and investments were modest ones; and support for the relationship from the couple's social network was a robust one. Personality measures added little. Paraphrased from the abstract only, which gives no effect sizes.

938.content: MacDonald and Hewlett compiled mating distances (how far apart spouses come from) within and across cultures and report that mating distance goes with population density among foragers and among farmers: the fewer people per area, the farther people go for a spouse. In every culture with data, men travelled farther than women over a lifetime, and among Aka foragers of Central Africa distance travelled varied with age and sex. Paraphrased from the abstract only; the abstract gives no distances.

939.content: Rowland retested the red-belly finding with dummies shown to territorial male three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus). The abstract reports that the males did not always attack a dummy with red undersides more than one without, and that overall they tended to bite the dummy without red more, both when the two were shown together and when they were shown one after the other. Attack rates rose once a male had eggs in his nest, and the tendency to attack the non-red dummy more stayed the same. The abstract gives no sample size.

940.content: Rowland and Sevenster repeated Tinbergen's dummy experiments with territorial male three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus) from a Long Island and a Dutch population. Males from both populations generally bit a silver male dummy more than a male dummy with red undersides and blue eyes; a few males in each population did the opposite. In the Dutch trials males backed off from the coloured dummy more often than from the silver one. Males directed more bites to a level dummy than to a head-up or head-down one, and courted a dummy female more the more swollen its abdomen was, also when the swelling was beyond the natural range. The abstract gives no sample sizes.

941.content: In a field experiment in two lakes on Vancouver Island, 3D-printed painted models of a male three-spined stickleback (Gasterosteus aculeatus) were hung 30 cm from the nests of wild males; usable video came from 16 males in Gosling Lake and 13 in Blackwater Lake. Where the resident males are mostly red (Gosling), red-throated models were inspected or bitten 20 percent more often than melanic models (medians 3 against 2.5). Where the resident males are mostly black (Blackwater), melanic models got 50 percent more bites than red ones (medians 1.5 against 1), a difference that was significant only with nest depth in the model. The authors conclude that no one colour is inherently attacked more; the colour attacked more is the locally common one.

In the pilot for the same experiment, nesting male three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus) attacked painted fish-shaped models and did not respond to unpainted models or to cylinders. The paper gives no numbers for the pilot.

942.content: In a tank experiment with 10 male and 10 female three-spined sticklebacks (Gasterosteus aculeatus), each fish first lived next to a territorial neighbour and was then shown photographs that combined the face and the body of that neighbour or of a stranger. Both sexes attacked photographs with a stranger's face for longer than photographs with the neighbour's face, whatever body was attached. The share of the photographed male's body that was red had no effect on how long focal males attacked (F1,16 = 0.05, p = 0.83), and on the first day four males without red were attacked intensively. The authors conclude that these fish tell a familiar neighbour from a stranger by the face.

943.content: Tagged pike (Esox lucius) in a drainable pond were fished by hook and line with either a spinner or a small live fish, and every pike caught was put back. With the spinner, catchability fell to very low levels after about half of the population had been caught that way, and it was difficult to catch the same pike on a spinner twice. With live bait, catchability stayed the same after intensive fishing of both kinds, and recaptures matched what chance predicts. The abstract gives no numbers of fish.

944.content: In a controlled catch-and-release experiment in a 25 ha lake north-east of Berlin, anglers fished 3232 sessions of 15 minutes for northern pike (Esox lucius) with two standard artificial lures at 30 fixed sites and caught 313 pike. Soft plastic shads caught more pike than metal spoons (0.08 against 0.06 pike per 15 minutes). Catch rates fell over the seven days of a fishing week, which the authors read as learning or as pike moving out of reach after capture. The model explained little of the variation (pseudo-R2 0.16).

The authors, fisheries scientists working on northern pike (Esox lucius), state that the lure industry keeps releasing new lure types, colours, shapes and attractants, and that little is known scientifically about whether these innovations raise catch rates. This is their reading of the literature in 2017, with three exceptions named.

945.content: Subadult muskellunge (Esox masquinongy), a close relative of the northern pike, were filmed feeding on fathead minnows with their senses intact, with the lateral line chemically suppressed, blinded, or with one side of either sense removed. The fish stalk slowly and then lunge. Vision was used to pick up the prey at a distance; both vision and the lateral line (the sense for water movement) shaped when the strike began, and blinded fish did not stalk and lunged only at prey close by. The abstract gives no animal numbers.

946.content: Northern pike (Esox lucius) in tanks were offered fantail and regular-tail goldfish, or goldfish of different colours. The look of the prey did not change which fish the pike ate. In pool trials with four prey species the pike always took carp and fathead minnow over two sunfish species, whether the pike were fed or had gone 2 or 4 weeks without food. The abstract gives no numbers.

947.content: Among adult female American black bears (Ursus americanus) followed with GPS collars near Durango, Colorado, bears whose summer hair carried more carbon-13 (the study's marker of eating human food) hibernated for a shorter time the next winter. This link was tested on 15 bears over one winter; the model with the food marker alone had an adjusted R2 of 0.44. Across the 30 bears of the study, bears that hibernated for less time lost telomere length faster (adjusted R2 0.12), which the authors read as faster cellular ageing.

In the same study of 30 adult female American black bears (Ursus americanus) near Durango, Colorado, every bear hibernated. Hibernation lasted 170 days on average, with a range from 134 to 223 days. So the bears that ate more human food slept for fewer weeks; none stayed awake through the winter.

948.content: Among 104 female American black bears (Ursus americanus) followed in three areas of Maine from 1982 to 1988, most bears in the two northern areas entered dens in mid to late October in years when beechnuts were scarce and in mid to late November in the alternate years when nuts were abundant. Year-to-year variation in den entry was not strongly tied to autumn weather. Pregnant females tended to den earlier than other females. Bears came out in April within 7 days of the last snow melt, and denning lasted 134 to 197 days. The authors conclude that black bears generally stay active in autumn until they use more energy than they take in.

949.content: Using GPS collar data from 131 den events of 51 adult female American black bears (Ursus americanus), the authors report that weather and food both shaped hibernation. Warmer temperatures were most strongly associated with den timing: they shortened hibernation and brought spring emergence forward. More natural food and more use of human food around development both went with later den entry in autumn and shorter hibernation.

950.content: Brown bears (Ursus arctos) in Slovenia, where corn is put out at feeding sites all year including winter, were followed by GPS telemetry. They denned for 82 days (females) and 57 days (males) on average, 45 and 56 percent less than a comparison across bear populations gives for that latitude. 61 percent of the bears left their dens during winter, on average 1.9 times, and bears used the feeding sites 61 percent more in the winter period than outside it. The abstract gives no number of bears.

951.content: Fourteen free-ranging brown bears (Ursus arctos) in Sweden were followed over three winters with GPS collars, heart monitors and body temperature loggers. Activity, heart rate and body temperature began to fall slowly several weeks before the bears entered their dens. The bears entered dens when snow arrived and the air temperature reached 0 degrees Celsius. The authors conclude that hibernation was started mainly by cues from the environment and ended by cues from the body. Food supply was not measured.

952.content: A review of the brown bear (Ursus arctos) denning literature reports that den timing varies with snow, temperature, food availability, den altitude, sex and reproductive state. A fall in food availability is named as the main influence on the hibernation period, and food still available in late autumn delays den entry; pregnant females are the exception and den while berries are still abundant. Brown bears do not have to hibernate: where food stays available and the climate is mild, some bears spend the winter outside dens.

The same review reports that where brown bears (Ursus arctos) can get human-provided food, and above all where they are fed at feeding sites, studies have found denning periods cut by more than half, or more bears leaving their dens in winter, compared with populations at a similar latitude without such food. The authors call for more research on the effects.

953.content: African ball-rolling dung beetles (the abstract names no species; the same group's 2017 paper names Scarabaeus satyrus) rolled their dung balls along straight paths under a starlit sky with no moon and lost this ability when the sky was overcast. In a planetarium they kept their line equally well under a full starry sky and when only the Milky Way was shown. The abstract adds that these beetles also use the sun, the moon and the pattern of polarised light in the sky. It gives no numbers.

954.content: The nocturnal dung beetle (Scarabaeus satyrus) shapes a ball at a fresh dung pile and rolls it away in a straight line, away from the pile and from competing beetles, until it can bury and eat the ball undisturbed. To hold the line it uses the sky cues available, which the authors list as the moon, the pattern of polarised moonlight and the Milky Way. This is the authors' summary of earlier work by the same group, given as the background of the paper.

In laboratory tests nocturnal dung beetles (Scarabaeus satyrus) were given artificial light patterns in place of the night sky. With two light spots of equal brightness they were not oriented (n = 24); with two spots that differed in brightness they held their line well (n = 20). The authors conclude that the beetle steers by comparing brightness between regions of the Milky Way, and they measured a contrast threshold of 13 percent, enough to tell the brighter southern arm of the Milky Way from the northern arm.

955.content: In behavioural experiments at light-polluted and dark-sky sites, paired with photographs of each sky, the authors report that light pollution hid the natural sky cues from dung beetles (the abstract names no species). The beetles then relied on bright lights on the ground in place of their sky compass. The abstract states that this change brings attraction toward artificial lights, more competition between individual beetles and less efficient dispersal. It gives no numbers.

956.content: Two independent mark and recapture studies of common toads (Bufo bufo), one in England and one in Sweden, followed adults between spawning ponds in 1987 to 1990. In any year, 79 to 96 percent of the adults that lived to breed the next year came back to the same pond. In England large numbers of toadlets were also marked in 1984 and 1985: of the males that later came back as breeding adults, 81 percent were caught in the pond they came from. Moves between ponds were rarer the further apart the ponds were. The abstract gives no figure for females marked as toadlets.

957.content: During the 1971 breeding migration of common toads (Bufo bufo), the author counted the females killed by traffic on an asphalt road carrying about 10 cars an hour and estimated the total number of females from the egg strings in the water. About 30 percent of the females that crossed the road were run over, and the author expects a similar share for males. The abstract names no site and gives no counts.

958.content: Volunteers in the United Kingdom and Switzerland have carried common toads (Bufo bufo) across roads on their spring breeding migration since the 1970s, and counted them. Using the 153 UK and 141 Swiss populations with at least 5 years of counts, the authors estimate that toads declined in each decade since the 1980s in both countries; in the UK the mean yearly growth rate was 0.989 for 1985 to 1994, 0.929 for 1995 to 2004 and 0.973 for 2005 to 2014. The authors state that the reasons remain unknown and that road deaths are one possible reason next to climate, farming, habitat loss and disease.

The same paper reports, from another author's records, that at three sites in Cambridgeshire where nobody carried common toads (Bufo bufo) across the road and road deaths and traffic were recorded every year from 1974, all three populations had collapsed by 2010. The authors also state that toads on spring migration typically make up the largest share of road-killed amphibians across much of Europe.

959.content: At 37 places in the Austrian state of Salzburg where amphibians cross a road on their spring migration, temporary fences with pitfall traps were set up each year from 1995 to 2015 and the animals were counted and carried over. Across these sites the common toad (Bufo bufo) was stable: the index for 2015 stood at 96 percent (plus or minus 21) of the 1995 value. The common frog (Rana temporaria) at the same sites fell to 17 percent (plus or minus 4) of its 1995 value, for which the authors name habitat destruction as the main likely reason.

960.content: Green turtle (Chelonia mydas) and loggerhead (Caretta caretta) hatchlings were tested in an arena where light and slope could be set. Both species headed toward the more brightly lit part of the arena, and both headed away from dark shapes that stood for a raised horizon, as the view toward land has. They responded mainly to what was at or near eye level. When a dark shape and a brightness difference pointed in different directions, the hatchlings headed away from the dark shape and ignored the brightness. The authors conclude that hatchlings of both species usually find the sea by heading away from raised dark shapes. The abstract gives no numbers.

961.content: From hatchling tracks at natural nests, at chosen release sites and in a walled wooden arena on the beach, the authors propose a ranking of cues for marine turtle hatchlings (the abstract names no species). Hatchlings move toward the lowest line of the horizon. They move away from high dark shapes while staying close to the lowest horizon. Only where it is unclear which way the horizon is lowest do they move toward the brightest low horizon. The authors propose that bright lights near a beach hide the horizon line, so the lights become the only horizon the hatchling can see, and it moves toward them. The abstract gives no numbers.

962.content: On Barrow Island, Western Australia, 595 flatback turtle hatchlings (genus Natator, which has this one species; the full Latin name is in the scope line) were released in a beach arena 150 m from a bank of industrial lights of three types at three brightness levels. With no lights the hatchlings headed for the ocean (mean bearing 358 degrees, r = 0.96). With the lights behind a high dune (a dark skyline 16 degrees high) the hatchlings stayed more ocean-oriented than with the same lights in a low creek bed (a bright skyline 2 degrees high): at medium and high brightness of all three light types they were significantly less ocean-oriented at 2 degrees than at 16 degrees.

963.content: Loggerhead turtle (Caretta caretta) hatchlings from a Florida hatchery were made to crawl toward a light on the landward side of a dark beach and were then released. After a 2 minute crawl toward land they still swam offshore when there were waves, and failed to swim offshore in a calm sea (10 turtles per group). After a 2 hour crawl toward the light they took longer to find the sea (14.4 minutes on average against 9.3 for undisturbed turtles, 10 per group), many on winding paths, and 2 of the 10 did not reach the surf within 25 minutes.

The same paper sums up earlier work on sea turtle hatchlings (loggerhead, Caretta caretta, and other species). Hatchlings come out of the nest at night and head away from raised, darker skylines on the land side and toward the open, lower, brighter horizon over the sea. Artificial light makes them crawl toward the lights, or leaves them unable to hold any direction; they may then crawl for hours, tire, dry out and meet more predators. The authors cite an estimate that tens of thousands of hatchlings die each year in this way (Witherington 1997, a book chapter I did not read; the paper names no region for the figure).

964.content: On a nesting beach on Lanyu Island, Taiwan, green turtle (Chelonia mydas) hatchlings from 21 nests were released in a 3 m arena beside a portable street lamp. With the lamp off most hatchlings crawled toward the ocean. Under white light, of 261 hatchlings 173 (69 percent) ended on the lamp side and 13 (5 percent) on the ocean side. Under yellow light, of 273 hatchlings 33 (13 percent) ended on the lamp side and 81 (31 percent) on the ocean side. The brightness setting of the lamp made no difference, and a shield on the lamp let more hatchlings find the sea on moonlit nights.

965.content: In the RADAR trial, 253 adults in 19 NHS Trusts in England who were diagnosed with schizophrenia or another recurrent non-affective psychotic disorder and were prescribed an antipsychotic were randomised to a gradual, flexible dose reduction over months (126) or to maintenance (127), open label with masked assessors. By 24 months 32 (25 percent) of the reduction group and 17 (13 percent) of the maintenance group had a severe relapse, which the trial defined as admission to hospital (hazard ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.2 to 4.0), and any relapse was recorded in 52 (41 percent) against 28 (22 percent). Totals on the self-report Social Functioning Scale, the primary outcome, did not differ at 24 months (difference 0.19 points, 95% CI -1.94 to 2.33).

In RADAR the reduction group reached a median cut of 67 percent from the baseline dose at some point and 33 percent at 24 months, the trial reported; 34 of 126 (27 percent) stopped the antipsychotic completely at some time, as did 13 of 127 (10 percent) of the maintenance group. Of the 34 who stopped in the reduction group, 9 (26 percent) had a relapse with hospital admission, and of 88 who cut the dose by half or more, 25 (28 percent) did. Eight people died in the reduction group and four in the maintenance group.

RADAR put nothing social or psychological in place of the reduced drug. Participants in both arms were monitored by their treating psychiatrist and care team according to usual practice and could receive other drugs and psychological therapies as clinically indicated. The authors write that future studies could explore whether additional psychological and social support could lower the excess relapse seen with antipsychotic dose reduction and discontinuation, and whether a reduction over years would do so.

966.content: A Cochrane review of 75 randomised trials (9,145 participants, published 1959 to 2017) compared staying on an antipsychotic with a switch to placebo in people diagnosed with schizophrenia. At seven to 12 months 24 percent on the drug and 61 percent on placebo had relapsed by each trial's definition (30 trials, 4,249 people, risk ratio 0.38, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.45), and 7 percent against 18 percent were admitted to hospital (21 trials, 3,558 people). The reviewers report more movement problems, sedation and weight gain on the drug, and too few data to compare suicide or employment.

In the same review, relapse by 12 months did not clearly differ between trials that stopped the antipsychotic abruptly (27 percent on drug against 62 percent on placebo, 18 trials) and trials that tapered it for at least three weeks or followed a depot (18 percent against 56 percent, 11 trials), the reviewers reported. Trials of first-episode patients showed a similar gap (26 percent against 61 percent, 8 trials, 528 people). The reviewers state that most trials lasted no longer than one year and the longest three years, that the gap between drug and placebo shrank as trial length grew, and that nothing is known about the very long term.

967.content: A meta-analysis of 65 randomised trials (6,493 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia, stabilised on an antipsychotic and then continued or withdrawn) reported relapse within 1 year in 27 percent on the drug and 64 percent on placebo (risk ratio 0.40, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.49) and readmission in 10 percent against 26 percent. The abstract reports that abrupt or gradual withdrawal did not significantly change the result, that the gap between drug and placebo decreased with study length, and that weight gain, movement problems and sedation were more common on the drug.

968.content: Seven-year follow-up of a 2-year open randomised trial in the Netherlands: 128 patients diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis and in remission for 6 months were assigned to dose reduction or discontinuation or to maintenance for 18 months, after which treatment was at the clinician's discretion; 103 (80.5 percent) were assessed at 7 years. Recovery, which the authors defined as meeting criteria for both symptomatic and functional remission, was reported in 40.4 percent of the reduction group and 17.6 percent of the maintenance group (odds ratio 3.49, P = .01). The abstract reports that the difference came from functional remission and that symptomatic remission did not differ.

969.content: Ten-year follow-up of a double-blind trial in Hong Kong: 178 patients diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis, free of positive symptoms after at least one year on an antipsychotic, were randomised to 12 months of quetiapine 400 mg daily or placebo and then treated as usual. A poor outcome at 10 years, which the authors defined as persistent psychotic symptoms, a need for clozapine or death by suicide, was reported in 35 of 89 (39 percent) of the discontinuation group and 19 of 89 (21 percent) of the maintenance group (risk ratio 1.84, 95% CI 1.15 to 2.96). The authors report that relapse during the trial year statistically accounted for part of the difference, and that about 80 percent of both groups relapsed at some time over the 10 years.

970.content: Twelve women aged 14 to 44 with an encephalitis and a teratoma all had antibodies in serum or cerebrospinal fluid that bound NR2B and NR2A heteromers of the NMDA receptor; the paper names this receptor as the target antigen for the first time and offers the antibody as a test. Nine of the 12 first presented with personality and behaviour change, agitation or paranoid thoughts; six were first evaluated by psychiatrists and five were admitted to psychiatric units. The authors write that most were initially considered to have a psychiatric illness or viral encephalitis, and that 10 were seen at several institutions before the tumour was found and removed.

Serum antibody titres were followed in eight of the 12 patients: all seven who improved neurologically showed a fall in titre (five to undetectable) and the one who died of neurological progression showed a rise from 1:200 to 1:1,600. Nine of the 12 recovered substantially and seven returned to their jobs after tumour removal, immunotherapy or both. All five tumours examined contained nervous tissue that expressed NR2 subunits and bound the patients' antibodies.

971.content: A systematic review of 26 prospective first-episode cohorts (4,490 participants) reported that a longer duration of untreated psychosis was associated with worse ratings at 6 and 12 months on total symptoms, depression and anxiety, negative symptoms, positive symptoms, overall functioning and social functioning, and with a lower chance of remission. The authors report that premorbid adjustment did not explain the association, call it modest, and say it supports trials of shortening the delay.

972.content: A meta-analysis of 33 samples from 39 articles on people diagnosed with schizophrenia or related psychoses (mean follow-up 8.1 years, range 2 to 28; mean delay before treatment 61 weeks) found that a longer duration of untreated psychosis went with worse general symptom ratings, more positive and negative symptoms, a lower chance of remission and poorer social functioning and global outcome, with correlations between 0.13 and 0.18. It found no significant association with employment, quality of life or hospital treatment.

The authors of the same meta-analysis write that most of the pooled correlations were unadjusted, that the original studies rarely examined confounders such as mode of onset, and that conclusions from observational designs are problematic because nobody can be randomised to a delay. They state that in the long term other factors, such as individual characteristics, social support and treatment, are likely to matter more than the duration of untreated psychosis.

973.content: In the Suffolk County Mental Health Project, 287 people first admitted with psychosis between 1989 and 1995 and later diagnosed with schizophrenia or schizoaffective disorder were followed for 20 years (2,137 observations from childhood on). Duration of untreated psychosis was associated with psychosocial function scores at first admission (Cohen's d 0.75), at 6 months and at 24 months, and with neither premorbid nor long-term function. Patients with a long delay had most of their decline before first admission and patients with a short delay declined after it; when function was set against time since the first psychotic symptom, the delay no longer separated the trajectories, the authors report.

The authors state that their result should not be read as evidence that early intervention is ineffective or that decline is inevitable: the cohort received care that relied mainly on antipsychotic drugs, and stronger treatments might change the trajectory. They report that the findings argue against untreated psychosis being toxic and against a long delay marking a more severe form.

974.content: The ICHD-3 criteria of the International Headache Society define migraine without aura from the patient's history: at least five attacks lasting 4 to 72 hours, with at least two of four pain features (one-sided, pulsating, moderate or severe, made worse by routine physical activity), with nausea or vomiting or sensitivity to both light and sound, and not better accounted for by another ICHD-3 diagnosis. No laboratory, imaging or genetic finding is among the criteria for migraine without aura.

The same classification states that migraine without aura is now clearly a neurobiological condition in which nitric oxide, serotonin and CGRP are involved, while the criteria remain clinical. For familial hemiplegic migraine it adds a genetic criterion: type 1, 2 or 3 is coded when a mutation in CACNA1A, ATP1A2 or SCN1A has been demonstrated.

975.content: A consensus statement endorsed by the European Headache Federation and the European Academy of Neurology states that the medical history is the mainstay of migraine diagnosis by ICHD-3 criteria, that physical examination is mostly confirmatory, and that neuroimaging, blood samples or lumbar puncture are used only now and then to confirm or reject a suspected secondary cause of headache. It names no test that confirms migraine itself.

976.content: A 2017 review of migraine pathophysiology reports that familial hemiplegic migraine is a monogenic subtype of migraine with aura, with three genes found by linkage analysis (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A), all acting on ion transport, and that mice carrying the human mutations show a raised susceptibility to cortical spreading depression. For common migraine it reports a 4-fold relative risk in first-degree relatives of people who have migraine with aura and 1.9-fold for migraine without aura, and higher concordance in identical than in fraternal twins.

The same review reports that CGRP is released during migraine attacks, that CGRP given to people who have migraine triggers attacks, and that small-molecule CGRP receptor blockers and monoclonal antibodies against CGRP or its receptor gave positive results in randomised placebo-controlled trials. The review reports that cortical spreading depression, a slow wave of neuronal depolarisation, is the believed mechanism of migraine aura, and that its electrical signature has not been recorded in a human during an aura.

977.content: A genome-wide association meta-analysis of 102,084 people with migraine and 771,257 controls found 123 risk loci, 86 of them new, including one locus holding the genes for CGRP (CALCA and CALCB) and one holding the gene for the serotonin 5-HT1F receptor (HTR1F), both targets of migraine drugs. Common variants accounted for an estimated 11.2 percent of liability, and the authors cite family and twin work for a heritability of 40 to 60 percent. In the added cohorts migraine status was mostly self-reported.

978.content: Functional MRI recorded during five visual auras in three men who met International Headache Society criteria for migraine with aura showed a signal change that began in extrastriate visual cortex (area V3A) and moved across occipital cortex at 3.5 mm per minute, following the path of the visual percept on the retinotopic map. The authors conclude that an electrophysiological event such as cortical spreading depression generates the aura in human visual cortex.

979.content: The Soteria project (San Francisco Bay Area, 1971 to 1983) assigned 179 unmarried people aged 15 to 32, newly diagnosed with schizophrenia by DSM-II and judged to need hospital admission, to a small home-like house with nonprofessional staff or to a general hospital psychiatric ward; assignment went by bed availability in the first cohort (79) and was random in the second (100). In the house antipsychotic drugs were ordinarily not used in the first 6 weeks and 76 percent (62 of 82) received none in the first 45 days, while 94 percent (85 of 90) of the hospital group received continuous antipsychotic drugs, the authors report. Over the two years 58 percent of Soteria subjects received an antipsychotic at some time and 19 percent were kept on one continuously, by the authors' count.

At two years, among the 129 subjects who completed follow-up, the Soteria group had a better composite outcome by 0.47 standard deviations (p = .03), and by 0.81 among completers classified as schizophrenia after conversion to DSM-IV (p = .02); among all 160 endpoint subjects the authors report small to medium trends in the same direction. Completion differed between arms (83 percent at Soteria against 63 percent in hospital), and 29 of 68 Soteria completers against 2 of 61 hospital completers received no antipsychotic during follow-up, by the authors' count.

980.content: A systematic review found three controlled trials of the Soteria approach (two cohorts in California and one in Berne, Switzerland) with 223 participants diagnosed with first-episode or second-episode schizophrenia spectrum conditions. At two years there were few significant differences between Soteria and usual hospital treatment (5 of the Californian comparisons and 2 of the Berne comparisons reached significance), and the reviewers conclude that Soteria did as well as drug-based treatment, and better in some areas, with much less medication. They state that the data were too few for a meta-analysis and that the quantity and quality of the evidence are too low to recommend Soteria as a standard treatment.

981.content: In Western Lapland, Finland, a historical comparison followed two groups of patients diagnosed with first-episode nonaffective psychosis for 5 years: 33 treated before and 42 treated during the fully developed phase of Open Dialogue, a family and social network approach that starts within 24 hours of contact. The two periods did not differ significantly in 5-year outcomes. In the later group 82 percent were reported to have no residual psychotic symptoms, 86 percent had returned to studies or a full-time job, 14 percent were on disability allowance, 17 percent relapsed in the first 2 years and 19 percent in the next 3, and 29 percent had used neuroleptic medication at some phase.

982.content: A register study compared all 108 people diagnosed with a first episode of psychosis whose treatment began under Open Dialogue in Western Lapland (inclusion periods 1992 to 1993, 1994 to 1997 and 2003 to 2005) with all 1,763 Finnish first-episode patients with a 19 to 20 year follow-up who were treated elsewhere. Almost all of the comparison group (97.3 percent) received neuroleptics at some point; in the Open Dialogue group 46 percent were treated with no neuroleptics at all, and 36 percent were on medication at the end of follow-up against 81 percent. Treatment begun outside Open Dialogue was associated with still being in treatment (adjusted odds ratio 2.2, 95% CI 1.3 to 3.7), on neuroleptics (7.1) and on a disability allowance (2.6) at the end of follow-up; suicide rates did not differ.

The paper describes the approach it followed up: staff teams hold network meetings to which family members and other members of the patient's social network (fellow workers, neighbours, friends) are always invited, the first within 24 hours of contact and daily for the first 10 to 12 days of a crisis, and neuroleptic medication is not introduced at the first meeting and is started only if other efforts prove insufficient. The authors state that selection bias and unmeasured variables may have affected the result and that randomised trials are still needed to establish effectiveness.

983.content: A systematic review of 23 Open Dialogue studies (search to January 2018; 1,777 articles screened) concluded that the quantitative studies lacked methodological rigour and carried a high risk of bias, which the reviewers report precludes any conclusion about efficacy among people with psychosis, and that randomised controlled trials are required.

984.content: ODDESSI, a cluster-randomised trial in five NHS trusts in England (30 clusters of general practices; 494 adults presenting in crisis, recruited June 2019 to December 2021), compared Open Dialogue with usual crisis and community care over 2 years. Time to first relapse after initial recovery, the primary outcome, did not differ (marginal hazard ratio 0.95, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.32). Open Dialogue was associated with fewer psychiatric inpatient admissions and re-referrals and with better self-rated recovery, quality of life and satisfaction, and with no difference in the size or quality of participants' social networks.

In ODDESSI 77 of 494 participants (16 percent) had a primary diagnosis of a psychotic disorder at referral and the most common primary label was a diagnosis of depressive disorder (127, 26 percent), so the trial is no test of first-episode psychosis care. The paper as read reports nothing on drugs: the words medication and antipsychotic do not occur in it. The authors report that network meetings with family members present were not the majority of contacts in the Open Dialogue arm, that social network involvement was more limited than intended, and that formal family interventions were not routinely provided in either arm.

985.content: STAGES, a triple-blind trial in Melbourne, randomised 90 people aged 15 to 25 who met DSM-IV criteria for a first-episode psychotic disorder to placebo (46) or low-dose risperidone or paliperidone (44) for 6 months; all received cognitive-behavioural case management from a specialised early psychosis service. Entry required low suicidality and aggression ratings, less than 6 months of untreated psychosis and stable accommodation with social support, criteria the authors set for safety. At 6 months the groups did not differ on the Social and Occupational Functioning Scale (mean difference -0.2, 95% CI -7.5 to 7.0), inside the noninferiority margin of 10.5 points.

In STAGES one third of those who started trial medication completed the 6 months on it, and those who discontinued were given usual care including an antipsychotic, the authors report. At 12 and 24 months noninferiority of the placebo group was not established, and negative symptom ratings were higher in the placebo group at 12 months. The authors state that the sample cannot be considered representative and that the result applies only to the small subgroup defined by the entry criteria.

986.content: COMPARE, a single-blind pilot trial in Greater Manchester, randomised 75 people who met ICD-10 criteria for schizophrenia, schizoaffective disorder or delusional disorder, or the entry criteria of an early intervention service, to cognitive behavioural therapy alone (26), antipsychotics alone (24) or both (25), and followed them for a year. PANSS total scores were lower with the combination than with therapy alone (difference -5.65, 95% CI -10.37 to -0.93) and did not differ significantly between antipsychotics alone and therapy alone (-1.13, 95% CI -5.81 to 3.55), the authors report. Therapy was up to 26 sessions over 6 months plus up to four boosters, side-effect scale scores were lower in the therapy-alone group, and the trial was designed to test feasibility and was not sized to compare the arms.

987.content: In a single-blind trial at two UK centres, 74 people aged 16 to 65 whom the trial classified as having schizophrenia spectrum disorders and who had chosen not to take antipsychotic drugs were randomised to cognitive therapy plus treatment as usual (37) or treatment as usual alone (37). Mean PANSS total scores over 18 months were lower in the cognitive therapy group (estimated between-group difference -6.52, 95% CI -10.79 to -2.25), the authors report.

988.content: PREVENT randomised 424 adults from 95 UK general practices, who had three or more previous episodes classified as major depression and were on maintenance antidepressants, to stay on the drug (212) or to join an 8-week group class of mindfulness-based cognitive therapy with support to taper or stop the drug (212). Over 24 months 94 (44 percent) of the class group and 100 (47 percent) of the maintenance group relapsed as rated by interview (hazard ratio 0.89, 95% CI 0.67 to 1.18). Of those who attended four or more sessions, 71 percent stopped the antidepressant, 17 percent reduced it and 13 percent did not reduce it, the authors report.

989.content: In the Dunedin birth cohort (1,037 children born 1972 to 1973, followed to age 32 with 96 percent retention), the 35 members later diagnosed with schizophrenia had a mean childhood IQ of 94, against 98 for the 145 later diagnosed with recurrent depression and 101 for 556 healthy comparison members. On tests of verbal and visual knowledge, reasoning and conceptualisation the group later diagnosed with schizophrenia already scored lower at age 7 and stayed lower; on processing speed, attention, visual-spatial problem solving and working memory they gained more slowly between ages 7 and 13. Their test results did not fall over those years, and neither pattern was seen in the group later diagnosed with recurrent depression.

990.content: A review in World Psychiatry reports that poor insight, meaning unawareness of symptoms, of the need for treatment and of the consequences, is found in people diagnosed with schizophrenia across cultures and in early, late, acute and non-acute phases. It reports that poor insight goes with refusing antipsychotic medication, a weaker therapeutic alliance, higher symptom ratings and poorer community function, while good insight goes with more reported depression and demoralisation, especially together with stigma and social disadvantage. The authors argue that the model of poor insight as a neurological unawareness (anosognosia) is far from a complete account and that biological, experiential, social and political factors all contribute.

991.content: A meta-analysis of 18 case-control studies (2,048 patients diagnosed with psychosis and 1,856 controls), 10 prospective or quasi-prospective studies (41,803 people) and 8 population cross-sectional studies (35,546 people) found that reported childhood adversity (sexual, physical and emotional abuse, neglect, parental death, bullying) was associated with psychosis outcomes, with an overall odds ratio of 2.78 (95% CI 2.34 to 3.31) and 2.75 in the prospective studies. The authors estimate that 33 percent of cases (range 16 to 47) would not occur if these adversities were removed, on the assumption that the association is causal.

992.content: A meta-analysis of 49 population-based incidence studies published 1977 to 2017 (43 in Europe, 3 in Israel, 2 in Canada, 1 in Australia) found a relative risk of being diagnosed with a non-affective psychotic disorder among migrants and their children of 2.13 (95% CI 1.99 to 2.27), adjusted for age and sex. The figure was 2.94 for migration to Europe from outside Europe, 1.88 for migration within Europe, 1.22 in Israel and 1.21 in Canada, and 4.19 for people from regions where most of the population is black. After adjustment for socioeconomic status the rates at which people from developing countries and from mostly black regions were diagnosed stayed raised (1.84 and 2.70), and first and second generation did not differ significantly within the same studies.

993.content: Abstract only. In a randomised controlled trial, 99 mother-infant pairs were assigned to increased carrying (carrying through the day, on top of the carrying that happens during feeding and in response to crying) or to a control group. At 6 weeks of age, the age of peak crying, the carried infants cried and fussed 43 percent less overall (1.23 against 2.16 hours a day) and 51 percent less in the evening (0.63 against 1.28 hours, 4 PM to midnight). Similar but smaller decreases were found at 4, 8 and 12 weeks. Less crying and fussing went with more contentment and more frequent feeding, with no change in feeding duration or sleep. The authors conclude that the relative lack of carrying in their society may predispose normal infants to crying and colic.

994.content: The NICE clinical guideline on borderline personality disorder (CG78, published 28 January 2009) recommends that drug treatment should not be used specifically for the diagnosis or for the individual symptoms or behaviour that go with it, naming repeated self-harm, marked emotional instability, risk-taking behaviour and transient psychotic symptoms, and that antipsychotic drugs should not be used for its medium- and long-term treatment. It allows drug treatment for comorbid conditions and the cautious short-term use of sedative medication in a crisis, for no longer than 1 week. It tells clinicians to review people with the diagnosis who have no diagnosed comorbid mental or physical illness and are being prescribed drugs, with the aim of reducing and stopping unnecessary drug treatment.
